Why Peak Expiratory Flow Rate Is Correct Simple, rapid bedside test Quantifies airway obstruction Helps classify severity (mild, moderate, severe, life-threatening) Guides treatment decisions and monitoring Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Arterial blood gas Used in severe/life-threatening asthma, not first-line for initial assessment. B. Chest X-ray Not routine unless complications suspected. C. D-dimer Used for suspected PE, not asthma. E. Sputum culture Not useful acutely. Key Exam Principle 👉 Asthma severity = PEFR measurement 👉 ABG only in severe or life-threatening cases 👉 Always quantify airflow obstruction early 👉 "Asthma attack = check peak flow"

question_text: A 28 year old woman, with a background of chronic alcoholism presents with bright-red haematemesis and abdominal pains. On examination, she has cool extremities and is seen to be confused. Her blood pressure is 85/60 mmHg and her heart rate is 120 beats/minute. What is the SINGLE most appropriate next step in management?
explanation: Why? This patient has massive upper gastrointestinal bleeding (likely variceal) with haemodynamic instability (hypotension, tachycardia, confusion). The immediate priority is resuscitation following the ABC approach—specifically circulation—by giving intravenous fluids. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Bright red haematemesis (active upper GI bleed) ✅ Chronic alcoholism (risk of varices) ✅ Hypotension (85/60 mmHg) ✅ Tachycardia (120 bpm) ✅ Confusion and cool extremities (shock) These indicate haemorrhagic shock. Why Intravenous Fluids Is Correct First step in haemorrhagic shock (ABC approach) Restores circulating volume Improves perfusion to vital organs Must be done before definitive treatments Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A/B. Endoscopic treatments Definitive but only after stabilisation. C. Octreotide Useful in variceal bleeding but after initial resuscitation. D. Terlipressin Important in variceal bleeding but not before stabilisation. Key Exam Principle 👉 Shock = resuscitate first (ABC) 👉 GI bleed + hypotension = IV fluids immediately 👉 Definitive therapy comes AFTER stabilisation 👉 "Bleeding + shock = fluids first"

question_text: A 20 year old was found unconscious on the floor at the park in the early morning after a night out with his friends in the pub. The paramedics are unable to arouse him. He smells of alcohol and has an empty bottle of alcohol in his hand. He has a heart rate of 100 beats/minute, respiratory rate of 18 breaths/minute and a capillary blood glucose level of 1.2. What is the SINGLE most appropriate management?

options.c: Administer 4 g of buccal oral glucose gel
options.d: Insert an intravenous line and administer 75 ml of 20% glucose intravenously

explanation: Why? This patient has severe hypoglycaemia (glucose 1.2 mmol/L) with reduced consciousness. The immediate management is rapid correction with intravenous glucose. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Very low glucose (1.2 mmol/L) ✅ Unconscious patient ✅ Alcohol ingestion (risk of hypoglycaemia) These indicate severe, life-threatening hypoglycaemia. Why IV Glucose Is Correct Fastest way to restore blood glucose Effective even in unconscious patients First-line in severe hypoglycaemia with reduced consciousness Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A/B. IM glucagon Used if IV access is not available; less effective in alcohol-related hypoglycaemia (depleted glycogen stores). C. Buccal glucose Requires conscious patient. E. Insulin Would worsen hypoglycaemia. Key Exam Principle 👉 Hypoglycaemia + unconscious = IV glucose immediately 👉 Alcohol → reduced glycogen → glucagon less effective 👉 Always correct glucose urgently 👉 "Unconscious + low sugar = IV glucose"

question_text: A 30 year old man is brought to the Emergency Department by paramedics after collapsing at a nightclub. On arrival, he is agitated and sweating profusely. His friends reveal that he has been using cocaine during the night. His vital signs are as follows: Blood pressure 179/110 mmHg, heart rate 130 beats per minute, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, temperature 37.8°C, oxygen saturation 98% on room air. ECG shows sinus tachycardia without ischaemic changes. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?
explanation: Why? This patient has acute cocaine toxicity with sympathetic overactivity (agitation, hypertension, tachycardia). The first-line treatment is benzodiazepines (e.g., diazepam) to reduce central sympathetic stimulation. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Cocaine use ✅ Agitation and sweating ✅ Severe hypertension (179/110 mmHg) ✅ Tachycardia (130 bpm) These indicate sympathomimetic toxidrome. Why Diazepam Is Correct Reduces CNS stimulation Decreases sympathetic outflow Helps control agitation, heart rate, and blood pressure First-line in cocaine toxicity Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Labetalol Beta-blockers are generally avoided initially due to risk of unopposed alpha stimulation. C. Nitroprusside May be used later for severe hypertension, not first-line. D. Flumazenil Used in benzodiazepine overdose, not cocaine toxicity. E. Furosemide No role here. Key Exam Principle 👉 Cocaine toxicity = benzodiazepines first-line 👉 Treat agitation → improves vitals 👉 Avoid pure beta-blockers initially 👉 "Cocaine overdose = sedate with benzos"

question_text: A 9 year old girl is brought by her mother to the A&E with stridor, wheezing and a rash. The young girl came from visiting her friend at her farm house. Her lips are beginning to swell. She has a very itchy generalised urticarial rash. What is the SINGLE most appropriate treatment?
explanation: Why? This is a clear case of anaphylaxis (airway involvement + breathing + skin features). The immediate treatment is intramuscular adrenaline. For children aged 6–12 years, the correct dose is 0.3 ml of 1:1000 adrenaline IM. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Stridor (airway compromise) ✅ Wheezing (bronchospasm) ✅ Lip swelling (angioedema) ✅ Generalised urticarial rash These indicate severe anaphylaxis. Why 0.3 ml IM Adrenaline Is Correct First-line, life-saving treatment Dose for age 6–12 years = 0.3 ml (1:1000) Given IM into the anterolateral thigh Acts rapidly to reverse airway swelling and shock Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. 0.15 ml Dose for younger children (<6 years). C. 0.5 ml Adult dose. D. Oral adrenaline Not used—too slow and ineffective. E. IV chlorpheniramine Adjunct only, not life-saving. Key Exam Principle 👉 Anaphylaxis = IM adrenaline immediately 👉 Dose depends on age: - <6 years → 0.15 ml - 6–12 years → 0.3 ml - >12 years → 0.5 ml 👉 "Child + anaphylaxis = correct IM adrenaline dose"

question_text: A 20 year old woman brings herself into the Emergency Department after having a paracetamol overdose 6 hours ago. She intended to commit suicide however she now regrets her decision. She recently received news that she failed a university exam. She lives with her boyfriend who is supportive. Her plasma paracetamol level was plotted just below the treatment line on the paracetamol treatment graph. What is the most appropriate action for the A&E doctor?

options.a: Discharge home with outpatient follow up
options.b: Continue to observe for the next 8 hours

explanation: Why? This patient presented with a deliberate self-harm (suicide attempt) via paracetamol overdose. Even though her paracetamol level is below the treatment threshold and she is medically stable, she requires a full psychosocial assessment by the psychiatric liaison team before discharge. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Intentional overdose (suicide attempt) ✅ Emotional trigger (exam failure) ✅ Regret after attempt ✅ Medically stable (below treatment line) These indicate need for mental health assessment. Why Psychiatric Liaison Referral Is Correct All deliberate self-harm requires psychosocial assessment Assesses suicide risk and safeguarding Guides safe discharge planning Mandatory before discharge Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Discharge home Unsafe without psychiatric assessment. B. Observe 8 hours Not necessary once medically stable. C. Refer to medical team No further medical intervention needed. E. Psychiatric ward admission May be needed, but only after assessment. Key Exam Principle 👉 Any suicide attempt = psychiatric assessment required 👉 Even if medically stable 👉 Do NOT discharge without review 👉 "Self-harm = psych review before discharge"

question_text: A 19 year old boy presents with nervousness, a runny nose, watering eyes, tremors and muscle cramps. He says that he has also been having trouble sleeping and feels like he lacks mental clarity. He is a known drug addict and he claims that he has been trying to stop taking drugs for the past three days. He looks agitated and sweaty: What is the SINGLE most likely drug that he has been taking?
explanation: Why? This patient is showing classic features of opioid (heroin) withdrawal. The combination of rhinorrhoea, lacrimation, muscle cramps, agitation, sweating, and insomnia strongly supports this diagnosis. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Runny nose (rhinorrhoea) ✅ Watering eyes (lacrimation) ✅ Muscle cramps and tremors ✅ Agitation and sweating ✅ Insomnia and poor concentration ✅ Timeline of 3 days since stopping drugs These are hallmark features of opioid withdrawal. Why Heroin Is Correct Heroin is a short-acting opioid → withdrawal occurs within 1–3 days Produces "flu-like" symptoms Causes agitation, sweating, and insomnia Classic exam presentation Why the Other Options Are Less Likely B. Benzodiazepines Withdrawal causes anxiety, seizures, tremors—not rhinorrhoea/lacrimation. C. Cocaine Withdrawal causes depression and fatigue, not these physical symptoms. D. Ecstasy Causes mood changes, not withdrawal syndrome like this. E. LSD No typical withdrawal syndrome. Key Exam Principle 👉 Opioid withdrawal = rhinorrhoea + lacrimation + myalgia 👉 Timeline: 1–3 days after stopping 👉 Opposite of opioid intoxication (pinpoint pupils) 👉 "Runny nose + cramps + agitation = heroin withdrawal"

question_text: A 26 year old woman presents to the Emergency Department 12 hours after ingesting 50 tablets of paracetamol. She reports feeling generally well but admits to nausea. On examination, she is alert and haemodynamically stable. Blood tests, including liver function tests and coagulation profile, have been sent. Paracetamol levels have been taken but the results are not yet available. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.c: Observe until paracetamol levels are available

explanation: Why? This patient presents late (12 hours post ingestion) after a significant paracetamol overdose (50 tablets). At this stage, treatment with N-acetylcysteine (NAC) should be started immediately without waiting for paracetamol levels. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Large overdose (50 tablets) ✅ Presentation at 12 hours (late) ✅ Paracetamol levels not yet available These indicate high risk of toxicity with delayed presentation. Why Intravenous NAC Is Correct Should be started if presentation is >8 hours after overdose Delay increases risk of liver failure Safe and effective antidote Do NOT wait for levels in late presenters Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Activated charcoal Only useful within 1–2 hours of ingestion. C. Observe Dangerous delay in treatment. D. Oral methionine Alternative if NAC unavailable, but IV NAC is preferred. E. Psychiatric assessment Important but only after medical stabilization. Key Exam Principle 👉 >8 hours post paracetamol overdose = start NAC immediately 👉 Do NOT wait for levels 👉 Early treatment prevents liver damage 👉 "Late presentation = treat first, check later"

question_text: A 32 year old man presents to A&E in hypovolaemic shock immediately following a road traffic accident. He is tachycardic, sweating and anxious. He was also noted to have bruises on his abdomen. What mechanism explains the manifested symptoms?
explanation: Why? This patient is in hypovolaemic shock due to trauma. The body responds by activating the sympathetic nervous system to maintain perfusion to vital organs. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Tachycardia ✅ Sweating ✅ Anxiety/restlessness ✅ Trauma with likely blood loss These are classic signs of sympathetic activation. Why Increased Sympathetic Activity Is Correct Triggers tachycardia to maintain cardiac output Causes vasoconstriction to preserve blood flow to vital organs Leads to sweating and anxiety Part of compensatory response in shock Why the Other Options Are Less Likely B. Parasympathetic activity Would cause bradycardia and hypotension. C. Decreased cortisol Cortisol typically increases in stress. D. Decreased catecholamines Catecholamines actually increase in shock. E. Vasodilatation Occurs in distributive shock, not hypovolaemic shock. Key Exam Principle 👉 Hypovolaemic shock = sympathetic activation 👉 Signs: tachycardia, sweating, anxiety 👉 Body tries to compensate for volume loss 👉 "Shock = SNS overdrive"

question_text: A 3 year old child presented to the Emergency Department with his mother. The mother tells you that the child was playing with his small toys and suddenly became breathless and started to cough. She says that the child remained conscious throughout and has been able to vocalise. The child has been previously well. On examination, the child is afebrile, heart rate is 90 beats/minute, respiratory rate is 24/minute, blood pressure is 120/70 mmHg and SpO2 is 96%. A wheeze is present over the right side of the chest on auscultation. There is no stridor or cyanosis. What is the SINGLE next most appropriate investigation?

options.e: CT scan of neck and chest

explanation: Why? This is a classic case of suspected foreign body aspiration (FBA) in a child. The most appropriate initial investigation is a chest X-ray. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Sudden onset coughing and breathlessness while playing ✅ Previously well child ✅ Unilateral wheeze (right-sided) ✅ No stridor → suggests lower airway involvement ✅ Stable vitals and oxygen saturation These features strongly suggest a foreign body lodged in the bronchial tree (commonly right main bronchus). Why Chest X-ray Is Correct Initial imaging of choice in suspected foreign body aspiration May show indirect signs: • Hyperinflation (air trapping) • Collapse (atelectasis) • Mediastinal shift Helps guide further management (e.g., bronchoscopy) Quick, accessible, and low radiation Why the Other Options Are Less Likely B. Lateral X-ray of neck Used for upper airway obstruction (e.g., epiglottitis, croup), not lower airway foreign body. C. Fluoroscopy Can detect air trapping but not first-line; used if X-ray is inconclusive. D. Nasendoscopy Evaluates upper airway; not useful for bronchial foreign body. E. CT scan of neck and chest Too high radiation for initial investigation in a stable child. Key Exam Principle 👉 Sudden cough + unilateral wheeze in a child = Foreign body aspiration until proven otherwise 👉 First-line investigation = Chest X-ray 👉 Definitive diagnosis and treatment = Bronchoscopy

question_text: A 45 years old man is brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance. He was found collapsed at home. According to his wife, he had complained of severe abdominal pain and repeated vomiting earlier in the day. On arrival, he is unresponsive to voice but withdraws to pain. On examination, airway is patent and breathing is spontaneous. Respiratory rate is 20 breaths per minute. Oxygen saturations are 95% on air. Heart rate is 102 beats per minute and blood pressure is 100/70 mmHg. What is the most appropriate immediate next step?

options.b: Check bedside capillary blood glucose immediately
options.c: Commence high flow oxygen via non rebreather mask
options.e: Refer to the acute medical team

explanation: Why? This patient is acutely unconscious (GCS ≈ 9: withdraws to pain only) with an unclear cause. The most important immediate reversible cause of reduced consciousness that must be checked is hypoglycaemia. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Reduced level of consciousness (responds only to pain) ✅ Cause unclear (collapse at home) ✅ Airway and breathing are currently adequate ✅ Mild tachycardia but no severe hypotension These point to the need for rapid assessment of reversible causes before further interventions. Why Check Capillary Blood Glucose Is Correct Hypoglycaemia is a life-threatening but rapidly reversible cause of coma Bedside glucose testing is quick, non-invasive, and immediately actionable Part of the primary survey in any patient with altered consciousness ("D" in ABCDE) Delay can lead to permanent brain injury Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Admit to ICU Premature before initial assessment and stabilisation. C. High flow oxygen Not indicated as oxygen saturation is already 95% on room air. D. IV crystalloid bolus Blood pressure is borderline but not critically low; not the immediate priority over reversible causes of unconsciousness. E. Refer to acute medical team Referral comes after initial emergency assessment and stabilisation. Key Exam Principle 👉 In any unconscious patient → ALWAYS check glucose immediately 👉 "Unconscious = Hypoglycaemia until proven otherwise" 👉 ABCDE approach: D (Disability) includes glucose check

question_text: A 58 year old woman presents to the Emergency Department with shortness of breath that started 12 hours ago. Her blood pressure is 145/98 mmHg, heart rate is 111 beats/minute, respiratory rate is 23 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation is 92% on room air. Physical examination reveals a mildly distressed woman with tachypnoea. What is the most appropriate initial investigation?
explanation: Why? This patient presents with acute shortness of breath and mild hypoxia. The most appropriate initial investigation in any patient with undifferentiated dyspnoea is a chest X-ray. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Acute onset dyspnoea (12 hours) ✅ Tachycardia and tachypnoea ✅ Oxygen saturation 92% (mild hypoxia) ✅ No confirmed diagnosis yet These findings suggest a broad differential diagnosis including pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, pneumothorax, or heart failure. Why Chest X-ray Is Correct First-line investigation for undifferentiated shortness of breath Helps identify common causes: • Pneumonia (consolidation) • Pneumothorax • Pulmonary oedema • Pleural effusion Quick, widely available, and low radiation Guides further investigations (e.g., CTPA if PE suspected) Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. CTPA Used when pulmonary embolism is strongly suspected after initial assessment; not the first investigation in undifferentiated dyspnoea. B. Echocardiogram Useful for cardiac causes but not first-line in acute dyspnoea without clear cardiac findings. C. Creatine kinase Used for muscle injury or myocardial infarction; not helpful in evaluating dyspnoea. D. Lower limb Doppler ultrasound May detect DVT but does not confirm pulmonary embolism and is not the first step. Key Exam Principle 👉 First-line investigation in acute dyspnoea = Chest X-ray 👉 Always start broad before moving to specific tests (e.g., CTPA) 👉 "Unexplained SOB → Do CXR first"

question_text: A 75 year old man presents to the Emergency Department with severe neck pain. He reports that he has been taking 6 grams of paracetamol every day for the past 5 days, which has kept his pain somewhat under control. On examination, he has tenderness over his cervical spine and his observations are normal. His liver function test are seen below: Serum alanine transferase (ALT) 119 U/L (5-35), Serum alkaline phosphatase (ALP) 240 U/L (30-150). His serum paracetamol level is 15mg/L. What is the most appropriate management?

options.a: Offer naproxen and advice to reduce his paracetamol intake
options.d: Prescribe a short course of co-codamol and refer for a routine MRI C-spine

explanation: Why? This patient has chronic supratherapeutic paracetamol ingestion (6 g daily for 5 days) with evidence of liver injury. In such cases, the paracetamol nomogram is NOT applicable, and treatment with N-acetylcysteine (NAC) should be started immediately. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Repeated supratherapeutic dosing (6 g/day > recommended 4 g/day) ✅ Duration of 5 days (chronic ingestion) ✅ Elevated ALT (119 U/L) → evidence of hepatocellular injury ✅ Detectable paracetamol level (15 mg/L) These indicate ongoing toxicity and risk of liver damage. Why Intravenous Acetylcysteine Is Correct NAC replenishes glutathione and prevents further liver injury Indicated in: • Chronic excessive ingestion • Any detectable paracetamol level with raised ALT Nomogram cannot be used in staggered or repeated overdoses Early treatment reduces risk of acute liver failure Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Naproxen + advice Inappropriate—patient already has evidence of toxicity. B. Reassure Dangerous—misses evolving liver injury. D. Co-codamol Contains paracetamol → worsens toxicity. E. IV fluids Supportive only; does not treat underlying toxicity. Key Exam Principle 👉 Chronic/staggered paracetamol overdose = IGNORE nomogram 👉 If ALT elevated + detectable paracetamol → START NAC 👉 "Any doubt → Treat with NAC"

question_text: A 24 year old man is brought to the Emergency Department by paramedics following a road traffic accident. He was a restrained driver involved in a head-on collision with another vehicle. Paramedics report he has been on oxygen via a non-rebreather mask at 15 litres per minute during transport. On arrival, he is alert but in significant respiratory distress. Observations reveal a respiratory rate of 34 breaths per minute, a pulse of 132 beats per minute, and a blood pressure of 94/68 mmg. On examination, there is a large bruise over the left side of the chest with absent breath sounds and hyper-resonance on percussion over the left hemithorax. His trachea is shifted to the right, and there is reduced chest wall movement on the left. Oxygen saturation remains 89% despite high-flow oxygen. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
explanation: Why? This patient has a tension pneumothorax, a life-threatening emergency that requires immediate decompression without waiting for imaging. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Severe respiratory distress ✅ Hypotension (94/68 mmHg) ✅ Tachycardia (132 bpm) ✅ Absent breath sounds on the left ✅ Hyper-resonance on percussion ✅ Tracheal deviation to the right ✅ Hypoxia despite high-flow oxygen These are classic signs of tension pneumothorax. Why Needle Thoracocentesis Is Correct Immediate life-saving procedure Relieves pressure in the pleural space Improves venous return and cardiac output Should be done immediately (do NOT wait for imaging) Followed by definitive chest tube insertion Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Oxygen Already given and ineffective; does not treat the cause. B. Intubation May worsen the condition by increasing intrathoracic pressure before decompression. C. Pericardiocentesis Used for cardiac tamponade, not pneumothorax. E. Thoracotomy Too invasive; reserved for specific severe trauma cases. Key Exam Principle 👉 Tension pneumothorax = clinical diagnosis 👉 Immediate needle decompression FIRST 👉 Do NOT delay for imaging 👉 "Air under pressure = release immediately"

question_text: A 12 year old girl when playing in the garden accidentally stepped on a hive and was bitten several times. She has numerous wheals on her body and complains of severe itching which is worsening in the last few hours. Her medical history includes penicillin allergy. Her observations are within normal limits. What is the SINGLE most appropriate management?
explanation: Why? This child has a localized allergic reaction (urticaria) following multiple insect stings, with no features of anaphylaxis. The most appropriate management is an oral antihistamine. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Multiple insect stings (trigger for allergic reaction) ✅ Wheals (urticaria) ✅ Severe itching ✅ Normal vital signs ✅ No airway, breathing, or circulatory compromise These indicate a mild to moderate allergic reaction, not anaphylaxis. Why Oral Antihistamine Is Correct First-line treatment for urticaria and itching Blocks histamine-mediated symptoms Safe and effective in stable patients No need for aggressive treatment in absence of systemic involvement Why the Other Options Are Less Likely B. Intravenous antihistamine Reserved for more severe reactions or if oral route not possible. C. Intramuscular adrenaline Indicated only in anaphylaxis (e.g., airway compromise, hypotension, bronchospasm). D. Ciprofloxacin No role—this is not a bacterial infection. E. Reassurance Inadequate—patient is symptomatic and requires treatment. Key Exam Principle 👉 Urticaria + stable vitals = antihistamine 👉 Anaphylaxis signs (ABCDE compromise) = IM adrenaline 👉 "Itch + wheals only → antihistamine"

question_text: A 38 year old man is brought to the Accident and Emergency department after being involved in a road traffic collision. He was the cyclist and did not have a helmet on at the time of the accident. He sustained a blow to the right side of his head when he fell. On examination, apart from a visible abrasion over the right temporal region, there is a clear discharge leaking from his right ear. The patient mentions that this discharge started shortly after the trauma and has been persistent. Which of the following is the most likely composition of the leaking discharge?
explanation: Why? This patient has signs of a basilar skull fracture (specifically temporal bone fracture), leading to CSF otorrhoea. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Head trauma (RTA, no helmet) ✅ Blow to temporal region ✅ Clear fluid leaking from ear (otorrhoea) ✅ Persistent discharge after trauma These are classic features of a skull base fracture with cerebrospinal fluid leak. Why Cerebrospinal Fluid Is Correct Temporal bone fractures can tear the dura This allows CSF to leak through the middle ear and out of the ear canal Clear, watery discharge is characteristic May test positive for β-2 transferrin (specific for CSF) Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Endolymph Located in the inner ear; not typically seen leaking externally. B. Blood plasma Would not present as clear persistent ear discharge. C. Synovial fluid Found in joints, unrelated to ear discharge. D. Sebaceous secretions Normal ear wax (cerumen) is not clear and watery. Key Exam Principle 👉 Head trauma + clear ear/nose discharge = CSF leak until proven otherwise 👉 Suggests basilar skull fracture 👉 Risk of meningitis → requires urgent evaluation 👉 "Clear fluid after head injury = CSF"

question_text: An 88 year old man is brought to the hospital by his daughter as he has been increasingly confused over the past week. He has not been eating or drinking well over the past few days. He is lethargic and irritable. His medical history includes dementia and diabetes mellitus type 2. His pulse rate is 99 beats/minute. His blood pressure was recorded as 101/65 mmHg on lying down and 80/50 mmHg on standing. On examination, his mucous membranes are dry and his skin turgor is reduced. His blood results show the following: Haemoglobin 119 g/L (130-180), White cell count 9 x 10^9/L (4-11), Platelets 305 x 10^9/L (150-400), Serum urea 9.5 mmol/L (2.0-7), Serum creatinine 170 µmol/L (70-150), Serum calcium 2.52 mmol/L (2.1-2.6), eGFR 65 mL/min, Sodium 152 mmol/L (135-145), Potassium 3.9 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), Glucose (fasting) 6.9 mmol/L (3.5-5.5). What is the SINGLE most appropriate solution to be administered intravenously?
explanation: Why? This patient has hypovolaemic hypernatraemia due to dehydration. The immediate priority is restoration of intravascular volume using isotonic fluid (0.9% sodium chloride) before correcting the sodium. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Elderly with poor oral intake ✅ Confusion and lethargy (hypernatraemia symptoms) ✅ Orthostatic hypotension (101/65 → 80/50) ✅ Dry mucous membranes and reduced skin turgor ✅ Elevated urea and creatinine (pre-renal AKI) ✅ Sodium 152 mmol/L (hypernatraemia) These indicate volume depletion with hypernatraemia. Why 0.9% Sodium Chloride Is Correct First step is volume resuscitation Isotonic saline restores circulating volume Improves renal perfusion Only after volume correction should hypotonic fluids be used to gradually correct sodium Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. 0.45% sodium chloride Hypotonic—used later to correct sodium, not for initial resuscitation. C. 0.9% sodium chloride + 5% dextrose Not first-line for resuscitation; dextrose lowers sodium too quickly. D. 0.45% sodium chloride + potassium Not appropriate initially; potassium is normal and patient is hypovolaemic. E. 1.8% sodium chloride Would worsen hypernatraemia. Key Exam Principle 👉 Hypovolaemic hypernatraemia = FIRST give isotonic saline 👉 Restore volume before correcting sodium 👉 Correct sodium slowly to avoid cerebral oedema 👉 "Shock/dehydration first, sodium later"

question_text: A 7 year old boy is brought to the Emergency Department by his parents after collapsing at a birthday party. He developed widespread urticaria, facial swelling, and wheeze. On arrival, he is drowsy, his respiratory rate is 30 breaths per minute; heart rate is 140 beats per minute, blood pressure is 80/45, and oxygen saturation is 89% on air. What is the SINGLE most appropriate immediate management step?
explanation: Why? This child is in anaphylactic shock, a life-threatening emergency requiring immediate intramuscular (IM) adrenaline. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Widespread urticaria ✅ Facial swelling (angioedema) ✅ Wheeze (airway involvement) ✅ Hypotension (80/45 mmHg) ✅ Tachycardia (140 bpm) ✅ Hypoxia (SpO2 89%) ✅ Reduced consciousness (drowsy) These fulfill criteria for anaphylaxis with airway, breathing, and circulation compromise. Why IM Adrenaline Is Correct First-line, life-saving treatment Acts rapidly to: • Reverse airway edema • Bronchodilate • Increase blood pressure (vasoconstriction) • Improve cardiac output Given IM into the anterolateral thigh Should be administered immediately without delay Why the Other Options Are Less Likely B. IV adrenaline Reserved for refractory cases in ICU; high risk if given incorrectly. C. IV chlorphenamine Adjunct only; too slow and not life-saving. D. IV corticosteroids Delayed effect; not useful acutely. E. Nebulised salbutamol Helps bronchospasm but does not treat systemic anaphylaxis. Key Exam Principle 👉 Anaphylaxis = IM adrenaline FIRST 👉 Do not delay for IV access or other drugs 👉 ABC compromise = adrenaline immediately 👉 "Adrenaline saves lives"

question_text: A 17 year old girl has taken an overdose of 30 paracetamol tablets 3 hours ago. She is extremely anxious but otherwise asymptomatic. She has no past medical history. She weighs 50kg. Her blood pressure is 120/70 mmHg, heart rate is 100 beats/minute, and oxygen saturation is 98% on air. Which is the SINGLE most appropriate next step?

options.d: Paracetamol plasma level 4 hours after overdose
options.e: Urgent liver function tests + clotting screen + paracetamol plasma levels immediately

explanation: Why? This patient presents within 3 hours of a significant paracetamol overdose. The most appropriate immediate step is activated charcoal to reduce further absorption of the drug. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Overdose occurred 3 hours ago (within 4-hour window) ✅ Large ingestion (30 tablets → potentially toxic) ✅ Currently asymptomatic ✅ Early presentation These indicate a window where decontamination is still effective. Why Activated Charcoal Is Correct Effective if given within 1–4 hours of ingestion Reduces further absorption of paracetamol Simple and immediate intervention Improves overall outcome if given early Why the Other Options Are Less Likely B. Gastric lavage Rarely used; higher risk and not routinely recommended. C. N-acetylcysteine Indicated based on 4-hour paracetamol level or if presentation is late (>8 hours). D. Paracetamol level at 4 hours Important, but immediate management (charcoal) should not be delayed while waiting. E. Immediate blood tests Paracetamol level before 4 hours is unreliable and not useful. Key Exam Principle 👉 <4 hours post-overdose = give activated charcoal 👉 ≥4 hours = check paracetamol level (nomogram) 👉 NAC based on level or delayed presentation 👉 "Early overdose → charcoal first"

question_text: A 54 year old smoker is seen in the Emergency Department with extensive wheeze and breathlessness. He is known to have COPD. On auscultation, he has widespread wheezing throughout his chest. He has a temperature of 36.7°C, heart rate of 115 beats/minute, blood pressure of 130/80 mmHg, respiratory rate of 28 breaths/minute and an oxygen saturation of 85%. He is started on 24% oxygen by Venturi face mask. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
explanation: Why? This patient is having an acute exacerbation of COPD with significant bronchospasm. The next immediate step after controlled oxygen is bronchodilation with nebulised salbutamol. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Known COPD patient ✅ Severe breathlessness and widespread wheeze ✅ Hypoxia (SpO2 85%) ✅ Tachypnoea (RR 28) and tachycardia ✅ Already started on controlled oxygen (24% Venturi) These indicate acute COPD exacerbation with bronchospasm. Why Salbutamol Nebulisers Is Correct First-line bronchodilator in COPD exacerbation Relieves airway obstruction rapidly Given via nebuliser (often with oxygen) Improves ventilation and oxygenation Part of initial ABC management Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Oral amoxicillin Antibiotics may be needed later but not the immediate priority. B. IV co-amoxiclav Reserved for severe infection; no signs of infection here. C. Intubation Indicated only if respiratory failure or deterioration. D. IV aminophylline Second-line; used if poor response to nebulisers. Key Exam Principle 👉 Acute COPD exacerbation = O2 (controlled) + bronchodilators 👉 First bronchodilator = nebulised salbutamol 👉 Then add steroids ± antibiotics 👉 "Wheeze = bronchodilate first"

question_text: A 35 year old patient is brought to the Emergency Department after having a road traffic accident. He has bruises on his chest. A chest X-ray shows a widened mediastinum. He has a pulse of 129 beats/minute, a blood pressure of 80/40 mmHg and a respiratory rate of 34 breaths/minute. What is the SINGLE most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Why? This patient has sustained major blunt chest trauma and presents with haemodynamic instability and a widened mediastinum on chest X-ray—classic for thoracic aortic rupture. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ High-speed trauma (road traffic accident) ✅ Chest bruising (significant blunt force) ✅ Hypotension (80/40 mmHg) ✅ Tachycardia (129 bpm) ✅ Widened mediastinum on chest X-ray These findings strongly point toward traumatic aortic injury. Why Thoracic Aortic Rupture Is Correct Most common cause of widened mediastinum after trauma Results from rapid deceleration injury (e.g., RTA) Leads to internal bleeding and shock Life-threatening emergency requiring urgent intervention Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Myocardial infarction Does not cause widened mediastinum or relate to trauma. B. Abdominal aortic aneurysm Occurs in abdomen, not associated with widened mediastinum. D. Flail chest Causes paradoxical chest movement, not widened mediastinum. E. Pleural effusion Would show fluid level, not mediastinal widening. Key Exam Principle 👉 Trauma + widened mediastinum = aortic injury until proven otherwise 👉 Especially with hypotension and tachycardia 👉 "Widened mediastinum = think aortic rupture"

question_text: A 42 year old woman is brought to the Emergency Department by her husband who states that she has swallowed the contents of his heart medication propranolol. It has been approximately two hours since the overdose. She feels dizzy but remains alert and orientated. Her temperature is 37.3°C, heart rate is 50 beats/minute, blood pressure is 70/40 mmHg, respiratory rate 12 breaths/minute and oxygen saturations 98% breathing room air. A 12-lead ECG shows a normal QRS duration and QT interval. She has been started on intravenous fluids and her blood pressure was retaken with a reading of 95/66 mmHg. What is the most appropriate next management?
explanation: Why? This patient has beta-blocker (propranolol) overdose with bradycardia and hypotension. The specific antidote is glucagon. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Known propranolol overdose ✅ Bradycardia (HR 50 bpm) ✅ Hypotension (initially 70/40 mmHg) ✅ Partial response to IV fluids but still unstable ✅ Normal QRS (no sodium channel blockade yet) These indicate beta-blocker toxicity affecting cardiac output. Why Glucagon Is Correct Acts via non-beta receptor pathways to increase cAMP Improves heart rate and contractility First-line antidote in beta-blocker overdose with haemodynamic compromise Effective even when beta receptors are blocked Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Activated charcoal May be considered within 1–2 hours, but patient is already unstable—antidote takes priority. B. Intubation Not required—airway and breathing are adequate. C. Atropine May help mild bradycardia but often ineffective in beta-blocker overdose. E. Diazepam Used for seizures, not present here. Key Exam Principle 👉 Beta-blocker overdose = bradycardia + hypotension 👉 First-line antidote = glucagon 👉 Fluids first, then glucagon if unstable 👉 "BB overdose → give glucagon"

question_text: A 60 year old man was involved in a high-speed road traffic accident. He was brought into the Emergency Department resuscitation room by the paramedics. He complains of severe right upper quadrant pain. On examination, there are no external bleeding. He has normal breath sounds. His abdomen is slightly distended. His right upper quadrant is tender with bruising. He has a temperature of 36.7°C, heart rate of 120 beats/minute, blood pressure of 89/56 mmHg, respiratory rate of 28 breaths/minute and an oxygen saturation of 96%. His capillary refill time is 4 seconds. Intravenous fluids have been started. What is the SINGLE most appropriate investigation?
explanation: Why? This patient has suspected intra-abdominal bleeding following trauma and is haemodynamically unstable. The most appropriate immediate investigation is a FAST (Focused Assessment with Sonography in Trauma) ultrasound. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ High-speed trauma (RTA) ✅ Hypotension (89/56 mmHg) ✅ Tachycardia (120 bpm) ✅ Delayed capillary refill (4 seconds) ✅ Abdominal distension and RUQ tenderness/bruising These strongly suggest internal bleeding, likely from liver injury. Why Ultrasound (FAST) Is Correct Rapid bedside investigation Detects free intra-abdominal fluid (blood) Used in haemodynamically unstable trauma patients Guides urgent surgical decision-making Does not delay resuscitation Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Chest X-ray May be useful but does not assess abdominal bleeding. B. Abdominal X-ray Poor sensitivity for intra-abdominal injury. C. CT scan abdomen Gold standard but only for haemodynamically stable patients. E. MRI scan Too slow and impractical in emergency trauma. Key Exam Principle 👉 Unstable trauma patient = FAST ultrasound FIRST 👉 Stable patient = CT scan 👉 "Unstable = FAST, Stable = CT"

question_text: A 48 year old man with a known history of type 1 diabetes mellitus presents to the Emergency Department. The patient is found unconscious by a family member at home. On assessment, the patient has a low blood glucose level of 2.5 mmol/L (45 mg/dL). There are no other apparent causes of his altered mental status. What is the most appropriate initial action for this patient with hypoglycaemia and unconsciousness?
explanation: Why? This patient has severe hypoglycaemia with unconsciousness. The most appropriate immediate treatment is intravenous glucose. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Known type 1 diabetes ✅ Unconscious state ✅ Blood glucose = 2.5 mmol/L (severely low) ✅ No other cause identified These indicate life-threatening hypoglycaemia requiring urgent correction. Why IV Glucose Is Correct Fastest way to raise blood glucose Restores consciousness quickly Preferred in unconscious patients (cannot take oral glucose) 20% glucose (or 10% depending on protocol) is standard emergency treatment Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. IM glucose Glucose is not given IM; incorrect option (glucagon would be used if no IV access). B. Oral glucose gel Contraindicated in unconscious patients (risk of aspiration). C. Subcutaneous glucose Not used; ineffective and inappropriate route. E. CT head Not indicated before correcting hypoglycaemia. Key Exam Principle 👉 Unconscious + hypoglycaemia = IV glucose immediately 👉 If no IV access → IM glucagon 👉 "Low sugar first, everything else later"

question_text: A 28 year old man is brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance after intentionally ingesting a large number of his propranolol tablets. His partner found him unresponsive and immediately sought medical help. On arrival, he is conscious but drowsy. His pulse is 55 beats per minute, and his blood pressure is 89/58 mmHg. He complains of feeling light-headed. He has been started on intravenous fluid. Which is the most appropriate initial management?
explanation: Why? This patient has beta-blocker (propranolol) overdose causing bradycardia and hypotension despite initial fluid resuscitation. The most appropriate initial treatment is glucagon. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Known propranolol overdose ✅ Bradycardia (HR 55 bpm) ✅ Hypotension (89/58 mmHg) ✅ Drowsiness/light-headedness ✅ Already started on IV fluids These indicate haemodynamic compromise due to beta-blocker toxicity. Why Glucagon Is Correct First-line antidote for beta-blocker overdose Increases intracellular cAMP independent of beta receptors Improves heart rate and myocardial contractility Effective even when beta receptors are blocked Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Atropine May be used for mild bradycardia but often ineffective in beta-blocker toxicity. B. Calcium chloride Used mainly in calcium channel blocker overdose, not beta-blockers. D. HIET Used in severe/refractory cases after initial treatments fail. E. Intravenous lipid emulsion Reserved for severe refractory toxicity (especially lipophilic drugs like propranolol), not first-line. Key Exam Principle 👉 Beta-blocker overdose = bradycardia + hypotension 👉 First-line antidote = glucagon 👉 Escalate (HIET, lipid) if refractory 👉 "BB overdose → glucagon first"

question_text: A 32 year old man presents to the Emergency Department. He experienced chest pain 8 hours back while playing football. The chest pain was central, non-radiating and dull. It lasted for 20 minutes. The patient had taken aspirin 300 mg before he arrived at the hospital. On examination, he is afebrile. His heart rate is 85 beats/minute, blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg, respiratory rate is 15 breaths/minute and SpO2 is 96%. Investigations were performed which show ECG - No abnormalities detected. Troponin T on arrival 2 ng/L (<12). Creatine kinase 300 U/L (25-195). What is the SINGLE most appropriate next step?

options.d: Discharge home with outpatient cardiology review

explanation: Why? This patient presents with possible acute coronary syndrome (ACS), but initial ECG and troponin are normal. The correct next step is serial troponin testing at 12 hours to rule out myocardial infarction. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ History of chest pain suggestive of cardiac origin ✅ Pain occurred 8 hours ago (troponin may still be rising) ✅ Normal ECG ✅ Initial troponin normal (2 ng/L) ✅ Elevated CK (non-specific) These suggest ACS cannot yet be ruled out. Why Admit for 12-hour Troponin Is Correct Troponin may take several hours to rise Serial measurement improves diagnostic accuracy Standard approach for suspected ACS with initial negative tests Ensures safe exclusion of myocardial infarction Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Coronary angiography Indicated in confirmed or high-risk ACS, not with normal initial tests. B. Alteplase Used in STEMI; ECG is normal. C. Fondaparinux + dual antiplatelet therapy Indicated in confirmed NSTEMI/ACS, not yet established. D. Discharge home Unsafe—ACS not yet excluded. Key Exam Principle 👉 Suspected ACS + normal initial troponin = repeat troponin at 12 hours 👉 Do not rule out MI with a single test 👉 "One troponin is not enough"

question_text: A 27 year old man is brought into A&E with burn wounds over both his arms after a house fire. On inspection, the skin is red and painful with blistering. Capillary refill is delayed. What is the next immediate action for this patient?

options.d: Clean the area with 0.9% normal saline
options.e: Cover the burn using cling film immediately after cooling

explanation: Why? In any burn patient, especially from a house fire, the priority is primary survey using the ABCDE approach. Airway compromise (e.g., inhalational injury) can be life-threatening and must be assessed immediately. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ House fire (risk of inhalational injury) ✅ Burn injuries present ✅ No mention of airway assessment yet These indicate the need for immediate primary survey. Why Assess Airway, Breathing, and Circulation Is Correct First step in ALL trauma and burn patients Identifies life-threatening issues early (e.g., airway burns, carbon monoxide poisoning) Airway compromise can rapidly deteriorate Management must follow ABCDE sequence before local burn care Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Reassure Inappropriate—potentially serious injury. C. Cold compresses Burn cooling is important but only AFTER ABC assessment. D. Clean with saline Not the immediate priority. E. Cling film Correct step in burn care, but only after initial resuscitation and cooling. Key Exam Principle 👉 Burns = treat as trauma (ABCDE first) 👉 Always assess airway early (risk of inhalation injury) 👉 Local burn care comes AFTER resuscitation 👉 "Burns = ABC before anything else"

question_text: An 18 month old boy accidentally pulled a cup of hot tea off a high table. The hot liquid splashed over him, and he now presents with a partial thickness burn covering 6% of his total body surface area (TBSA), localised to his chest. What is the best treatment for him?
explanation: Why? This child has a minor burn (<10% TBSA in children). IV fluid resuscitation is not required; oral fluids and local wound care are sufficient. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ TBSA = 6% (small burn) ✅ Partial thickness burn ✅ Localised to chest ✅ No signs of shock or dehydration These indicate a minor burn. Why No IV Treatment Is Correct Fluid resuscitation is only required when: • Children: >10% TBSA • Adults: >15% TBSA Small burns can be managed with oral fluids Focus is on analgesia, wound care, and monitoring Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. IV crystalloids Not indicated for burns <10% TBSA in children. B. IV colloids Not used in initial burn management. D. IV dextrose bolus No indication unless hypoglycaemia. E. IV albumin Not used acutely; reserved for specific cases later. Key Exam Principle 👉 Burn fluid resuscitation thresholds: • Children: >10% TBSA • Adults: >15% TBSA 👉 <10% in children = NO IV fluids 👉 "Small burn → oral fluids, not IV"

question_text: A 23 year old woman presents to the Emergency Department with symptoms of dizziness, sweating, and tinnitus. She admits to having ingested a large number of aspirin tablets approximately three hours prior to arrival. On examination, she is tachypnoeic with a respiratory rate of 30 breaths per minute and appears agitated. An arterial blood gas (ABG) analysis reveals the following: pH 7.49 (7.35 - 7.45), PaO2: 12.0 kPa (10-14), PaCO2: 2.9 kPa (4.7-6.0), Bicarbonate 22 mmol/L (22-26). Which of the following best describes the primary acid-base disturbance in this patient?

options.e: Mixed respiratory alkalosis and metabolic acidosis

explanation: Why? This patient has early salicylate (aspirin) poisoning, which primarily causes respiratory alkalosis due to stimulation of the respiratory centre. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Aspirin overdose (3 hours ago → early phase) ✅ Tachypnoea (RR 30) ✅ Alkalemic pH (7.49) ✅ Low PaCO2 (2.9 kPa) ✅ Normal bicarbonate (22 mmol/L) These findings indicate a primary respiratory process. Why Respiratory Alkalosis Is Correct Salicylates stimulate the medullary respiratory centre Leads to hyperventilation → ↓ PaCO2 Results in alkalosis (↑ pH) Occurs early in overdose before metabolic acidosis develops Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Respiratory acidosis Would show ↑ PaCO2, not decreased. B. Respiratory acidosis with compensation Inconsistent with alkalemia and low CO2. D. Metabolic acidosis Would show ↓ bicarbonate and low pH. E. Mixed disorder Occurs later in salicylate toxicity; bicarbonate would be low, which it is not here. Key Exam Principle 👉 Early salicylate poisoning = respiratory alkalosis 👉 Late salicylate poisoning = mixed respiratory alkalosis + metabolic acidosis 👉 "Aspirin early = blow off CO2"

question_text: A 16 year old female teenager was brought to the Emergency Department after being stabbed on the upper right side of her back 2 hours ago. An erect chest X-ray revealed homogenous opacity on the lower right lung. The trachea is centrally placed. She has a blood pressure of 80/60 mmHg, a pulse of 122 beats/minute, and a respiratory rate of 34 breaths/minute. What is the SINGLE most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Why? This patient has a haemothorax following penetrating chest trauma, leading to accumulation of blood in the pleural space. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Penetrating trauma (stab wound) ✅ Hypotension (80/60 mmHg) → suggests blood loss ✅ Tachycardia (122 bpm) ✅ Homogenous opacity on chest X-ray (fluid) ✅ Trachea central (no shift) These findings strongly indicate blood in the pleural cavity. Why Haemothorax Is Correct Blood collects in pleural space after trauma Appears as homogenous opacity on CXR Causes hypovolaemic shock No tracheal deviation unless massive Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Pneumothorax Would show hyperlucency (dark area), not opacity. C. Pneumonia Develops over time; unlikely acute post-trauma. D. Tension pneumothorax Would show tracheal deviation and hyperresonance, not opacity. E. Empyema Pus in pleural space; subacute condition, not immediate trauma. Key Exam Principle 👉 Trauma + opacity on CXR = fluid (blood) → haemothorax 👉 Trauma + hyperlucency = air → pneumothorax 👉 Tracheal shift = tension 👉 "White = fluid, Black = air"

question_text: A 33 year old man fell from a ladder onto his back earlier in the day. He presents to the Emergency Department with severe back pain with macroscopic haematuria. There are bruises on his right flank. He initially presented with a heart rate of 120 beats/minute and blood pressure of 85/60 mmHg. After giving him intravenous fluids and pain relief, his pulse dropped to 85 beats/minute and his blood pressure was recorded at 120/76 mmHg. What is the SINGLE most appropriate initial diagnostic step?
explanation: Why? This patient has suspected renal trauma (flank injury + haematuria) and is now haemodynamically stable after resuscitation. The most appropriate initial investigation is a CT scan of the abdomen. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Blunt trauma (fall onto back) ✅ Flank bruising (renal injury sign) ✅ Macroscopic haematuria ✅ Initially unstable but now stabilised after fluids These strongly suggest renal injury requiring imaging. Why CT Abdomen Is Correct Gold standard for evaluating renal trauma Assesses extent of injury (laceration, hematoma, vascular injury) Indicated in haemodynamically stable patients Guides further management (conservative vs surgical) Why the Other Options Are Less Likely B. Cystoscopy Used for lower urinary tract/bladder issues, not initial trauma assessment. C. Intravenous urography Outdated; replaced by CT in trauma settings. D. Renal arteriography Used for specific vascular interventions, not initial imaging. E. Laparoscopy Not a diagnostic first step in stable patients. Key Exam Principle 👉 Renal trauma + stable patient = CT scan 👉 Unstable patient = FAST ± immediate surgery 👉 "Stable = CT, Unstable = operate/FAST"

question_text: A 78 year old woman is brought to the Emergency Department by her carer due to increasing confusion and lethargy over the past two days. She has a history of hypertension and osteoarthritis. She has been experiencing reduced oral intake and vomiting for the past three days. On examination, she appears drowsy and confused. Her mucous membranes are dry, and capillary refill time is prolonged. Blood pressure is 88/58 mmHg, and pulse rate is 110 beats per minute. Investigations reveal: Serum sodium 156 mmol/L (135-145), Serum urea 12.4 mmol/L (2.5-7.8), Serum creatinine 135 µmol/L (45-90). What is the most appropriate initial fluid management?
explanation: Why? This patient has hypovolaemic hypernatraemia with haemodynamic instability. The priority is rapid restoration of intravascular volume using isotonic saline (0.9% sodium chloride). Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Hypotension (88/58 mmHg) ✅ Tachycardia (110 bpm) ✅ Dry mucous membranes and poor skin perfusion ✅ History of vomiting and poor intake ✅ Elevated sodium (156 mmol/L) ✅ Raised urea and creatinine (pre-renal AKI) These indicate dehydration with volume depletion and hypernatraemia. Why 0.9% Sodium Chloride Is Correct First-line for resuscitation in hypovolaemic patients Restores circulating volume and organ perfusion Stabilises patient before correcting sodium Prevents further renal injury Why the Other Options Are Less Likely B. 5% dextrose Hypotonic; may worsen haemodynamic instability if used first. C. Hypertonic saline Used for severe hyponatraemia, not hypernatraemia. D. 0.45% sodium chloride Used later to correct sodium, not for initial resuscitation. E. Fluid restriction Used in hypervolaemic or euvolaemic states, not dehydration. Key Exam Principle 👉 Hypovolaemic hypernatraemia = FIRST isotonic saline 👉 Correct volume before correcting sodium 👉 Avoid rapid sodium correction 👉 "Resuscitate first, correct sodium later"

question_text: A 42 years old man presents to the Emergency Department after experiencing chest pain while playing squash 8 hours ago. The pain occurred during a competitive game, was central, dull in nature, non-radiating, and lasted approximately 20 minutes before resolving spontaneously with rest. On examination, he is comfortable at rest and afebrile. Heart rate 82 beats/minute, blood pressure 112/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths/minute, SpO2 97% on air. Investigations show: ECG Normal sinus rhythm, Troponin T on arrival 3 ng/L (<12), Creatine kinase 320 U/L (25-195). What is the SINGLE most appropriate next step?

options.a: Admit for serial troponin testing at 12 hours

explanation: Why? This patient has possible acute coronary syndrome (ACS), but initial ECG and troponin are normal. A single normal troponin does not exclude myocardial infarction, so serial testing is required. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Typical exertional chest pain (suggestive of cardiac origin) ✅ Pain resolved with rest (possible angina/ACS) ✅ Presentation 8 hours after event ✅ Normal ECG ✅ Normal initial troponin These indicate ACS cannot yet be ruled out. Why Serial Troponin Testing Is Correct Troponin may rise several hours after myocardial injury Serial measurement increases diagnostic sensitivity Standard protocol for suspected ACS Ensures safe exclusion before discharge Why the Other Options Are Less Likely B. CT coronary angiography Not first-line in acute ED setting with suspected ACS. C. Alteplase Indicated in STEMI; ECG is normal. D. Fondaparinux + DAPT Used in confirmed NSTEMI/ACS, not yet diagnosed. E. Discharge Unsafe without ruling out MI. Key Exam Principle 👉 Suspected ACS + normal initial tests = repeat troponin 👉 Never rely on a single troponin 👉 "Rule out before you rule out"

question_text: A mother brings her two year old daughter into the Emergency Department. The child was eating some peanuts whilst the mother was preparing food. When the mother returned to check on her she could hear a high pitched noise when the daughter was breathing. The daughter is well and talks to you saying "a peanut went down my throat". On auscultation you hear an expiratory wheeze on the right side of the child's chest. There is no hoarseness of voice and no drooling. Her observations are within normal limits. She is afebrile. A chest X-ray was performed which was normal. What is the SINGLE most appropriate next step?
explanation: Why? This child has a high clinical suspicion of foreign body aspiration (peanut) despite a normal chest X-ray. The definitive next step is bronchoscopy. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Sudden onset during eating (peanuts) ✅ Child reports aspiration event ✅ Unilateral expiratory wheeze (right side) ✅ Normal vitals but persistent focal signs ✅ Normal chest X-ray (does NOT exclude foreign body) These strongly indicate a bronchial foreign body. Why Bronchoscopy Is Correct Gold standard for diagnosis and treatment Allows direct visualization and removal of foreign body Indicated when clinical suspicion is high, regardless of imaging Prevents complications (e.g., pneumonia, collapse) Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Flexible nasal endoscopy Examines upper airway, not bronchi. B. Lateral neck X-ray Used for upper airway obstruction, not lower airway foreign body. C. Repeat chest X-ray Delays definitive treatment; normal X-ray does not rule out FBA. E. IV antibiotics No evidence of infection. Key Exam Principle 👉 Suspected foreign body aspiration + focal signs = bronchoscopy 👉 Normal CXR does NOT exclude FBA 👉 "History > X-ray in FBA" 👉 "If you suspect it, scope it"

question_text: A 29 year old man is brought to the Emergency Department following a high speed road traffic accident. He was the driver of a car that collided head-on with another vehicle. On arrival, he is conscious but appears pale and clammy. His pulse is 120 beats per minute and blood pressure is 85/60 mmHg. He complains of severe pain in the left upper abdomen. A bedside ultrasound scan shows free fluid within the abdomen. What is the most likely organ injured?
explanation: Why? This patient has intra-abdominal bleeding following blunt trauma, with left upper quadrant pain—most consistent with splenic injury. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ High-speed trauma (RTA) ✅ Hypotension (85/60 mmHg) and tachycardia → shock ✅ Pale and clammy → hypovolaemia ✅ Left upper quadrant pain ✅ FAST scan showing free fluid (likely blood) These strongly indicate splenic rupture. Why Spleen Is Correct Most commonly injured organ in blunt abdominal trauma Located in left upper quadrant Highly vascular → causes significant intra-abdominal bleeding Classic cause of haemodynamic instability after trauma Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Aorta Injury usually causes immediate death or thoracic signs. B. Small bowel Less vascular; less likely to cause rapid shock. C. Liver More commonly causes right upper quadrant pain. D. Pancreas Retroperitoneal; less likely to cause free fluid early. Key Exam Principle 👉 LUQ pain + shock + free fluid = splenic injury 👉 Most common organ injured in blunt abdominal trauma 👉 "LUQ trauma → think spleen first"

question_text: A 34 year old woman presents to the Emergency Department with complaints of persistent nausea. She reports having taken paracetamol at a dose of 6 grams per day over the past 4 days to manage her lower back pain. On examination, she is alert but appears uncomfortable. Her vital signs are within normal limits. Initial blood tests reveal a serum paracetamol concentration of 15 µg/ml. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?

options.a: Administer intravenous fluids and reassess in 24 hours
options.b: Prescribe an antiemetic and review in one week
options.d: Discharge with advice to reduce paracetamol use

explanation: Why? This patient has chronic supratherapeutic paracetamol ingestion with a detectable drug level. In such cases, the nomogram cannot be used, and treatment with N-acetylcysteine (NAC) should be started immediately. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Repeated high dosing (6 g/day > safe limit) ✅ Duration over several days (staggered/chronic ingestion) ✅ Symptoms (persistent nausea) ✅ Detectable paracetamol level (15 µg/ml) These indicate ongoing risk of hepatotoxicity. Why NAC Is Correct Replenishes glutathione and prevents liver injury Indicated in chronic or staggered overdose Nomogram is NOT applicable in repeated dosing Treatment should not be delayed when toxicity is suspected Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. IV fluids Supportive only; does not treat toxicity. B. Antiemetic only Misses underlying toxic process. D. Discharge Unsafe—risk of delayed liver failure. E. Abdominal ultrasound Not useful in acute paracetamol toxicity. Key Exam Principle 👉 Chronic/staggered overdose = treat regardless of level 👉 Detectable paracetamol + symptoms = give NAC 👉 Do NOT use nomogram in repeated ingestion 👉 "If in doubt → start NAC"

question_text: A 19 year old man is urgently brought into the emergency department (ED) by his friends, who leave swiftly before the medical staff can interview them. The patient is in a semiconscious state with a respiratory rate of 7 breaths per minute, blood pressure of 120/75 mmHg, and a pulse rate of 60 beats per minute. His previous admission records show that he has type 1 diabetes mellitus. On examination, he exhibits needle track marks on his arms and his pupils are notably pinpoint in size. He is sweating profusely. What is the SINGLE most appropriate management?
explanation: Why? This patient has opioid overdose, presenting with the classic triad of respiratory depression, reduced consciousness, and pinpoint pupils. The immediate treatment is naloxone. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Reduced consciousness (semiconscious) ✅ Respiratory depression (RR 7) ✅ Pinpoint pupils (miosis) ✅ Needle track marks (IV drug use) These are classic for opioid toxicity. Why Naloxone Is Correct Opioid antagonist Rapidly reverses respiratory depression Life-saving and first-line treatment Can be given IV/IM/IN Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Insulin No evidence of hyperglycaemia or DKA. C. Methadone Used for opioid substitution, not overdose treatment. D. Gastric lavage Not appropriate; overdose likely parenteral. E. Flumazenil Used for benzodiazepine overdose, not opioids. Key Exam Principle 👉 Opioid overdose triad: • CNS depression • Respiratory depression • Miosis 👉 Treatment = naloxone immediately 👉 "Pinpoint pupils + low RR = give naloxone"

question_text: A 28 year old man is brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance after collapsing at a nightclub. On examination, he is agitated, sweating profusely, and reports chest pain. His blood pressure is 182/110 mmHg, heart rate is 130 beats per minute, and he appears to be hyperventilating. He admits to using cocaine earlier in the evening. An ECG shows sinus tachycardia. Blood tests, including cardiac enzymes, are within normal limits. What is the most appropriate initial management to manage his elevated heart rate and blood pressure?
explanation: Why? This patient has acute cocaine toxicity causing sympathetic overactivity (tachycardia, hypertension, agitation). The first-line treatment is benzodiazepines to reduce central sympathetic stimulation. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Cocaine use ✅ Agitation and sweating ✅ Severe hypertension (182/110 mmHg) ✅ Tachycardia (130 bpm) ✅ Chest pain with normal ECG/troponin These indicate cocaine-induced sympathetic excess. Why Benzodiazepine Is Correct Reduces CNS stimulation and sympathetic outflow Lowers heart rate and blood pressure Relieves agitation and anxiety First-line treatment in cocaine toxicity Why the Other Options Are Less Likely B. Beta blockers Contraindicated—can cause unopposed alpha stimulation → worsen hypertension. C. Calcium channel blockers May be used later but not first-line. D. IV fluids Supportive but does not address sympathetic overactivity. E. Nitrates May help chest pain but not primary initial treatment. Key Exam Principle 👉 Cocaine toxicity = sympathetic overdrive 👉 First-line = benzodiazepines 👉 Avoid beta blockers (unopposed alpha effect) 👉 "Cocaine → sedate first"

question_text: A 10 year old boy is brought unconscious to the Emergency Department by his parents. His parents report that he was playing with his brother in the park when he sat down and then fell unconscious. There was no head injury. The incident occurred 25 minutes ago, and he has not regained consciousness since. He is unresponsive but breathing normally. His airways are patent. He has vesicular breath sounds. His heart rate is 120 beats/minute. There are no visible wounds. What is the SINGLE next most appropriate management?

options.d: Arrange for a CT scan of the head

explanation: Why? This child is unconscious but has a patent airway, is breathing normally, and has circulation (HR 120). Therefore, the immediate next step in management follows the ABCDE approach, specifically assessing reversible causes of decreased consciousness. The most urgent and rapidly correctable cause is hypoglycaemia, so capillary blood glucose must be checked immediately. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Unconscious but breathing normally ✅ Airway patent and stable respiratory exam ✅ Circulation present (HR 120) ✅ Sudden collapse without trauma ✅ No obvious cause identified These point toward a metabolic or reversible cause such as hypoglycaemia. Why Check Capillary Blood Glucose Is Correct Quick, bedside test Hypoglycaemia is a common reversible cause of unconsciousness in children Can be rapidly treated (e.g., IV dextrose) Part of 'D' (Disability) in ABCDE assessment Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Intubate Not needed—airway is patent and breathing is adequate. B. Intravenous fluids Not immediately indicated without signs of shock or dehydration. D. CT scan of the head Important later, but only after stabilisation and ruling out reversible causes. E. Chest compressions Not indicated—patient has a pulse and is breathing. Key Exam Principle 👉 Always follow ABCDE in emergencies 👉 In unconscious patients with stable ABC → check glucose immediately 👉 "Unconscious = check sugar first"

question_text: A 42 year old man is called on the telephone by his GP following receiving results of his lithium level. His lithium level is 1.6 mmol/L (0.6-1.0). He takes lithium regularly for his bipolar disorder. On further questioning, he admits to having tremors, muscle weakness and dizziness over the last week. What is the SINGLE most appropriate action?

options.d: Refer to the acute medical unit (AMU) for a same-day assessment

explanation: Why? This patient has lithium toxicity. His lithium level is elevated (1.6 mmol/L), and he has clinical symptoms (tremor, muscle weakness, dizziness), indicating symptomatic toxicity. This requires urgent medical assessment and monitoring in an acute setting. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Lithium level above therapeutic range (1.6 mmol/L) ✅ Neurological symptoms (tremor, weakness, dizziness) ✅ Symptoms ongoing for a week These indicate established lithium toxicity rather than a mild or incidental elevation. Why Referral to AMU Is Correct Symptomatic lithium toxicity requires urgent assessment Risk of progression to severe toxicity (confusion, seizures, coma) Requires monitoring of lithium levels, renal function, and electrolytes May require IV fluids or even dialysis in severe cases Same-day hospital review is essential Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Referral to neurology Not appropriate—this is a toxicological emergency, not a primary neurological disorder. B. Referral to psychiatry Not urgent priority—medical stabilisation comes first. C. Repeat lithium levels in 24 hours Unsafe delay in a symptomatic patient with toxic levels. E. Request renal function test Important but should be done urgently in hospital, not as an outpatient step. Key Exam Principle 👉 Lithium level >1.5 mmol/L + symptoms = toxicity 👉 Symptomatic toxicity = urgent hospital referral 👉 "Lithium toxicity → admit, monitor, hydrate"

question_text: A 43 year old woman is brought to the Emergency Department following a fall from a ladder while cleaning her windows. She landed awkwardly and now complains of severe neck pain. She is fully alert but appears anxious and reports a tingling sensation in both upper limbs. On examination, there is marked cervical spine tenderness and restricted neck movement. Her respiratory rate is 22 breaths per minute, and her oxygen saturation is 92% on room air. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?
explanation: Why? This patient has a suspected cervical spine injury following trauma (fall from height) with red flag symptoms (neck pain, cervical tenderness, and bilateral upper limb tingling suggesting possible spinal cord involvement). The most important immediate step is to prevent further spinal cord damage by immobilising the cervical spine. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Fall from height (mechanism of injury) ✅ Severe neck pain and cervical spine tenderness ✅ Neurological symptoms (bilateral upper limb tingling) ✅ Restricted neck movement These strongly suggest a potential cervical spine injury. Why Cervical Spine Immobilisation Is Correct Prevents further movement and secondary spinal cord injury First priority in trauma with suspected spinal injury Part of 'A' (Airway with cervical spine protection) in ABCDE Applied immediately (e.g., hard collar, blocks, spinal board) Why the Other Options Are Less Likely B. Administer oxygen Important (SpO₂ 92%), but does not address the immediate risk of spinal cord injury—can be given alongside but not the primary priority. C. Intubation Not indicated—patient is conscious with adequate airway. D. Urgent chest X-ray Not first step—imaging comes after initial stabilisation. E. CT head May be needed later but not before spinal immobilisation. Key Exam Principle 👉 Trauma = always think ABCDE 👉 Airway WITH cervical spine protection is first 👉 "Suspected C-spine injury → immobilise immediately before anything else"

question_text: A 32 year old man with a history of asthma presents to the Emergency Department with worsening breathlessness and wheeze over the past six hours. He has been using his salbutamol inhaler frequently at home with little relief. On arrival, he is tachypnoeic, using accessory muscles, and unable to complete full sentences. His respiratory rate is 36 breaths per minute, and his oxygen saturation is 88% despite receiving 15 litres of oxygen via a non-rebreathe mask. His pulse is 128 beats per minute, and auscultation reveals widespread wheeze with reduced air entry. He has been treated with nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium bromide, intravenous hydrocortisone, and high-flow oxygen, but his condition has not improved. Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
explanation: Why? This patient has a life-threatening acute severe asthma attack (near-fatal features): hypoxia despite high-flow oxygen, inability to speak, tachypnoea, tachycardia, and poor response to initial standard therapy. The next step in management is intravenous magnesium sulphate, which acts as a bronchodilator in severe refractory asthma. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Severe asthma features (RR 36, unable to complete sentences) ✅ Hypoxia (SpO₂ 88% despite 15L O₂) ✅ Tachycardia (128 bpm) ✅ Reduced air entry (suggests severe airway obstruction) ✅ No improvement after initial treatment (nebulised β2-agonist + ipratropium + steroids) These indicate life-threatening asthma requiring escalation. Why Intravenous Magnesium Sulphate Is Correct Potent bronchodilator via smooth muscle relaxation Recommended in severe or life-threatening asthma not responding to initial therapy Improves airflow and reduces hospital admission risk Given as a single IV infusion (e.g., 1.2–2 g over 20 minutes) Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Intravenous aminophylline Second-line and less preferred due to side effects and narrow therapeutic index. B. Intravenous hydrocortisone Already given—no role in repeating immediately. D. Intravenous salbutamol May be used later, but magnesium sulphate is preferred next step. E. Oral prednisolone Too slow and inappropriate in severe, deteriorating patient (IV steroids already given). Key Exam Principle 👉 Severe asthma not responding to initial therapy → give IV magnesium sulphate 👉 "Refractory asthma = magnesium next" 👉 Always escalate stepwise after standard treatment

question_text: A 33 year old woman has recurring tightness in her chest accompanied by palpitations and sweating. These episodes occur several times a week and are associated with increased respiratory rate and tingling and numbness around the mouth and fingers. What is the SINGLE most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Why? This patient’s symptoms are classic for panic attacks with hyperventilation. The key feature is respiratory alkalosis from rapid breathing, which leads to paraesthesia (tingling around the mouth and fingers) due to reduced ionised calcium. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Recurrent episodes ✅ Palpitations and sweating (autonomic symptoms) ✅ Increased respiratory rate (hyperventilation) ✅ Tingling around mouth and fingers (paraesthesia) These are hallmark features of panic attacks with hyperventilation syndrome. Why Panic Attack Is Correct Hyperventilation → ↓ CO₂ → respiratory alkalosis Leads to ↓ ionised calcium → paraesthesia (perioral + fingers) Associated with autonomic symptoms (palpitations, sweating) Episodic and recurrent in nature Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Hypercalcaemia Causes weakness, constipation, confusion—not paraesthesia. B. Stable angina Exertional chest pain, not associated with tingling or hyperventilation. D. Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease Burning chest pain related to meals, no autonomic or neurological symptoms. E. Prinzmetal's angina Causes chest pain at rest due to coronary vasospasm, but not hyperventilation or paraesthesia. Key Exam Principle 👉 Hyperventilation → respiratory alkalosis → ↓ ionised Ca²⁺ → paraesthesia 👉 Panic attack = episodic chest tightness + autonomic symptoms + tingling 👉 "Tingling + fast breathing = think panic"

question_text: A 24 year old woman is brought to the Emergency Department after ingesting an unknown quantity of aspirin tablets approximately four hours ago in a suicide attempt. She is alert but complains of nausea, ringing in her ears, and dizziness. On examination, her respiratory rate is 28 breaths per minute and she has a mild tremor. Her arterial blood gas on air shows: pH 7.46 (7.35-7.45), pCO2 3.8 kPa (4.7-6.0), bicarbonate 18 mmol/L (22-29). Plasma salicylate concentration is 480 mg/L. Her serum potassium is 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.0). Intravenous fluids are started. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
explanation: Why? This patient has moderate salicylate toxicity. Her symptoms (tinnitus, nausea, tachypnoea) and ABG (mixed respiratory alkalosis + metabolic acidosis) are classic. The next step is urinary alkalinisation with intravenous sodium bicarbonate to enhance salicylate excretion. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Aspirin overdose (4 hours ago) ✅ Tinnitus (classic salicylate toxicity sign) ✅ Tachypnoea (RR 28) ✅ ABG: high pH + low pCO2 + low HCO3⁻ → mixed respiratory alkalosis + metabolic acidosis ✅ Salicylate level 480 mg/L (elevated, significant toxicity) ✅ Hypokalaemia (K⁺ 3.2 mmol/L) These indicate clinically significant salicylate poisoning requiring active elimination. Why Intravenous Sodium Bicarbonate Is Correct Alkalinises blood and urine Increases ionisation of salicylate → reduces CNS penetration Enhances renal excretion (ion trapping) Standard treatment for moderate toxicity Also helps correct metabolic acidosis Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Activated charcoal Useful early (<1–2 hours), but at 4 hours benefit is limited (though may still be considered in some cases, not the best next step here). B. Haemodialysis Indicated in severe toxicity (very high levels, severe acidosis, renal failure, altered consciousness)—not yet indicated here. D. Intubation Avoid if possible—can worsen acidosis if ventilation is not carefully controlled. E. N-acetylcysteine Used for paracetamol overdose, not aspirin. Key Exam Principle 👉 Salicylate toxicity = respiratory alkalosis + metabolic acidosis 👉 Moderate toxicity → give IV sodium bicarbonate 👉 Severe toxicity → consider dialysis 👉 "Aspirin overdose → alkalinise urine"

question_text: A 59 year old man is found not fully conscious on the street and brought to A&E by paramedics. Bystanders report that he was walking when he suddenly collapsed. On arrival, paramedics found him confused but breathing. His Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score is 11/15, with no signs of trauma. Blood glucose is measured at 1.6 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
explanation: Why? This patient has severe hypoglycaemia (glucose 1.6 mmol/L) with impaired consciousness (GCS 11). The most appropriate and fastest treatment is intravenous glucose to rapidly restore blood glucose levels. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Very low blood glucose (1.6 mmol/L) ✅ Reduced consciousness (GCS 11) ✅ Unable to safely take oral treatment These indicate severe hypoglycaemia requiring urgent IV correction. Why IV Glucose Is Correct Rapidly increases blood glucose levels First-line in hypoglycaemia with reduced consciousness Reliable and immediate effect Prevents progression to seizures, coma, or death Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Buccal glucose gel Used in conscious patients who can cooperate—not suitable here. B. IM Glucagon Used if IV access is not available; IV glucose is preferred when access exists. D. Oral glucose solution Unsafe due to risk of aspiration in reduced consciousness. E. Subcutaneous insulin Would worsen hypoglycaemia—contraindicated. Key Exam Principle 👉 Hypoglycaemia + reduced consciousness → IV glucose immediately 👉 If no IV access → IM glucagon 👉 "Low sugar + low GCS = give IV dextrose NOW"

question_text: An 18 year old female was brought into the ED after ingestion of 28 paracetamol tablets after breaking up with her boyfriend. She came in confused and unwell. She was admitted in the medical ward and N-acetylcysteine was given. 24 hours later, her laboratory results show a normal FBC, an arterial pH of 7.1, Prothrombin time of 17 seconds and creatinine of 255 umol/L. She is still confused and lethargic. What is the SINGLE most appropriate management?
explanation: Why? This patient has developed acute liver failure following paracetamol overdose despite treatment with N-acetylcysteine. She meets poor prognostic criteria (King’s College criteria), indicating the need for urgent liver transplantation. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Paracetamol overdose (28 tablets) ✅ Persistent confusion (hepatic encephalopathy) ✅ Severe metabolic acidosis (pH 7.1) ✅ Prolonged PT (17 seconds → coagulopathy) ✅ Elevated creatinine (255 µmol/L → renal failure) These indicate multi-organ involvement and severe liver failure. Why Liver Transplantation Is Correct King’s College criteria for paracetamol toxicity: ➡️ Arterial pH < 7.3 OR ➡️ PT > 100 sec + creatinine > 300 µmol/L + encephalopathy This patient already meets the critical pH criterion (<7.3), which alone is sufficient Indicates very poor prognosis without transplant Requires urgent referral to a transplant centre Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Observe for another 24 hours Dangerous delay—patient is critically unwell. B. Admit to psychiatric ward Medical stabilisation takes priority over psychiatric care. C.
