Intravenous fluids Supportive only—does not address liver failure. D. Administer charcoal Only useful early after ingestion—not 24 hours later. Key Exam Principle 👉 Paracetamol overdose + pH < 7.3 = urgent transplant 👉 Always think King’s College criteria 👉 "Acidosis in paracetamol toxicity = transplant referral"

question_text: A 10 year old boy is brought to the Emergency Department after falling onto a barbecue grill, resulting in partial-thickness burns covering 8% of his total body surface area, primarily on his arm and chest. He is crying and reports severe pain. He is haemodynamically stable, and IV access has not yet been established. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial analgesia for managing his pain?
explanation: Why? This child has severe acute pain from partial-thickness burns and requires rapid, effective analgesia. Since IV access is not yet established, the best option is intranasal fentanyl, which provides fast, potent analgesia without the need for IV access. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Severe pain (crying, burns) ✅ Partial-thickness burns (very painful) ✅ No IV access yet ✅ Haemodynamically stable These indicate the need for strong, rapid analgesia via a non-invasive route. Why Intranasal Fentanyl Is Correct Rapid onset of action Potent opioid analgesic suitable for severe pain No need for IV access Commonly used in paediatric emergency settings Well tolerated and easy to administer Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Oral ibuprofen Too slow and insufficient for severe burn pain. B. Oral codeine Weak opioid with variable metabolism in children; not ideal for acute severe pain. D. Oral paracetamol Insufficient alone for severe pain. E. Intramuscular morphine Painful injection, unpredictable absorption, and generally avoided in children. Key Exam Principle 👉 Severe pain + no IV access → intranasal fentanyl 👉 Burns = very painful → require strong opioids 👉 "No IV? Go intranasal"

question_text: A 59 year old man is brought to the Emergency Department following a motor vehicle accident. He is speaking in full sentences but is unable to hear. The patient is breathing without difficulty and his extremities are well perfused. On examination, you note mastoid ecchymosis and rhinorrhoea. His pulse rate is 86 beats/minute, blood pressure is 128/84 mmHg and respiratory rate is 17 breaths/min. Which bone is most likely fractured?
explanation: Why? This patient has classic signs of a basilar skull fracture involving the temporal bone. Mastoid ecchymosis (Battle’s sign), hearing loss, and CSF rhinorrhoea strongly point to temporal bone involvement. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Mastoid ecchymosis (Battle’s sign) ✅ Hearing loss ✅ CSF rhinorrhoea ✅ History of trauma (motor vehicle accident) These are hallmark features of a basilar skull fracture, particularly involving the temporal bone. Why Temporal Bone Is Correct Temporal bone houses structures of the ear → explains hearing loss Commonly involved in basilar skull fractures Associated with Battle’s sign (mastoid bruising) Can cause CSF leak (rhinorrhoea or otorrhoea) Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Occipital Less commonly associated with these specific signs. B. Sphenoid Can be involved in skull base fractures but less associated with Battle’s sign and hearing loss. C. Parietal Typically causes scalp swelling or fracture without CSF leak or mastoid bruising. D. Ethmoid Associated with CSF rhinorrhoea but not mastoid ecchymosis or hearing loss. Key Exam Principle 👉 Battle’s sign = temporal bone fracture 👉 Hearing loss + CSF leak → think base of skull (temporal) 👉 "Mastoid bruising = temporal bone injury"

question_text: You are working in the Emergency Department. A patient, who has presented feeling generally unwell, collapses. In resus, he is found to have a heart rate of 36 beats/minute and a blood pressure of 87/62 mmHg. An ECG reveals sinus bradycardia. What is the most appropriate initial management?
explanation: Why? This patient has symptomatic bradycardia with hypotension (HR 36, BP 87/62). The first-line treatment according to ACLS guidelines is intravenous atropine to increase heart rate and improve cardiac output. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Severe bradycardia (HR 36 bpm) ✅ Hypotension (BP 87/62 mmHg) ✅ Collapse (hemodynamic instability) ✅ ECG shows sinus bradycardia These indicate symptomatic bradycardia requiring urgent intervention. Why Atropine Is Correct First-line treatment for symptomatic bradycardia Works by inhibiting vagal tone → increases heart rate Rapid onset of action Improves cardiac output and blood pressure Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. IV fluids May support BP but does not correct bradycardia. C. Adenosine Used for supraventricular tachycardia, not bradycardia. D. Amiodarone Used for tachyarrhythmias, not bradycardia. E. External pacing Used if atropine fails or in severe cases—not first-line. Key Exam Principle 👉 Symptomatic bradycardia → give atropine first 👉 If ineffective → pacing 👉 "Brady + hypotension = atropine first"

question_text: An 11 year old boy fell from his bicycle earlier in the day and hit his head on a lampost. He was brought in by his mother to the Emergency Department. He cannot remember the event and cannot remember riding the bicycle. The accident was witnessed by his mother. She says he was not going at a high speed as he was cycling uphill. He lost consciousness for a few seconds after the injury but recovered well. He was not wearing a helmet. On examination, there is a small swelling on the frontal area with no visible lacerations or bleeding. He has a Glasgow Coma Scale of 15/15. His neurological examination was unremarkable. What is the SINGLE most appropriate management?

options.c: Observe for a minimum of 4 hours post head injury
options.d: Observe for a minimum of 24 hours post head injury

explanation: Why? This child has a mild head injury with risk factors (brief loss of consciousness and amnesia), but no red flag features requiring immediate CT. According to head injury guidelines, such patients should be observed for at least 4 hours in the Emergency Department. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Brief loss of consciousness ✅ Amnesia (cannot remember event) ✅ GCS 15/15 ✅ Normal neurological exam ✅ Low-impact mechanism (slow cycling uphill) These indicate a mild head injury with intermediate risk. Why Observation for 4 Hours Is Correct Recommended for children with mild head injury + risk factors Allows monitoring for deterioration Avoids unnecessary radiation from CT If stable after observation → safe discharge Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. CT head within 1 hour Indicated only if red flags (e.g., GCS <14, focal deficit, persistent vomiting, signs of skull fracture). B. MRI head within 6 hours Not used in acute head injury assessment. D. Observe for 24 hours Unnecessary if patient remains stable. E. Discharge immediately Unsafe due to history of LOC and amnesia—requires observation first. Key Exam Principle 👉 Mild head injury + LOC/amnesia → observe for 4 hours 👉 CT only if red flags present 👉 "Head injury + GCS 15 but symptoms = observe first"

question_text: A 23 year old single male was brought to emergency department by his father exhausted and frightened. His father tells you that his son, who was previously healthy, had, for no apparent reason, a sudden attack of fear, dizziness, sweating, palpitations and the feeling that his heart is going to stop beating. The symptoms started to decrease gradually after about 10 minutes. Which is the SINGLE most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Why? This presentation is classic for a panic attack: sudden onset of intense fear with autonomic symptoms that peak rapidly and resolve within minutes. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Sudden onset of fear without trigger ✅ Palpitations, sweating, dizziness (autonomic symptoms) ✅ Feeling of impending doom ("heart is going to stop") ✅ Short duration (~10 minutes) ✅ Previously healthy individual These are hallmark features of panic attacks. Why Panic Attack Is Correct Abrupt onset and short duration Prominent autonomic symptoms Peaks within minutes and resolves spontaneously Common in young adults No underlying organic trigger identified Why the Other Options Are Less Likely B. Delirious state Would present with confusion, disorientation, and fluctuating consciousness—not brief episodic fear. C. Alcohol withdrawal Requires history of alcohol dependence and typically presents with tremors, agitation, and symptoms over hours–days. D. Drug overdose Usually causes persistent symptoms, altered consciousness, or specific toxidromes—not brief self-resolving episodes. E. Phaeochromocytoma Causes recurrent episodes but typically associated with sustained hypertension and not such brief isolated events. Key Exam Principle 👉 Sudden fear + palpitations + sweating + short duration = panic attack 👉 Episodes peak within minutes and resolve 👉 "Short, intense, self-limiting = panic"

question_text: A 22 year old man attends the Emergency Department with a stab wound to the chest. The man complains of left-sided chest pain and difficulty in breathing. On examination, there is a single stab wound to his left chest just below his clavicle. His trachea deviates to the right. On auscultation, the patient has an absence of breath sounds on the left side chest. His pulse rate is 122 beats/minute and BP 95/55 mmHg. The patient has been started on high-flow oxygen. What is the most appropriate next step in his management?
explanation: Why? This patient has a tension pneumothorax, a life-threatening condition requiring immediate decompression. The key features include tracheal deviation away from the affected side, absent breath sounds, hypotension, and tachycardia following chest trauma. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Penetrating chest trauma (stab wound) ✅ Tracheal deviation to the right (away from left side) ✅ Absent breath sounds on the left ✅ Hypotension (95/55 mmHg) ✅ Tachycardia (122 bpm) These are classic signs of tension pneumothorax. Why Needle Thoracentesis Is Correct Immediate life-saving decompression Relieves pressure in pleural space Restores venous return and cardiac output Done before imaging or definitive management Followed by chest drain insertion Why the Other Options Are Less Likely B. Chest drain Definitive treatment but must be preceded by emergency needle decompression in unstable patients. C. Intubate and ventilate May worsen tension pneumothorax if done before decompression. D. Tracheostomy Not indicated—airway is patent. E. Pericardiocentesis Used for cardiac tamponade, not pneumothorax. Key Exam Principle 👉 Tension pneumothorax = clinical diagnosis 👉 Do NOT wait for imaging 👉 Immediate needle decompression first, then chest drain 👉 "Shock + tracheal deviation + absent breath sounds = decompress NOW"

question_text: A 46 year old man presents to the Emergency Department requesting help to stop drinking alcohol. He has been drinking heavily for over ten years, typically consuming more than 25 units per day. He reports no history of seizures, confusion, or hallucinations. His last alcoholic drink was earlier today. He is alert and orientated, and his physical examination is unremarkable. His vital signs are within normal limits. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.b: Arrange urgent referral to community alcohol services
options.c: Arrange urgent referral to general practice
options.e: Refer to liaison psychiatry for assessment

explanation: Why? This patient has alcohol dependence but is currently stable with no features of withdrawal or complications (e.g., seizures, delirium tremens). The most appropriate next step is referral to community alcohol services for structured outpatient detoxification and support. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Chronic heavy alcohol use (>25 units/day) ✅ No history of withdrawal complications (no seizures, hallucinations) ✅ Currently stable (normal vitals, alert, oriented) ✅ Motivated to stop drinking These suggest suitability for outpatient (community-based) management. Why Community Alcohol Services Is Correct Provides structured detox programmes Offers psychosocial support and relapse prevention Appropriate for low-risk, stable patients Avoids unnecessary hospital admission Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Admit for inpatient detoxification Reserved for high-risk patients (history of seizures, delirium tremens, severe comorbidities). C. Referral to general practice Too indirect—specialist alcohol services are more appropriate. D. Community psychiatry Not indicated unless there is a comorbid psychiatric disorder. E. Liaison psychiatry Typically for acute mental health crises or overdose—not needed here. Key Exam Principle 👉 Stable alcohol dependence → community detox 👉 Inpatient only if high risk (seizures, DTs, severe illness) 👉 "Stable + motivated = outpatient referral"

question_text: A 24 year old male presents to A&E with 40% partial thickness burns after having been in a house fire. His pulse rate is 115 bpm and respiratory rate is 29 breaths per minute. His systolic blood pressure is 80 mmHg. What is the SINGLE most appropriate management?

options.a: IV fluids calculated from the time of hospital arrival
options.b: IV fluids calculated from the time of burn

explanation: Why? This patient has major burns (40% TBSA) with signs of burn shock (tachycardia, hypotension). The most important immediate management is aggressive fluid resuscitation using a formula (e.g., Parkland formula), which must be calculated from the time of the burn, not hospital arrival. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Extensive burns (40% TBSA) ✅ Hypotension (SBP 80 mmHg) ✅ Tachycardia (115 bpm) ✅ Tachypnoea (29 breaths/min) These indicate burn shock requiring urgent fluid resuscitation. Why IV Fluids from Time of Burn Is Correct Parkland formula: 4 mL × body weight (kg) × %TBSA burned Half given in first 8 hours from time of burn Remaining half over next 16 hours Timing is critical—delay increases mortality Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. IV fluids from hospital arrival Incorrect timing—must count from time of injury. C. Oral rehydration Inadequate for major burns. D. IV dextrose stat Not indicated—needs crystalloid (e.g., Hartmann’s solution). E. IV morphine Important for pain but not priority over life-saving fluid resuscitation. Key Exam Principle 👉 Burns >10–15% TBSA → IV fluid resuscitation required 👉 Use Parkland formula 👉 ALWAYS calculate from time of burn 👉 "Burns clock starts at injury, not arrival"

question_text: A 21 year old man has been found unconscious in an alleyway with a respiratory rate of 5 breaths/minute and a pulse of 55 beats/minute. His pupils are constricted. What is SINGLE most appropriate management?
explanation: Why? This patient has classic opioid overdose: reduced consciousness, severe respiratory depression (RR 5), bradycardia, and pinpoint pupils (miosis). The immediate life-saving treatment is naloxone, an opioid antagonist. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Unconscious patient ✅ Respiratory depression (RR 5) ✅ Bradycardia (pulse 55) ✅ Constricted pupils (miosis) These are the classic triad of opioid toxicity. Why Naloxone Is Correct Competitive opioid receptor antagonist Rapidly reverses respiratory depression Restores consciousness Life-saving first-line treatment Can be given IV, IM, or intranasal Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Methadone Opioid agonist—would worsen overdose. C. Flumazenil Reverses benzodiazepines, not opioids. D. Thiamine Used in alcohol dependence (Wernicke’s), not acute overdose. E. Dextrose Used for hypoglycaemia, not indicated here. Key Exam Principle 👉 Opioid overdose = triad (coma + respiratory depression + miosis) 👉 Immediate treatment = naloxone 👉 "Pinpoint pupils + slow breathing = give naloxone"

question_text: A 6 month old boy has been brought A&E following an apnoeic episode at home. He is now completely well but his parents are very anxious as their family friend's child died of sudden infant death syndrome at a similar age. The parents would like to know how to perform CPR on a baby of his age. What is the SINGLE most recommended technique for cardiac compressions?

options.e: Index and middle fingertips of one hand

explanation: Why? In infant CPR (less than 1 year old), the recommended technique for chest compressions by a single rescuer is using two fingers (index and middle) placed on the lower half of the sternum. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Infant (6 months old) ✅ CPR technique being asked These indicate infant basic life support guidelines. Why Index and Middle Fingertips Is Correct Standard technique for single rescuer infant CPR Provides adequate depth and control Allows effective compressions without excessive force Positioned on lower half of sternum Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. All fingers of both hands Not a recognized CPR technique. B. All fingers of one hand Not recommended—poor control and incorrect positioning. C. Palm of one hand Used in older children/adults, not infants. D. Thumb of one hand Incorrect—thumb technique requires both thumbs encircling chest (two-rescuer method). Key Exam Principle 👉 Infant CPR (single rescuer) → 2 fingers (index + middle) 👉 Two rescuers → 2-thumb encircling technique 👉 "Baby CPR = two fingers"

question_text: A 78 year old woman presents to the Emergency Department with severe epigastric pain and vomiting for the past 2 days. The pain is referred to her right shoulder. Generalised rigidity of the abdomen is noted when examining. She denies chest pain. She has a temperature of 37.2°C, a respiratory rate of 22 breaths/minute and a pulse of 102 beats/minute. Her medical history is significant for rheumatoid arthritis. What is the SINGLE most appropriate initial investigation?
explanation: Why? This patient has features of a perforated peptic ulcer causing peritonitis. The most appropriate initial investigation is an erect chest X-ray to look for free air under the diaphragm (pneumoperitoneum). Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Severe epigastric pain ✅ Pain referred to shoulder (diaphragmatic irritation) ✅ Generalised abdominal rigidity (peritonitis) ✅ Elderly patient with rheumatoid arthritis (likely NSAID use → ulcer risk) These strongly suggest a perforated viscus, most commonly a perforated peptic ulcer. Why Erect Chest X-ray Is Correct Quick, bedside investigation Detects free air under diaphragm (hallmark of perforation) Guides urgent surgical management First-line imaging in suspected perforation Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Ultrasound abdomen Limited for detecting free intraperitoneal air. B. Pelvic X-ray Not relevant for abdominal pathology. C. Colonoscopy Contraindicated in suspected perforation. E. Upper GI endoscopy Contraindicated—risk of worsening perforation. Key Exam Principle 👉 Suspected perforation → erect chest X-ray first 👉 Look for air under diaphragm 👉 "Rigid abdomen + shoulder pain = think perforation → X-ray"

question_text: A 48 year old woman presents to the Emergency Department with concerns that she might be taking too much paracetamol. She reports that she has been taking paracetamol for the past five days due to persistent headaches. She mentions taking a total of 6 grams of paracetamol each day. A paracetamol concentration shows 16 µg/ml. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in managing this patient?

options.a: Discharge home with advice to cease paracetamol use and arrange follow-up in a week
options.b: Admit for observation without any specific treatment
options.c: Calculate the paracetamol concentration 4 hours post last dose and use the standard paracetamol overdose nomogram to guide treatment
options.e: Refer to a hepatologist for evaluation

explanation: Why? This is a case of repeated supratherapeutic ingestion (staggered overdose) of paracetamol. The patient has been taking 6 g daily for 5 days, which exceeds the safe maximum dose (4 g/day). In such cases, the standard paracetamol nomogram is NOT applicable, and treatment with N-acetylcysteine (NAC) should be started immediately. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Repeated high dosing (6 g/day for 5 days) ✅ Exceeds safe limit (>4 g/day) ✅ Staggered ingestion (not a single overdose) ✅ Detectable paracetamol level (16 µg/ml) These indicate risk of toxicity despite not appearing acutely unwell. Why NAC Is Correct Indicated in staggered or repeated supratherapeutic ingestion Prevents liver damage by replenishing glutathione Nomogram cannot be used in this scenario Early treatment reduces risk of acute liver failure Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Discharge home Unsafe—patient is at risk of hepatotoxicity. B. Observe only Delays definitive treatment. C. Use nomogram Only valid for single acute overdose with known timing. E. Refer to hepatologist Not first step—initial management is NAC. Key Exam Principle 👉 Staggered paracetamol overdose = treat with NAC regardless of level 👉 Nomogram ONLY for single acute ingestion 👉 "Repeated dosing → NAC immediately"

question_text: A 28 year old man presents to the Emergency Department with a history of recreational drug use. He exhibits symptoms of hyperthermia, with a body temperature of 39.6°C. His blood pressure is recorded at 172/90 mmHg, and he has a heart rate of 110 beats per minute. He appears agitated and is sweating profusely. His pupils are dilated. Which substance overdose is consistent with his clinical presentation?
explanation: Why? This patient shows features of a sympathomimetic toxidrome: hyperthermia, hypertension, tachycardia, agitation, sweating, and mydriasis (dilated pupils). Cocaine is a classic cause of this presentation. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Hyperthermia (39.6°C) ✅ Hypertension (172/90 mmHg) ✅ Tachycardia (110 bpm) ✅ Agitation and sweating ✅ Dilated pupils (mydriasis) These are hallmark signs of sympathetic overactivity. Why Cocaine Is Correct Powerful sympathomimetic → ↑ catecholamines Causes agitation, hyperthermia, tachycardia, hypertension Leads to mydriasis and diaphoresis Classic exam toxidrome Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. LSD Causes hallucinations but not marked autonomic instability. B. Heroin Causes CNS depression, respiratory depression, and pinpoint pupils (opposite picture). C. Ketamine Can cause dissociation but less pronounced hyperthermia and sympathetic excess. E. Cannabis Causes mild tachycardia and relaxation—not severe agitation or hyperthermia. Key Exam Principle 👉 Sympathomimetic toxidrome = cocaine/amphetamines 👉 Features: hyperthermia + hypertension + tachycardia + agitation + mydriasis 👉 "Hot, fast, sweaty, wide pupils = cocaine"

question_text: A 33 year old woman was painting her room when she developed a severe headache, vomited and fell off the stool. She feels well now and has a Glasgow Coma Scale of 15. On examination, there is a small bruise on her forehead. What is the SINGLE next appropriate investigation to identify the cause?
explanation: Why? This scenario strongly suggests carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning. The key clue is that she was painting in an enclosed environment, followed by headache, vomiting, and collapse. CO poisoning commonly presents with these nonspecific symptoms and must be confirmed by measuring carboxyhaemoglobin levels. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Indoor activity (painting → possible poor ventilation) ✅ Headache and vomiting ✅ Sudden collapse ✅ Now recovered with normal GCS These are classic early features of carbon monoxide exposure. Why Carboxyhaemoglobin Level Is Correct Confirms carbon monoxide poisoning CO binds haemoglobin → reduces oxygen delivery Levels correlate with severity Essential diagnostic test Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. CT head Would assess trauma but does not explain preceding symptoms. C. ECG May be useful but not diagnostic of cause. D. Full blood count Not helpful in this context. E. Echocardiography Not relevant for this presentation. Key Exam Principle 👉 Headache + vomiting + collapse in enclosed space = CO poisoning 👉 Diagnose with carboxyhaemoglobin level 👉 "Think CO before CT if environmental clue present"

question_text: A 62 year old woman is brought to the Emergency Department by her daughter due to confusion, agitation, and difficulty passing urine. Her family reports that she has been taking medication for chronic pain. On examination, she has dilated pupils, dry skin, and a heart rate of 110 beats per minute. Her bladder is palpable on abdominal examination. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her presentation?
explanation: Why? This patient has features of an anticholinergic toxidrome: confusion, agitation, tachycardia, dry skin, mydriasis (dilated pupils), and urinary retention. Amitriptyline, a tricyclic antidepressant, has strong anticholinergic effects and is commonly used for chronic pain. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Confusion and agitation ✅ Dilated pupils (mydriasis) ✅ Dry skin ✅ Tachycardia (110 bpm) ✅ Urinary retention (palpable bladder) ✅ Medication for chronic pain These are classic features of anticholinergic toxicity. Why Amitriptyline Is Correct Tricyclic antidepressant with strong anticholinergic effects Commonly used for neuropathic/chronic pain Causes central (confusion, agitation) and peripheral (dry skin, urinary retention, mydriasis) effects Classic toxidrome: "hot, dry, blind, mad, full" Why the Other Options Are Less Likely B. Carbamazepine Causes CNS depression, ataxia—not anticholinergic features. C. Gabapentin Causes sedation and dizziness, not anticholinergic toxicity. D. Metformin Associated with lactic acidosis, not these symptoms. E. Sertraline SSRI—may cause serotonin syndrome (hyperreflexia, clonus), not dry skin or urinary retention. Key Exam Principle 👉 Anticholinergic toxidrome = dry, hot, confused, urinary retention, mydriasis 👉 Common cause = tricyclic antidepressants (e.g., amitriptyline) 👉 "Hot, dry, blind, mad, full = anticholinergic"

question_text: A 31 year old man was involved in a road traffic accident and has severe pain at the right outer upper thigh and groin. There is clear deformity of the hip and shortening of the right leg. A femoral shaft fracture is suspected. His blood pressure is 100/70 mmHg. He has a heart rate of 90 beats/minute and a respiratory rate of 19 breaths/minute. He is saturating at 97% at room air. What is the SINGLE most appropriate next action?

options.a: Anteroposterior pelvic and lateral hip X-rays
options.d: Full blood count and cross match

explanation: Why? This patient has a suspected femoral shaft fracture, which can cause significant blood loss and severe pain. The most important immediate step is immobilisation using a Thomas' splint to reduce pain, prevent further bleeding, and stabilise the fracture. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ High-energy trauma (RTA) ✅ Severe thigh/groin pain ✅ Limb shortening and deformity ✅ Suspected femoral shaft fracture ✅ Haemodynamically stable but at risk of bleeding These indicate the need for urgent stabilisation. Why Thomas' Splint Is Correct Immobilises femur and reduces movement Decreases pain and muscle spasm Reduces blood loss (femur can bleed up to 1–1.5 L) Standard initial management in suspected femoral shaft fracture Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. X-rays Important but should follow initial stabilisation. B. IV fluids Not immediately required—patient is relatively stable. D. FBC and cross match Important but not the first step. E. MRI Not used acutely in trauma. Key Exam Principle 👉 Suspected femoral shaft fracture → immobilise first (Thomas' splint) 👉 Prevent bleeding and pain before imaging 👉 "Femur fracture = splint immediately"

question_text: A 19 year old woman is brought to the Emergency Department by a friend after taking an overdose of paracetamol 2 hours ago. She admits to ingesting 35 tablets of 500 mg paracetamol, following an argument with her partner. When should the paracetamol concentration be taken?
explanation: Why? Paracetamol levels should be measured at least 4 hours after ingestion, as this is when absorption is complete and levels can be accurately plotted on the Rumack-Matthew nomogram. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Known time of overdose (2 hours ago) ✅ Acute single ingestion These indicate use of the standard paracetamol nomogram. Why 4 Hours Is Correct Levels taken before 4 hours are unreliable Allows accurate risk assessment using nomogram Guides need for N-acetylcysteine (NAC) Standard practice in overdose management Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. After 8 hours Too late—delays treatment unnecessarily. B. Immediately Too early—levels not yet reliable. C. In 2 hours time Would be at 4 hours total, but the correct principle is to take at 4 hours post ingestion (not relative timing from now unless explicitly stated). D. In 30 minutes Far too early for accurate measurement. Key Exam Principle 👉 Paracetamol level = take at 4 hours post ingestion 👉 Use nomogram ONLY after 4 hours 👉 "Too early = unreliable, 4 hours = accurate"

question_text: A 48 year old man was being evaluated for hypertensive retinopathy in the eye clinic before he was referred to the Emergency Department for insidious and progressive onset of nausea, drowsiness and palpitations. Apart from hypertension, he had no other significant past medical history. An ECG taken revealed tall tented T waves, flattened P waves and widened QRS. Investigations showed the following: Sodium 142 mmol/L (135-145), Potassium 7.1 mmol/L (3.5-5), Blood glucose 5.2 mmol/L. IV calcium chloride was administered by the junior doctor on duty and senior assistance has been requested. What is the SINGLE most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?

options.a: IV Actrapid insulin 10 units with 50 ml of 50% dextrose
options.b: IV Actrapid insulin 10 units with 50 ml of 5% dextrose
options.c: IV Actrapid insulin 50 units with 50 ml of 50% dextrose
options.d: IV Actrapid insulin 50 units with 50 ml of 5% dextrose
options.e: IV Actrapid insulin 10 units with 50 ml of 0.9% sodium chloride

explanation: Why? This patient has severe hyperkalaemia (K⁺ 7.1 mmol/L) with ECG changes (tall tented T waves, flattened P waves, widened QRS). After stabilising the cardiac membrane with IV calcium, the next step is to shift potassium intracellularly using insulin with glucose. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Potassium 7.1 mmol/L (severe hyperkalaemia) ✅ ECG changes (tented T waves, widened QRS) ✅ Already given IV calcium (membrane stabilisation) These indicate life-threatening hyperkalaemia requiring urgent treatment. Why Insulin + 50% Dextrose Is Correct Insulin drives potassium into cells Dextrose prevents hypoglycaemia Rapidly reduces serum potassium levels Standard next step after calcium administration Typical regimen: 10 units IV insulin + 50 mL of 50% dextrose Why the Other Options Are Less Likely B. 5% dextrose Insufficient glucose concentration to prevent hypoglycaemia. C & D. 50 units insulin Excessive dose → high risk of severe hypoglycaemia. E. Insulin with saline No glucose → dangerous hypoglycaemia risk. Key Exam Principle 👉 Hyperkalaemia management sequence: 1. Stabilise heart → IV calcium 2. Shift K⁺ into cells → insulin + glucose 3. Remove K⁺ → diuretics/dialysis 👉 "Calcium protects, insulin shifts"

question_text: A 44 year old man with a history of alcohol dependency presents with confusion. He responds poorly to questions and is seen to be irritable. He is unsteady and has uncoordinated walking. His blood glucose is 3.5 mmol/L. He has no other relevant medical history. What is the SINGLE most appropriate immediate action?
explanation: Why? This patient has features of Wernicke’s encephalopathy (confusion, ataxia) in the setting of chronic alcohol use. The most important immediate step is intravenous thiamine, which must be given before glucose to prevent worsening of neurological damage. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Alcohol dependency ✅ Confusion ✅ Ataxia (unsteady, uncoordinated walking) ✅ Irritability These are classic features of Wernicke’s encephalopathy. Why Intravenous Thiamine Is Correct Treats thiamine deficiency Prevents progression to Korsakoff syndrome Must be given BEFORE glucose Life-saving and prevents irreversible brain damage Why the Other Options Are Less Likely B. 50% glucose bolus Giving glucose first can worsen Wernicke’s encephalopathy. C. 5% dextrose Same issue—must give thiamine first. D. Normal saline Supportive but does not treat cause. E. CT head Not priority—clinical diagnosis, treat immediately. Key Exam Principle 👉 Alcoholic + confusion/ataxia → think Wernicke’s 👉 ALWAYS give thiamine before glucose 👉 "No glucose before thiamine"

question_text: A 54 year old man attends the Emergency Department after consumption of several tablets. He is nauseous and complains of ringing in both ears. He has been vomiting several times since coming to the department. He has a diagnosis of bipolar disorder and has been using lithium for several years. He also takes aspirin for secondary prevention following a myocardial infarction a year ago. He takes levothyroxine for his hypothyroidism. A few days ago, he started on diazepam and paracetamol for back muscle spasm. What is the SINGLE most likely overdose of medication causing his symptoms?
explanation: Why? This patient has classic features of salicylate (aspirin) toxicity, particularly tinnitus (ringing in the ears), nausea, and vomiting. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Tinnitus (ringing in ears) — hallmark sign ✅ Nausea and repeated vomiting ✅ History of aspirin use These strongly indicate salicylate toxicity. Why Aspirin Is Correct Tinnitus is a classic early symptom of salicylate overdose Also causes nausea, vomiting, and metabolic disturbances Commonly tested exam association Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Paracetamol Early symptoms are often minimal; tinnitus is not typical. C. Levothyroxine Causes hyperthyroid symptoms (tachycardia, tremor), not tinnitus. D. Diazepam Causes CNS depression, not agitation or tinnitus. E. Lithium Causes tremor, confusion, and GI upset, but not tinnitus. Key Exam Principle 👉 Tinnitus = think salicylate toxicity 👉 Aspirin overdose → nausea + vomiting + ringing ears 👉 "Ringing ears = salicylates"

question_text: A 21 year old man attends the urgent care centre with shortness of breath and wheezing. He has been taking his salbutamol and salmeterol inhalers regularly for his asthma. Over the past 2 days, he had to increase his salbutamol inhaler frequency to reduce his wheezing. Auscultation of his chest reveals a widespread wheeze. He has a heart rate of 109 beats/minute, a respiratory rate of 24 breaths/minute, a temperature of 37.3°C and an oxygen saturation of 93%. He is able to finish a sentence in one breath. What is the SINGLE most appropriate test to be performed to determine the severity of his asthma exacerbation?

options.a: Peak expiratory flow rate using a peak flow meter

explanation: Why? The severity of an asthma exacerbation is best assessed using peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR). It provides a quick, bedside, objective measurement of airway obstruction and is used to classify severity and guide management. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Known asthma patient ✅ Increased use of reliever inhaler ✅ Wheeze, tachycardia, tachypnoea ✅ Able to complete sentences (not life-threatening) These indicate an asthma exacerbation requiring severity assessment. Why PEFR Is Correct Simple, rapid bedside test Measures airflow limitation Helps classify severity (mild/moderate/severe) Guides treatment decisions and monitoring Why the Other Options Are Less Likely B. Arterial blood gas Reserved for severe or life-threatening asthma. C. Spirometry Not used in acute exacerbations—requires patient cooperation and is time-consuming. D. Chest X-ray Not routine—only if complications suspected. E. ECG Not relevant for assessing asthma severity. Key Exam Principle 👉 Asthma exacerbation → assess severity with PEFR 👉 ABG only if severe/life-threatening 👉 "Asthma severity = peak flow"

question_text: A 4 year old girl is brought to the Emergency Department after pulling a kettle of boiling water onto herself. She has sustained a 3% total body surface area burn across her chest. The affected area is red, blistered, and very painful. She is distressed, crying, and unable to tolerate assessment due to pain. She is haemodynamically stable. She does not have an IV line. What is the most appropriate pain management?
explanation: Why? This child has severe acute pain from a partial-thickness burn and requires rapid, effective analgesia. Since there is no IV access and she cannot tolerate oral medication, intranasal diamorphine is the best option for fast and potent pain relief. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Severe pain (crying, distressed) ✅ Partial-thickness burn (very painful) ✅ No IV access ✅ Unable to tolerate assessment (needs rapid analgesia) These indicate need for strong, fast, non-invasive analgesia. Why Intranasal Diamorphine Is Correct Rapid onset of action Potent opioid analgesic No need for IV access Widely used in paediatric emergency care Improves cooperation for assessment Why the Other Options Are Less Likely B. IV morphine Effective but not possible without IV access. C. Rectal diclofenac Insufficient for severe pain and slower onset. D. Oral paracetamol Too weak and slow for this level of pain. E. Buccal midazolam Used for seizures/sedation—not analgesia. Key Exam Principle 👉 Severe paediatric pain + no IV access → intranasal opioid 👉 Burns = very painful → strong analgesia needed 👉 "No IV + severe pain = intranasal opioid"

question_text: A 32 year old man is brought to A&E by his friends after they found him unresponsive at a party. His friends report that he has been using cocaine throughout the night. On examination, the man is agitated, sweating profusely, and has a heart rate of 130 beats per minute. His blood pressure is 185/100 mmHg. Pupillary dilation is noted, and he has increased muscle tone. An ECG shows sinus tachycardia, and his oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. What is the most appropriate management?
explanation: Why? This patient has cocaine toxicity with a sympathomimetic toxidrome: agitation, tachycardia, hypertension, sweating, mydriasis, and increased muscle tone. The first-line treatment is benzodiazepines (e.g., lorazepam) to reduce central sympathetic outflow. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Cocaine use ✅ Agitation and sweating ✅ Severe hypertension (185/100 mmHg) ✅ Tachycardia (130 bpm) ✅ Dilated pupils and increased muscle tone These indicate sympathetic overdrive due to stimulant toxicity. Why Lorazepam Is Correct First-line treatment in cocaine toxicity Reduces agitation and CNS stimulation Lowers heart rate and blood pressure indirectly Prevents complications (e.g., seizures, arrhythmias) Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Labetalol Mixed alpha/beta blocker—may be used cautiously, but not first-line. C. Nitroprusside Controls BP but does not address underlying agitation. D. Phentolamine Alpha-blocker used in refractory cases—not first-line. E. Propranolol Contraindicated—causes unopposed alpha stimulation → worsens hypertension. Key Exam Principle 👉 Cocaine toxicity = benzodiazepines first 👉 Avoid pure beta blockers (unopposed alpha effect) 👉 "Cocaine → sedate first"

question_text: A 75 year old man has sudden-onset shortness of breath and pleuritic chest pain. He underwent a transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) three days ago for benign prostatic hyperplasia. On examination, he has a pulse of 110 beats per minute, respiratory rate of 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation of 94% on room air. His blood pressure is 130/80 mmHg. Chest auscultation reveals clear lung fields with no added sounds. What is the most appropriate investigation?
explanation: Why? This patient has a high clinical probability of pulmonary embolism (PE): recent surgery (TURP), acute onset pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, and dyspnoea with clear lungs. In high-risk patients, the most appropriate investigation is CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA). Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Recent surgery (3 days post-op → major risk factor) ✅ Sudden onset dyspnoea and pleuritic chest pain ✅ Tachycardia (110 bpm) ✅ Clear chest exam These strongly suggest pulmonary embolism. Why CTPA Is Correct Gold standard investigation for PE Directly visualises pulmonary arteries Indicated in moderate-to-high probability cases Provides rapid and definitive diagnosis Why the Other Options Are Less Likely B. Chest X-ray Often normal in PE—used to exclude other causes, not diagnostic. C. D-dimer Used only in low-risk patients—this patient is high risk. D. Lower limb ultrasound May detect DVT but does not confirm PE. E. V/Q scan Used if CTPA contraindicated (e.g., renal failure, contrast allergy). Key Exam Principle 👉 High suspicion of PE → go straight to CTPA 👉 D-dimer only for low-risk patients 👉 "Post-op + pleuritic pain = CTPA"

question_text: A 60 year old man presents to the Emergency Department complaining of feeling exhausted and unwell in general since earlier in the day. He also reports that over the past hour, he feels his heart racing which is extremely distressing. On further discussion, he notes that he was diagnosed with diabetes mellitus ten years ago and is on metformin. Ramipril was added on to his treatment plan five years ago due to high blood pressure. An urgent ABG was performed, and the report is available. pH 7.33 (7.35-7.45), pCO2 5.0 kPa (4.7-6.0), pO2 12 kPa (12-14), Sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145), Potassium 6.8 mmol/L (3.5-5.0). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?
explanation: Why? This patient has severe hyperkalaemia (K⁺ 6.8 mmol/L), which can cause life-threatening cardiac arrhythmias. The immediate next step is to assess for ECG changes to determine urgency and guide treatment. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Potassium 6.8 mmol/L (severe hyperkalaemia) ✅ Palpitations (possible arrhythmia) ✅ Mild acidosis (pH 7.33) These indicate high risk of cardiac instability. Why 12-lead ECG Is Correct Detects dangerous cardiac effects of hyperkalaemia Guides urgent treatment (e.g., calcium gluconate if changes present) Must be performed immediately in severe hyperkalaemia Why the Other Options Are Less Likely B. Chest X-ray Not relevant to hyperkalaemia. C. Renal function test Important but not as urgent as assessing cardiac risk. D. Venous blood gas Already have ABG—no added value. E. Serum ramipril concentration Not clinically useful or urgent. Key Exam Principle 👉 Hyperkalaemia → check ECG immediately 👉 ECG changes determine urgency of treatment 👉 "High potassium = monitor the heart first"

question_text: A 24 years old man is brought to the Emergency Department after sustaining burns in a house fire 2 hours ago. He has deep partial thickness burns over the anterior chest and abdomen and superficial burns to both upper limbs. His urine output is minimal since arrival. Which intravenous fluid is most appropriate for initial resuscitation?
explanation: Why? This patient has significant burns requiring fluid resuscitation. The fluid of choice in initial burn management is a crystalloid solution—specifically Hartmann’s solution (compound sodium lactate)—as recommended by the Parkland formula. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Significant burns (chest, abdomen, upper limbs) ✅ Early phase (2 hours post injury) ✅ Reduced urine output (sign of hypovolaemia) These indicate need for aggressive fluid resuscitation. Why Compound Sodium Lactate Is Correct Preferred fluid in burn resuscitation (Parkland formula) Restores intravascular volume effectively Contains electrolytes similar to plasma Reduces risk of hyperchloraemic acidosis compared to normal saline Why the Other Options Are Less Likely B. Dextrose 5% Not suitable for volume resuscitation—distributes quickly into cells. C. Gelatin-based colloid Not recommended in initial 24 hours of burns. D. Human albumin Used later, not in initial resuscitation phase. E. Sodium chloride 0.9% Can be used but less preferred due to risk of acidosis. Key Exam Principle 👉 Burns resuscitation → use Hartmann’s (compound sodium lactate) 👉 Follow Parkland formula 👉 "Burns = Hartmann’s first"

question_text: A 58 years old man attends the Emergency Department with sudden onset severe central chest pain that started one hour ago while he was lifting a heavy object. The pain radiates to his back. He has a history of hypertension and is prescribed amlodipine but admits poor adherence. Blood pressure is 168/92 mmHg in the right arm and 152/88 mmHg in the left arm. Heart rate is 96 beats per minute and regular. Oxygen saturations are 98% on air. What is the most appropriate next investigation?
explanation: Why? This patient has classic features of an aortic dissection: sudden severe chest pain radiating to the back and a difference in blood pressure between arms. The most appropriate investigation is a CT aorta (CT angiography) to confirm the diagnosis. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Sudden severe chest pain ✅ Radiation to the back ✅ History of hypertension ✅ Inter-arm blood pressure difference These are hallmark features of aortic dissection. Why CT Aorta Is Correct Gold standard initial imaging in stable patients Rapidly confirms diagnosis Defines extent of dissection Guides urgent management (surgical vs medical) Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Chest X-ray May show widened mediastinum but not diagnostic. C. D-dimer Not routinely used in suspected dissection. D. Coronary angiogram Used for myocardial infarction, not dissection. E. Transthoracic echocardiography Limited sensitivity—used if CT unavailable or patient unstable. Key Exam Principle 👉 Tearing chest pain radiating to back + BP difference = aortic dissection 👉 Stable patient → CT aorta 👉 "Back pain + unequal BP = scan the aorta"

question_text: A 3 years old boy is brought to the Emergency Department after being found unconscious at his grandfather's house. Earlier in the day he was seen playing near his grandfather's bedside table where several medications were kept. On arrival, the child is unresponsive. Respiratory rate is 6 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 88% on room air. Examination reveals shallow breathing and markedly constricted pupils. What is the most appropriate management?
explanation: Why? This child has classic opioid toxicity: reduced consciousness, severe respiratory depression (RR 6), and pinpoint pupils (miosis). The most appropriate immediate treatment is IV naloxone, an opioid antagonist. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Unconscious child ✅ Respiratory depression (RR 6) ✅ Low oxygen saturation (88%) ✅ Constricted pupils (miosis) ✅ Access to medications (likely ingestion) These are hallmark features of opioid overdose. Why IV Naloxone Is Correct Reverses opioid effects rapidly Restores respiratory drive Life-saving in opioid toxicity Can be repeated if needed Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Activated charcoal Not appropriate in an unconscious patient without airway protection. B. Flumazenil Reverses benzodiazepines, not opioids. D. Sodium bicarbonate Used for TCA toxicity or metabolic acidosis—not indicated here. E. Supportive oxygen therapy Important but does not reverse the underlying cause—naloxone is definitive. Key Exam Principle 👉 Opioid overdose = coma + respiratory depression + miosis 👉 Immediate treatment = naloxone 👉 "Pinpoint pupils + slow breathing = naloxone NOW"

question_text: A 28 years old man is brought to the Emergency Department by friends because of agitation and restlessness. He is sweating and repeatedly asks for tissues because of a persistent runny nose. His friends report that he occasionally uses recreational drugs. On examination, he appears anxious and uncomfortable. There is marked rhinorrhoea and lacrimation. His pupils are dilated. He repeatedly complains of abdominal cramps. Which substance is most likely responsible for this presentation?
explanation: Why? This patient is showing features of opioid withdrawal, not intoxication. The key features include rhinorrhoea, lacrimation, abdominal cramps, agitation, sweating, and dilated pupils—all classic for heroin withdrawal. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Rhinorrhoea (runny nose) ✅ Lacrimation (tearing) ✅ Abdominal cramps ✅ Agitation and restlessness ✅ Dilated pupils (mydriasis) These are hallmark signs of opioid withdrawal. Why Heroin Is Correct Opioid withdrawal causes: Rhinorrhoea + lacrimation Abdominal cramps and diarrhoea Sweating and agitation Dilated pupils (opposite of overdose) Very characteristic exam pattern Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Amphetamine Causes agitation and sweating but not rhinorrhoea or abdominal cramps. B. Cannabis Causes relaxation and mild tachycardia—not this picture. C. Cocaine Causes sympathomimetic features but not lacrimation or abdominal cramps. E. Ketamine Causes dissociation and hallucinations—not withdrawal symptoms. Key Exam Principle 👉 Opioid withdrawal = runny nose + tearing + cramps + agitation + dilated pupils 👉 Opposite of opioid overdose (which causes miosis) 👉 "Runny nose + cramps = opioid withdrawal"

question_text: A 79 years old man is brought to the Emergency Department by his carer because of increasing forgetfulness over the past few weeks. The man states that he feels well and is unsure why he has been brought to hospital. During the consultation he provides inconsistent answers about recent events. Examination shows no focal neurological deficit. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
explanation: Why? In any patient presenting with cognitive impairment or confusion, especially when the history is unreliable, the most important initial step is to obtain a collateral history from a reliable informant (e.g., carer or family member). Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Elderly patient ✅ Progressive forgetfulness over weeks ✅ Inconsistent answers (unreliable history) ✅ No focal neurological deficit These suggest possible cognitive impairment (e.g., dementia or delirium), requiring further clarification. Why Collateral History Is Correct Provides accurate timeline and progression Helps differentiate delirium vs dementia Essential for diagnosis and management planning First step before investigations Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Full blood count May be useful later but not first priority. B. Palliative care Not appropriate without diagnosis. C. Psychiatry referral Premature without assessment. E. Urgent CT head Not indicated without red flags (e.g., focal deficits, acute deterioration). Key Exam Principle 👉 Confused patient = always get collateral history first 👉 Especially if history is unreliable 👉 "No history from patient? Get it from someone else"

question_text: A 62 years old man attends the Emergency Department with a three day history of worsening breathlessness and productive cough. He reports coughing up thick green sputum and feeling increasingly fatigued. On examination he appears mildly distressed with respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 88% on air. Chest auscultation reveals widespread polyphonic wheeze. Which investigation should be performed initially to assess this man's respiratory status?
explanation: Why? This patient is hypoxic (SpO₂ 88%) with signs of respiratory distress and likely an acute exacerbation of COPD or severe lower respiratory pathology. The most appropriate initial investigation is an arterial blood gas (ABG) to assess oxygenation, ventilation (CO₂), and acid-base status. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Low oxygen saturation (88%) ✅ Tachypnoea (RR 26) ✅ Respiratory distress ✅ Productive cough with green sputum These indicate significant respiratory compromise. Why ABG Is Correct Assesses severity of hypoxia Detects hypercapnia (CO₂ retention) Identifies respiratory acidosis Guides oxygen therapy and need for ventilation Why the Other Options Are Less Likely B. D-dimer Used for suspected PE—not primary concern here. C. Peak flow Useful in asthma but less helpful in acutely unwell hypoxic patients. D. Spirometry Not used in acute setting—requires stable patient. E. Sputum culture Useful later for identifying infection, not immediate severity assessment. Key Exam Principle 👉 Hypoxia or respiratory distress → do ABG first 👉 Determines severity and guides management 👉 "Low O₂ = check ABG"

question_text: A 32 year old male presents to Accident & Emergency (A&E) following a traumatic injury. He had gotten into a fight outside a pub and sustained a stab wound to his right inguinal area. He has no past medical history of note and is on no chronic medication. After stabilising the patient, a lower limb neurological examination was carried out. It revealed 4/5 power during extension of the right knee. The exam was also significant for a loss of sensation along the medial side of his right thigh and the anteromedial side of his right calf. What is the SINGLE most likely nerve that is injured in this patient?
explanation: Why? This patient has features of femoral nerve injury. The femoral nerve supplies the quadriceps (knee extension) and provides sensation to the anterior thigh and medial leg (via the saphenous nerve). Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Injury in inguinal region (femoral nerve location) ✅ Weak knee extension (quadriceps weakness) ✅ Sensory loss: - Medial thigh - Anteromedial calf (saphenous nerve distribution) These are classic for femoral nerve damage. Why Femoral Nerve Is Correct Motor: knee extension (quadriceps) Sensory: anterior thigh + medial leg (via saphenous nerve) Runs through inguinal region → vulnerable in this injury Why the Other Options Are Less Likely B. Obturator nerve Affects thigh adduction, not knee extension or medial leg sensation. C. Popliteal nerve Not a standard anatomical nerve (likely refers to tibial/peroneal branches). D. Sciatic nerve Affects posterior thigh and most of leg/foot—not isolated medial sensory loss. E. Superficial peroneal nerve Supplies lateral leg and dorsum of foot—not medial leg or thigh. Key Exam Principle 👉 Femoral nerve = knee extension + medial leg sensation 👉 Injury at inguinal region → think femoral nerve 👉 "Medial leg + weak knee extension = femoral nerve"

question_text: A 32 year old type 2 diabetes woman has recently been having some difficulty with buttoning up her shirt along with paraesthesias and numbness in her right hand. She works a desk job at a corporate office. On examination, there is a loss of pinprick sensation along the lateral three digits and the lateral half of the ring finger. Her 5th digit on the right hand has normal sensation. She has difficulty touching the right little finger with her right thumb. Her right hand seems less bulky than the left one. Which anatomical structure is most likely to be affected?
explanation: Why? This patient has classic features of median nerve compression/injury, most likely carpal tunnel syndrome. The sensory loss affects the lateral three and a half digits, while the little finger is spared. She also has thenar muscle weakness and wasting, shown by difficulty opposing the thumb and reduced bulk of the hand. These findings are characteristic of median nerve involvement. :contentReference[oaicite:0]{index=0} Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Paraesthesias and numbness in the lateral 3½ digits ✅ Normal sensation in the 5th digit ✅ Difficulty with fine hand tasks like buttoning clothes ✅ Difficulty touching thumb to little finger (impaired opposition) ✅ Hand appears less bulky (thenar wasting) ✅ Desk job + diabetes are risk factors for carpal tunnel syndrome. :contentReference[oaicite:1]{index=1} Why Median Nerve Is Correct The median nerve supplies sensation to the palmar surface of the lateral three and a half digits. It also supplies the thenar muscles responsible for thumb opposition. Compression of the median nerve can cause numbness, tingling, clumsiness, weakness of thumb opposition, and thenar wasting. :contentReference[oaicite:2]{index=2} Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Radial nerve Radial nerve injury causes weakness of wrist and finger extension with sensory loss over the dorsum of the hand, not the lateral 3½ digits. :contentReference[oaicite:3]{index=3} B. Axillary nerve Axillary nerve affects the shoulder, especially deltoid function and sensation over the regimental badge area, not the hand. C. Ulnar nerve Would affect the little finger and medial half of the ring finger, which are spared here. E. Suprascapular nerve Supplies supraspinatus and infraspinatus muscles, not hand sensation or thumb opposition. Key Exam Principle 👉 Sensory loss in lateral 3½ digits + thenar wasting + weak thumb opposition = median nerve lesion 👉 5th digit spared = not ulnar nerve 👉 "Buttoning difficulty + thenar wasting = median nerve"

question_text: A surgeon is performing a laparoscopic cholecystectomy. What anatomical structure(s) is first pierced during insertion of a port at the midway point between the anterior midline and mid-axillary line?

options.c: External oblique aponeurosis and internal oblique muscle

explanation: Why? The port is being inserted in the lateral abdominal wall (between the midline and mid-axillary line). The first muscle layer encountered in this region is the external oblique aponeurosis, followed by the internal oblique muscle. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Location: midway between anterior midline and mid-axillary line (lateral abdominal wall) This excludes midline structures like linea alba and rectus abdominis. Why External Oblique Aponeurosis and Internal Oblique Muscle Is Correct Layers of the lateral abdominal wall (superficial → deep): Skin → subcutaneous tissue → external oblique → internal oblique → transversus abdominis → peritoneum Thus, the first structure pierced is the external oblique aponeurosis, followed by the internal oblique muscle. Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Linea alba Midline structure—not encountered laterally. B. External thoracic muscles Located in the chest, not abdomen. D. Transversus abdominis Deeper layer—encountered after external and internal oblique. E. Rectus abdominis Located near midline—not at this lateral point. Key Exam Principle 👉 Lateral abdominal wall layers: external oblique → internal oblique → transversus abdominis 👉 First pierced laterally = external oblique 👉 "Lateral entry = oblique muscles first"

question_text: A 60 year old man screwing his cupboard to the wall when he suddenly felt a rupture at the cubital fossa resulting in a swollen elbow with weakness on flexion and supination. A lump in the distal arm is seen. What is the SINGLE most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Why? This patient has a distal biceps tendon rupture, which presents with sudden pain in the cubital fossa, weakness in elbow flexion and supination, and a visible bulge ("Popeye deformity") in the arm. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Sudden rupture sensation during activity ✅ Pain and swelling at cubital fossa ✅ Weakness in flexion and supination ✅ Visible lump in distal arm (muscle retraction) These are classic features of biceps tendon rupture. Why Biceps Tendon Rupture Is Correct Biceps is responsible for: Elbow flexion Forearm supination Rupture leads to weakness in both Muscle retracts → visible lump ("Popeye sign") Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Hand flexor tendon rupture Affects finger flexion, not elbow or supination. B. De Quervain's disease Causes wrist pain near thumb—not elbow symptoms. D. Tennis elbow Lateral epicondylitis—pain with wrist extension, no rupture or lump. E. Golfer's elbow Medial epicondylitis—pain with wrist flexion, no rupture or deformity. Key Exam Principle 👉 Sudden pain + weakness in flexion/supination + bulge = biceps rupture 👉 "Popeye deformity = biceps tendon rupture"

question_text: A 33 year old man had an ankle ligament reconstruction following an ankle injury and ankle instability. He was put in a below-knee cast which extends to the top of the foot for a few weeks. On removing the cast, he was unable to dorsiflex his foot for a few days. What is the SINGLE most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Why? This patient has foot drop (inability to dorsiflex), which is most commonly caused by injury to the common peroneal nerve. This nerve is particularly vulnerable to compression around the fibular neck, especially with casts or prolonged immobilisation. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Below-knee cast (risk of nerve compression) ✅ Inability to dorsiflex (foot drop) ✅ Onset after cast removal These are classic for common peroneal nerve palsy. Why Common Peroneal Nerve Injury Is Correct Supplies muscles responsible for dorsiflexion (via deep peroneal nerve) Superficial location at fibular neck → easily compressed Common complication of casts and immobilisation Leads to foot drop Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Sural nerve injury Sensory nerve only—does not affect dorsiflexion. C. Sciatic nerve injury Would cause more extensive deficits (hamstrings + entire leg below knee). D. Deep venous thrombosis Causes swelling and pain, not motor weakness. E. Achilles tendon rupture Affects plantarflexion (not dorsiflexion). Key Exam Principle 👉 Foot drop = common peroneal nerve injury 👉 Think compression at fibular neck (casts, immobilisation) 👉 "No dorsiflexion = peroneal nerve"

question_text: A 48 year old man with a known posterior gastric ulcer presents with excruciating pain which subsides after analgesia. 8 days later, he becomes unwell and has a temperature of 38.5°C. A collection in the peritoneum is suspected. Where is the SINGLE most likely location of the collection?
explanation: Why? A posterior gastric ulcer typically perforates into the lesser sac (omental bursa), which lies posterior to the stomach. This can lead to a localized collection or abscess in that space. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Posterior gastric ulcer ✅ Initial severe pain (suggesting perforation) ✅ Later fever (suggesting abscess formation) These indicate a contained perforation with collection formation. Why Lesser Sac Is Correct Located behind the stomach Posterior gastric ulcers perforate directly into this space Common site for localized collections following posterior perforation Why the Other Options Are Less Likely B. Inferior diaphragm More associated with subphrenic abscesses, not specifically posterior gastric perforation. C. Paracolic gutter Allows fluid spread but not the primary site of collection here. D. Pouch of Douglas Dependent pelvic space—fluid may track here but not initial site. E. Greater sac More involved in anterior perforations causing generalized peritonitis. Key Exam Principle 👉 Posterior gastric ulcer → perforates into lesser sac 👉 Anterior ulcer → free perforation into greater sac 👉 "Posterior stomach = lesser sac"

question_text: A 32 year old man has had pain on his neck which radiates down to his left shoulder and down his left middle finger. He has decreased sensation down his index and middle fingers on his left hand. On examination, he has reduced tricep reflexes on his left arm. He has difficulty straightening his left elbow. Which of the following nerve roots is likely affected?
explanation: Why? This patient has features of a C7 radiculopathy. The pain radiating to the middle finger, reduced triceps reflex, sensory changes in the index and middle fingers, and weakness of elbow extension all point to C7 nerve root involvement. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Neck pain radiating down the arm ✅ Pain radiates to the middle finger ✅ Reduced sensation in index and middle fingers ✅ Reduced triceps reflex ✅ Difficulty straightening the elbow (triceps weakness) These are classic findings of C7 nerve root compression. Why C7 Is Correct C7 dermatome includes the middle finger C7 myotome contributes to elbow extension (triceps) C7 reflex = triceps reflex Compression commonly causes neck pain radiating down the arm into the middle finger Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. C5 Would affect shoulder abduction and biceps area, not middle finger or triceps reflex. B. C6 Typically affects the thumb and index finger, with reduced biceps or brachioradialis reflex. D. C8 n Usually affects ring and little fingers, with finger flexion weakness rather than triceps weakness. E. T1 Primarily affects intrinsic hand muscles, not triceps reflex or middle finger pain. Key Exam Principle 👉 C7 radiculopathy = middle finger pain/numbness + weak elbow extension + reduced triceps reflex 👉 "Middle finger + triceps = C7"

question_text: A 25 year old rugby player presents to the Emergency Department following a direct blow to the shoulder during a match. He reports pain and a decreased range of motion in the affected shoulder. On examination, there is notable swelling and tenderness over the shoulder joint. Neurological examination reveals reduced sensation over the deltoid muscle area and weakness in arm abduction. Radiographs of the shoulder do not show any fractures. The clinical findings suggest a shoulder dislocation with associated nerve injury. Which nerve is most likely involved in this patient's presentation?
explanation: Why? This patient has signs of an axillary nerve injury, which is commonly associated with anterior shoulder dislocation. The axillary nerve wraps around the surgical neck of the humerus and is vulnerable during shoulder trauma. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Shoulder trauma (direct blow during rugby) ✅ Reduced sensation over the deltoid area ("regimental badge" area) ✅ Weakness in arm abduction ✅ No fracture seen → suggests soft tissue injury (e.g., dislocation with nerve injury) These findings are classic for axillary nerve damage. Why Axillary Nerve Is Correct Axillary nerve supplies the deltoid muscle → responsible for arm abduction (especially from 15° to 90°) Provides sensation over the lateral shoulder (regimental badge area) Commonly injured in shoulder dislocations and surgical neck fractures Why the Other Options Are Less Likely B. Median Affects forearm flexors and hand sensation (lateral palm), not shoulder abduction or deltoid sensation. C. Ulnar Affects intrinsic hand muscles and sensation over the little finger, not the shoulder. D. Radial Primarily affects wrist and finger extension (wrist drop), with sensation over the posterior arm/forearm—not isolated deltoid area. E. Musculocutaneous Supplies biceps (elbow flexion) and sensation to the lateral forearm, not deltoid or shoulder abduction. Key Exam Principle 👉 Shoulder dislocation + deltoid weakness + loss of sensation over lateral shoulder = Axillary nerve injury 👉 "Deltoid badge area + abduction problem = Axillary nerve"

question_text: A 46 year old man is being treated for a pleural effusion. A chest drain has been sited just below the 4th rib, anterior to the mid-axillary line on his right side. What SINGLE structure is at particular risk of injury?
explanation: Why? The intercostal neurovascular bundle (vein, artery, nerve) runs along the inferior border of each rib. Placing a chest drain just below a rib puts the intercostal artery at high risk of injury. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Chest drain inserted just below the 4th rib ✅ Location: anterior to mid-axillary line (typical chest drain site) ✅ Knowledge of intercostal neurovascular anatomy These point to risk of damaging structures running along the inferior rib margin. Why Intercostal Artery Is Correct The intercostal artery runs in the costal groove on the inferior border of the rib Chest drains should be inserted just above the rib to avoid this bundle Incorrect placement below the rib risks lacerating the artery → bleeding Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Azygos vein Located in the posterior mediastinum, not in the lateral chest wall. B. Diaphragm Lower down (around 5th–6th rib level and below), not typically at risk at 4th rib insertion. D. Internal thoracic artery Runs near the sternum, not in the mid-axillary region. E. Liver On the right side but lies inferiorly; risk is higher with lower intercostal insertions (below 5th rib). Key Exam Principle 👉 Intercostal neurovascular bundle lies along the inferior border of the rib 👉 Always insert chest drains just above the rib to avoid the intercostal artery 👉 "Below the rib = risk of bleeding (intercostal artery)"

question_text: A 73 year old woman with rheumatoid arthritis is unable to extend the fingers of her right hand at the metacarpophalangeal joint and interphalangeal joints following a fall. What is the SINGLE most likely tendon to have been damaged?
explanation: Why? This patient has loss of extension at both the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) and interphalangeal (IP) joints of the fingers, which is the primary function of the extensor digitorum tendon. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Inability to extend fingers ✅ Affects both MCP and IP joints ✅ Multiple fingers involved (not isolated) ✅ Rheumatoid arthritis (predisposes to tendon rupture) These strongly indicate damage to the main extensor tendon of the fingers. Why Extensor Digitorum Is Correct Extensor digitorum is the primary extensor of digits 2–5 Extends MCP joints directly and contributes to IP joint extension via extensor expansion Commonly ruptured in rheumatoid arthritis due to chronic synovial inflammation ("attrition rupture") Damage results in inability to extend multiple fingers Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Extensor carpi radialis Acts on the wrist (extension and abduction), not finger extension. B. Extensor carpi ulnaris Also acts on the wrist, not the fingers. D. Extensor indicis Extends only the index finger, not all fingers. E. Flexor digitorum profundus Responsible for finger flexion (especially DIP joints), not extension. Key Exam Principle 👉 Loss of extension of multiple fingers at MCP and IP joints = Extensor digitorum injury 👉 Rheumatoid arthritis commonly causes extensor tendon rupture in the hand 👉 "Can't extend fingers → think extensor digitorum"

question_text: A 21 year old woman complains of decreased taste sensation and decreased salivation. These symptoms began 24 hours after undergoing a right tympanoplasty for a chronic perforation of her tympanic membrane. Which of the following nerves is most likely to have been injured during the procedure?
explanation: Why? This patient’s symptoms are due to injury of the chorda tympani nerve, a branch of the facial nerve (CN VII), which runs through the middle ear and is at risk during tympanoplasty. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Recent tympanoplasty (middle ear surgery) ✅ Decreased taste sensation ✅ Decreased salivation These symptoms point to involvement of a nerve responsible for taste and salivary function in the middle ear. Why Facial Nerve Is Correct The chorda tympani (branch of facial nerve) passes through the middle ear Carries taste from the anterior 2/3 of the tongue Provides parasympathetic supply to submandibular and sublingual glands → salivation Frequently at risk during middle ear procedures (e.g., tympanoplasty) Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Hypoglossal nerve Controls tongue movement, not taste or salivation. B. Vagus nerve Supplies taste to a small area of the epiglottis and has no major role in salivation. D. Trigeminal nerve Provides general sensation to the face and anterior tongue (not taste) and does not control salivation directly. E. Glossopharyngeal nerve Supplies taste to the posterior 1/3 of the tongue and parotid gland, not typically affected in middle ear surgery. Key Exam Principle 👉 Middle ear surgery + loss of taste (anterior 2/3) + reduced salivation = Chorda tympani injury 👉 Chorda tympani is a branch of the facial nerve (CN VII) 👉 "Middle ear → think facial nerve (chorda tympani)"

question_text: A 75 year old man presents to the GP surgery complaining of frequent pain in the calf muscle of his left leg. He reports that the pain begins after he takes a few steps and worsens as he continues walking. His symptom started approximately two months ago and has worsened since he first noticed it; as of present, he can barely walk 50 meters without having to rest. He has a history of diabetes mellitus; however, he is not compliant with his medication. Additionally, he is a heavy smoker with a history of 40 pack-years. On examination, he does not have palpable popliteal or pedal pulses in the left leg. He has a palpable femoral pulse. Which of the following is the most likely site of arterial obstruction?
explanation: Why? This patient has intermittent claudication affecting the calf, which is most commonly due to femoropopliteal arterial disease. The presence of a palpable femoral pulse with absent popliteal and distal pulses localizes the obstruction to the femoropopliteal segment. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Calf pain on walking (intermittent claudication) ✅ Severe limitation (can only walk ~50 meters) ✅ Risk factors: diabetes + heavy smoking ✅ Femoral pulse present ✅ Popliteal and pedal pulses absent These findings help localize the level of arterial obstruction. Why Femoropopliteal Artery Is Correct Calf claudication classically indicates femoropopliteal disease Femoral pulse present → obstruction is distal to femoral artery Absent popliteal pulse → lesion is proximal to or at popliteal artery This localizes disease to the femoropopliteal segment Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Internal iliac artery Would cause buttock or hip claudication, not isolated calf pain. B. External iliac artery Would reduce femoral pulse (but femoral pulse is present here). C. Anterior tibial artery Distal vessel disease would still usually preserve popliteal pulse. D. Dorsalis pedis artery Very distal; would not explain absent popliteal pulse. Key Exam Principle 👉 Claudication site = level of arterial disease 👉 Calf pain = femoropopliteal disease 👉 "Femoral pulse present + popliteal absent = femoropopliteal obstruction"

question_text: A 45 year old man with a history of schizophrenia presents with a three-day history of stiffness in his neck, tremor in his hands, and a shuffling gait. He recently had an increase in his risperidone dose from 4 mg to 8 mg daily. On examination, he appears rigid with reduced arm swing when walking. His mental state examination reveals no acute psychotic symptoms. These symptoms started shortly after the dosage adjustment. Which part of the brain is most likely affected in this case?
explanation: Why? This patient has drug-induced parkinsonism, an extrapyramidal side effect caused by dopamine D2 receptor blockade after an increase in risperidone dose. The extrapyramidal system primarily involves the basal ganglia. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Recent increase in risperidone dose ✅ Neck stiffness and rigidity ✅ Tremor in the hands ✅ Shuffling gait ✅ Reduced arm swing ✅ No acute psychotic symptoms These are classic parkinsonian features developing after antipsychotic dose escalation. Why Basal Ganglia Is Correct Antipsychotics block dopamine receptors in the nigrostriatal pathway This disrupts basal ganglia motor control circuits The result is extrapyramidal symptoms such as rigidity, tremor, bradykinesia, and shuffling gait Drug-induced parkinsonism is therefore a disorder of basal ganglia function Why the Other Options Are Less Likely B. Brainstem Brainstem lesions may affect consciousness, cranial nerves, or vital functions, not typically isolated antipsychotic-induced parkinsonism. C. Cerebellum Cerebellar lesions cause ataxia, intention tremor, dysmetria, and poor coordination rather than rigidity and shuffling gait. D. Corpus callosum Involved in communication between the cerebral hemispheres, not extrapyramidal motor control. E. Substantia nigra This is involved in dopamine production and is part of the nigrostriatal system, but the broader functional disturbance producing these extrapyramidal symptoms is classically localized to the basal ganglia. Key Exam Principle 👉 Antipsychotic-induced rigidity, tremor, and shuffling gait = drug-induced parkinsonism 👉 Extrapyramidal symptoms are due to dopamine blockade in the basal ganglia 👉 "Risperidone + parkinsonian features = basal ganglia involvement"

question_text: A 54 year old man undergoes a radical neck dissection within the anterior triangle of the neck. The surgery is successful, and the patient is recovering as expected. A few days after the procedure, the attending surgeon notes a palpable crepitation at the surgical site, consistent with entrapped air. Upon physical examination, the crepitus is localised, and no signs of infection are observed. What is the name of the layer where the air has likely been entrapped?
explanation: Why? This patient has subcutaneous emphysema, which presents as palpable crepitus due to air trapped beneath the skin. This air is located in the subcutaneous tissue (hypodermis). Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Recent neck surgery (risk of air entry into tissues) ✅ Palpable crepitation (classic for subcutaneous emphysema) ✅ Localised swelling with no infection signs These features point to air trapped under the skin rather than deeper structures. Why Subcutaneous Layer Is Correct Subcutaneous tissue (hypodermis) contains loose connective tissue that allows air to accumulate and spread Air in this layer produces the characteristic "crackling" sensation on palpation (crepitus) Common after surgery, trauma, or air leaks from respiratory structures Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Stratum corneum Outermost layer of the epidermis, too superficial and compact to trap air. B. Stratum basale Deepest epidermal layer; does not accommodate air pockets. D. Muscular layer Air is not typically trapped within muscle; crepitus is not characteristic here. E. Dermis Dense connective tissue layer; air accumulation here is uncommon compared to the subcutaneous layer. Key Exam Principle 👉 Crepitus after surgery = subcutaneous emphysema 👉 Air collects in loose connective tissue → subcutaneous layer 👉 "Crackling under skin = subcutaneous tissue"

question_text: A 28 year old man presents to the clinic complaining of weakness in his right hand and difficulty in extending his wrist following a minor fall in which he injured his right leg. He has been using crutches for the past three weeks to assist with mobility. On examination, he has a wrist drop and decreased sensation on the back of his forearm. He has decreased sensation at the dorsolateral aspect of the hand, including the thumb, the index finger, and the dorsal aspect of the middle finger. Which nerve is most likely affected in this patient?
explanation: Why? This patient has a radial nerve palsy, most likely due to compression from prolonged crutch use. This is classically called crutch palsy. The combination of wrist drop and sensory loss over the posterior forearm and dorsolateral hand strongly points to radial nerve injury. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Recent prolonged crutch use ✅ Wrist drop ✅ Difficulty extending the wrist ✅ Reduced sensation on the back of the forearm ✅ Sensory loss over dorsolateral hand, including thumb, index finger, and dorsal middle finger These are classic findings of radial nerve compression. Why Radial Nerve Is Correct Radial nerve innervates the wrist and finger extensors → injury causes wrist drop Provides sensation to the posterior forearm Provides cutaneous sensation to the dorsolateral hand Can be compressed in the axilla by improper crutch use (crutch palsy) Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Median nerve Would cause thenar weakness, loss of thumb opposition, and sensory symptoms over the palmar lateral 3½ fingers, not wrist drop. B. C7 nerve root Can cause triceps weakness and sensory symptoms into the middle finger, but does not classically cause this pattern of posterior forearm sensory loss after crutch use. C.
