Ulnar nerve Would affect the little finger and medial half of the ring finger, with intrinsic hand muscle weakness, not wrist drop. D. Axillary nerve Would cause deltoid weakness and sensory loss over the lateral shoulder, not wrist drop or dorsolateral hand sensory loss. Key Exam Principle 👉 Wrist drop = radial nerve injury until proven otherwise 👉 Crutch use can compress the radial nerve in the axilla 👉 "Crutches + wrist drop = radial nerve palsy"

question_text: A 43 year old man presents with lower back pain radiating down the lateral aspect of his right leg into the dorsum of the foot. He reports difficulty in walking upstairs and finds it hard to lift his right big toe. On examination, there is weakness of dorsiflexion of the big toe and reduced sensation over the dorsum of the foot. The ankle reflex is preserved. What is the most likely affected nerve root?
explanation: Why? This patient has features of an L5 radiculopathy. The hallmark findings include pain radiating to the dorsum of the foot, weakness of big toe dorsiflexion, and preserved ankle reflex. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Pain radiating down lateral leg to dorsum of foot ✅ Weakness of big toe dorsiflexion ✅ Difficulty walking upstairs (foot dorsiflexion weakness) ✅ Reduced sensation over dorsum of foot ✅ Ankle reflex preserved These are classic features of L5 nerve root compression. Why L5 Is Correct L5 dermatome includes the dorsum of the foot and great toe L5 myotome controls dorsiflexion of the big toe (extensor hallucis longus) Reflexes are usually normal (no specific deep tendon reflex for L5) Compression commonly causes radicular pain down the lateral leg to the foot Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. L3 Would affect the anterior thigh, not the dorsum of the foot. B. L4 Associated with knee extension weakness and reduced knee jerk reflex, with pain to the medial leg. D. S1 Would cause weakness in plantarflexion and reduced ankle reflex, with sensory loss over the lateral foot. E. S2 Less commonly involved in isolated radiculopathy; affects posterior thigh and leg rather than dorsum of foot. Key Exam Principle 👉 L5 radiculopathy = big toe dorsiflexion weakness + dorsum foot sensory loss + normal ankle reflex 👉 "Big toe up = L5"

question_text: A 33 year old man undergoes fasciotomy and internal fixation for a proximal tibial fracture following a road traffic accident. Postoperatively, he is unable to dorsiflex the foot or extend the great toe. Sensory loss is noted over the dorsum of the foot, particularly between the first and second toes. Ankle reflexes are preserved. Which nerve root is most likely affected?
explanation: Why? This patient has classic features of L5 nerve root involvement. The key findings are weakness of dorsiflexion and great toe extension, sensory loss in the first web space, and preserved ankle reflex. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Inability to dorsiflex the foot (foot drop) ✅ Inability to extend the great toe ✅ Sensory loss between first and second toes (first web space) ✅ Ankle reflex preserved These findings strongly localize to the L5 nerve root. Why L5 Is Correct L5 myotome controls dorsiflexion (tibialis anterior) and great toe extension (extensor hallucis longus) L5 dermatome includes the dorsum of the foot and especially the first web space No specific reflex is associated with L5 → ankle reflex remains normal Commonly affected in trauma or compression syndromes Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. L3 Affects hip flexion and knee extension; sensation over anterior thigh. B. L4 Associated with knee extension and reduced knee jerk reflex; sensation over medial leg. D. S1 Causes plantarflexion weakness and reduced ankle reflex; sensation over lateral foot. E. S2 Affects posterior thigh and leg; not specific for dorsiflexion or first web space sensation. Key Exam Principle 👉 Foot drop + great toe extension weakness + first web space sensory loss = L5 👉 Normal ankle reflex helps distinguish L5 from S1 👉 "First web space + big toe up = L5"

question_text: A 63 year old man presents to the clinic with a history of progressive claudication affecting his right leg, which has worsened over the past six months. He reports that the pain starts in his calf after walking more than 100 metres and is relieved by rest. The patient has a smoking history of 40 pack-years and has been diagnosed with hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia, for which he is on medication. On examination, the right foot pulse is diminished compared to the left, and the right ankle-brachial index (ABI) is 0.6. Which is the most likely location of arterial occlusion in this patient?
explanation: Why? This patient has classic intermittent claudication affecting the calf, which most commonly localizes to femoropopliteal arterial disease. The reduced ABI (0.6) confirms moderate peripheral arterial disease. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Calf pain on walking (intermittent claudication) ✅ Pain relieved by rest ✅ Risk factors: smoking, hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia ✅ Reduced foot pulse ✅ ABI = 0.6 (moderate PAD) These findings strongly suggest peripheral arterial disease in the femoropopliteal segment. Why Femoropopliteal Is Correct Calf claudication is the hallmark of femoropopliteal disease This segment supplies the calf muscles Occlusion here leads to exertional calf pain relieved by rest Most common site of atherosclerotic disease in the lower limb Why the Other Options Are Less Likely B. External iliac Would cause more proximal symptoms and may reduce femoral pulse. C. Internal iliac Typically causes buttock or hip claudication, not calf pain. D. Anterior tibial Distal disease; often presents with foot symptoms rather than isolated calf claudication. E. Aortoiliac Causes buttock/thigh claudication and may be associated with erectile dysfunction (Leriche syndrome). Key Exam Principle 👉 Claudication location helps localize arterial disease 👉 Calf pain = femoropopliteal disease 👉 ABI < 0.9 confirms peripheral arterial disease (0.6 = moderate severity) 👉 "Calf claudication = femoropopliteal"

question_text: A 30 year old woman, who is 35 weeks pregnant, presents to her GP with a two-week history of pain and numbness in her right hand, particularly affecting the thumb, index, and middle fingers. She describes the pain as worse at night and is occasionally awakened by the discomfort. On examination, a positive Phalen's test is noted. What is the most likely anatomical structure involved in her symptoms?

options.a: Median nerve at the elbow joint
options.b: Median nerve at the wrist joint
options.c: Radial nerve at the wrist joint
options.d: Ulnar nerve at the elbow joint
options.e: Ulnar nerve at the wrist joint

explanation: Why? This patient has classic carpal tunnel syndrome, which is caused by compression of the median nerve at the wrist within the carpal tunnel. Pregnancy is a common risk factor due to fluid retention. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Numbness in thumb, index, and middle fingers ✅ Symptoms worse at night ✅ Positive Phalen's test ✅ Pregnancy (risk factor due to fluid retention) These are hallmark features of carpal tunnel syndrome. Why Median Nerve at the Wrist Is Correct Median nerve passes through the carpal tunnel at the wrist Compression causes sensory symptoms in lateral 3½ fingers (thumb, index, middle, and half of ring finger) Symptoms are often worse at night Phalen's test reproduces symptoms by flexing the wrist Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Median nerve at the elbow joint Would cause more proximal forearm symptoms, not classic carpal tunnel distribution. C. Radial nerve at the wrist joint Radial nerve supplies dorsum of the hand and does not affect palmar sensation of these fingers. D. Ulnar nerve at the elbow joint Would affect the little finger and medial half of the ring finger. E. Ulnar nerve at the wrist joint Also affects the medial 1½ fingers, not the thumb, index, and middle fingers. Key Exam Principle 👉 Thumb + index + middle finger numbness + night pain + positive Phalen's = carpal tunnel syndrome 👉 Carpal tunnel syndrome = median nerve compression at the wrist 👉 "LOAF muscles + lateral 3½ fingers = median nerve at wrist"

question_text: A 45 year old woman presents with pain and numbness over the right upper outer thigh. Which nerve is most likely affected?
explanation: Why? This patient has symptoms consistent with meralgia paresthetica, which is caused by compression of the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve. This nerve supplies sensation to the upper outer (anterolateral) thigh. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Pain and numbness ✅ Localized to upper outer thigh ✅ Purely sensory symptoms (no motor weakness mentioned) These findings point to a sensory nerve supplying the lateral thigh. Why Lateral Femoral Cutaneous Nerve Is Correct Supplies sensation to the anterolateral thigh Purely sensory nerve → no motor deficits Commonly compressed under the inguinal ligament (e.g., obesity, tight clothing, pregnancy) Causes burning, tingling, or numbness over the lateral thigh (meralgia paresthetica) Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Femoral nerve Supplies anterior thigh and quadriceps (motor + sensory); injury causes weakness in knee extension. B. Obturator nerve Supplies medial thigh and adductor muscles, not lateral thigh. D. Genitofemoral nerve Supplies upper anterior thigh and genital region, not the outer thigh. E. Sciatic nerve Supplies posterior thigh and most of the leg; injury causes major motor deficits, not isolated lateral thigh sensory symptoms. Key Exam Principle 👉 Lateral thigh numbness (no weakness) = lateral femoral cutaneous nerve 👉 "Outer thigh only = meralgia paresthetica"

question_text: A 54 year old woman attends the vascular surgery clinic following endovenous thermal ablation for varicose veins in her right leg. The procedure was performed one week ago. She now reports numbness and tingling along the inner side of her right leg extending from the knee to the ankle. There is no associated weakness or difficulty in movement. On examination, there is reduced sensation to light touch along the medial aspect of the leg, with no motor deficits. Which nerve has most likely been injured during the procedure?
explanation: Why? This patient has isolated sensory loss along the medial side of the leg from the knee to the ankle, which is the sensory distribution of the saphenous nerve. This nerve is at risk during varicose vein procedures because it runs alongside the great saphenous vein. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Recent endovenous thermal ablation for varicose veins ✅ Numbness and tingling along the inner side of the leg ✅ Sensory loss from knee to ankle ✅ No motor weakness These findings point to injury of a purely sensory nerve associated with the great saphenous vein. Why Saphenous Nerve Is Correct Saphenous nerve is a sensory branch of the femoral nerve Supplies the medial aspect of the leg from the knee to the ankle/foot Runs closely with the great saphenous vein Can be injured during stripping or thermal ablation of varicose veins Pure sensory nerve → no motor deficits Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Common peroneal nerve Would cause sensory loss over the lateral leg/dorsum of foot and may cause foot drop. B. Femoral nerve Would cause quadriceps weakness and reduced knee extension, not isolated medial leg sensory loss. D. Sciatic nerve Would produce major motor deficits affecting the hamstrings and below-knee muscles, not isolated medial leg numbness. E. Tibial nerve Would affect plantar sensation and plantarflexion, not the medial leg. Key Exam Principle 👉 Medial leg sensory loss with no weakness = saphenous nerve injury 👉 Varicose vein procedures risk injury to the saphenous nerve because it accompanies the great saphenous vein 👉 "Great saphenous vein procedure + medial leg numbness = saphenous nerve"

question_text: A 45 year old man presents to the GP clinic with complaints of weakness and numbness affecting his right hand. He reports that the symptoms began gradually over the past three weeks. He notes difficulty with fine motor tasks, such as writing and grasping objects. Examination reveals reduced strength in the extensor muscles of the wrist and fingers, with a marked decrease in the strength of the triceps muscle. There is also diminished sensation over the middle finger. Reflex examination reveals a reduced triceps reflex on the right side. Which of the following nerve roots is most likely affected?
explanation: Why? This patient has features of a C7 radiculopathy. The reduced triceps strength, diminished triceps reflex, weakness of wrist and finger extensors, and sensory loss over the middle finger all point to C7 nerve root involvement. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Weakness of wrist and finger extensors ✅ Marked triceps weakness ✅ Reduced triceps reflex ✅ Diminished sensation over the middle finger ✅ Gradual onset suggesting cervical nerve root compression These are classic findings of C7 nerve root dysfunction. Why C7 Is Correct C7 myotome contributes to triceps function C7 also contributes to wrist and finger extension C7 reflex = triceps reflex C7 dermatome includes the middle finger This combination strongly localizes to the C7 nerve root Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. C5 Would more likely affect shoulder abduction and elbow flexion, with biceps involvement rather than middle finger sensory loss. B. C6 Typically affects the biceps and brachioradialis reflexes, with sensory symptoms in the thumb and index finger. D. C8 Usually affects finger flexors and intrinsic hand muscles, with sensory loss in the ring and little fingers. E. T1 Primarily affects intrinsic hand muscles, not the triceps reflex or middle finger sensation. Key Exam Principle 👉 C7 radiculopathy = middle finger sensory loss + weak triceps + reduced triceps reflex 👉 Wrist/finger extensor weakness can also be seen with C7 involvement 👉 "Middle finger + triceps = C7"

question_text: A 30 year old male carpenter presents to the Emergency Department with a laceration to his right index finger. He states that he was working with a saw when the blade slipped and cut his finger. He reports that he is unable to bend his index finger. On physical examination, he has a 2-cm laceration to the palm side of his right index finger. The laceration is through the skin and subcutaneous tissue, but it does not appear to involve any tendon or bone. He is unable to actively flex the proximal interphalangeal joint of his finger but able to flex the distal interphalangeal joint of his finger. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Why? This patient cannot flex the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint but can still flex the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint. This indicates an isolated injury to the flexor digitorum superficialis (FDS), which is responsible for PIP flexion. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Laceration on the palmar side of the finger (flexor surface) ✅ Inability to flex the PIP joint ✅ Preserved flexion of the DIP joint These findings help distinguish between the two flexor tendons. Why Flexor Digitorum Superficialis Is Correct FDS inserts on the middle phalanx → flexes the PIP joint FDP inserts on the distal phalanx → flexes the DIP joint Since DIP flexion is intact, FDP is functional Loss of PIP flexion indicates FDS tendon injury Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Flexor digitorum profundus tendon tear Would cause inability to flex the DIP joint (not preserved here). C. Flexor pollicis longus tendon tear Affects thumb flexion, not the index finger. D. Flexor carpi radialis tendon tear Affects wrist flexion, not finger flexion. E. Extensor digitorum tendon tear Would impair finger extension, not flexion. Key Exam Principle 👉 PIP flexion = FDS 👉 DIP flexion = FDP 👉 "DIP works, PIP doesn't = FDS injury"

question_text: A 52 year old man presents to the Emergency Department following a head injury from a fall off a ladder. He complains of double vision, which he notices is worse when looking down. On examination, vertical diplopia is evident, and it is observed that his right eye deviates upward when attempting to look down and inwards. No other cranial nerve deficits are noted, and the rest of his neurological examination is unremarkable. The history and examination findings suggest an injury to one of the extraocular muscles, likely related to the trauma he experienced. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Why? This patient has a superior oblique palsy, most likely due to trochlear nerve injury after head trauma. The superior oblique muscle normally depresses the adducted eye, so when it is weak, the affected eye drifts upward and the patient develops vertical diplopia that is worse when looking down. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Head injury ✅ Vertical diplopia ✅ Diplopia worse when looking down ✅ Right eye deviates upward when attempting to look down and inwards ✅ No other cranial nerve deficits These are classic features of superior oblique muscle palsy. Why Superior Oblique Muscle Palsy Is Correct Superior oblique muscle depresses the eye when it is adducted It is supplied by the trochlear nerve (CN IV), which is vulnerable in head trauma Weakness causes difficulty looking down, especially when reading or walking downstairs The affected eye may appear relatively elevated because it cannot depress properly in adduction Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Abducens nerve palsy Would cause failure of eye abduction with horizontal diplopia, not vertical diplopia worse on downward gaze. C. Inferior oblique muscle palsy Would impair elevation in adduction, not cause an upward deviation on attempted downward gaze. D. Lateral rectus muscle palsy Also causes impaired abduction and horizontal diplopia. E. Medial rectus muscle palsy Would cause impaired adduction, not isolated vertical diplopia on looking down. Key Exam Principle 👉 Vertical diplopia that is worse when looking down = superior oblique palsy 👉 Superior oblique acts to depress the adducted eye 👉 "Down and in problem after trauma = superior oblique / trochlear nerve palsy"

question_text: A 52 year old man presents to the GP clinic with numbness and tingling affecting the right lower lip, chin, and lower teeth. The symptoms started gradually over the past two weeks. He also reports mild pain in the right lower jaw and has experienced unintentional weight loss over the past three months. On examination, there is reduced sensation over the right lower lip, chin, and lower gingiva. No facial asymmetry or lymphadenopathy is noted. Which nerve is most likely affected in this patient?
explanation: Why? This patient has numbness of the lower lip, chin, and lower teeth, which is the sensory distribution of the inferior alveolar nerve (a branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve, V3). The symptoms are characteristic of "numb chin syndrome," often associated with mandibular pathology or malignancy. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Numbness of lower lip and chin ✅ Involvement of lower teeth and gingiva ✅ Jaw pain ✅ Unintentional weight loss (red flag for malignancy) These findings point specifically to the inferior alveolar nerve. Why Inferior Alveolar Nerve Is Correct Supplies sensation to lower teeth via dental branches Gives rise to the mental nerve → supplies lower lip and chin Runs within the mandibular canal → vulnerable to mandibular pathology (tumor, metastasis, trauma) Compression or infiltration leads to numb chin syndrome Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Auriculotemporal nerve Supplies temple and ear region, not lower lip or chin. B. Buccal nerve Supplies cheek mucosa and skin, not the lower lip or teeth. D. Lingual nerve Supplies anterior 2/3 of the tongue sensation, not chin or lower lip. E. Mandibular nerve Main trunk (V3) supplies a wider area including motor function; isolated symptoms localize more specifically to the inferior alveolar branch. Key Exam Principle 👉 Lower lip + chin + lower teeth numbness = inferior alveolar nerve 👉 "Numb chin syndrome" is a red flag → consider malignancy 👉 "Chin + lower teeth = inferior alveolar (mental branch)"

question_text: A 50 year old woman presents with a number of symptoms that have come on over the past few days. She has a generalised headache and, on further questioning, reports blurring of vision and a painful left eye. On looking forwards, the left eye has deviated inferiorly and laterally. There is obvious ptosis of the upper left lid, and the pupil is dilated and unresponsive to light. Where is the most likely location of the lesion?
explanation: Why? This patient has a complete left oculomotor nerve (CN III) palsy. The affected eye is deviated down and out, there is ptosis, and the pupil is dilated and unreactive. The oculomotor nucleus and nerve fascicles are located in the midbrain, so the most likely lesion location is the midbrain. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Eye deviated inferiorly and laterally ("down and out") ✅ Ptosis of the upper eyelid ✅ Dilated pupil ✅ Pupil unresponsive to light ✅ Blurred vision and painful eye These are classic features of oculomotor nerve palsy. Why Midbrain Is Correct The oculomotor nerve arises from the oculomotor nucleus in the midbrain CN III supplies: - Levator palpebrae superioris → eyelid elevation - Superior rectus, inferior rectus, medial rectus, inferior oblique → most extraocular movements - Parasympathetic fibers to the pupil → constriction Loss of CN III function causes: - "Down and out" eye position due to unopposed lateral rectus and superior oblique - Ptosis due to levator palpebrae paralysis - Dilated, fixed pupil due to loss of parasympathetic supply Why the Other Options Are Less Likely B. Pons The pons is associated with CN V to VIII. It is not the site of the oculomotor nucleus. C. Medulla oblongata The medulla is associated with CN IX to XII, not CN III. D. Cerebellum Cerebellar lesions cause ataxia, nystagmus, and coordination problems, not an isolated complete third nerve palsy. E. Cerebrum Cerebral lesions may cause visual field defects or motor/sensory deficits, but not this classic cranial nerve III palsy pattern. Key Exam Principle 👉 "Down and out" eye + ptosis + dilated pupil = oculomotor nerve palsy 👉 Oculomotor nerve nucleus is in the midbrain 👉 "CN III = midbrain"

question_text: A 30 year old man complains of double vision when he looks to the left. When he closes either his right or left eye, his vision normalises. Which is the SINGLE most likely nerve to be involved?
explanation: Why? This patient has binocular diplopia, since the double vision disappears when either eye is closed. Diplopia that is worse on looking to the left suggests failure of left lateral gaze, most commonly due to a left abducens nerve (6th cranial nerve) palsy affecting the left lateral rectus muscle. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Double vision only when both eyes are open ✅ Vision normalises when either eye is closed → binocular diplopia ✅ Diplopia occurs when looking to the left These findings point to a problem with coordinated extraocular movement. Why Left 6th Cranial Nerve Is Correct The left 6th cranial nerve supplies the left lateral rectus muscle The lateral rectus abducts the left eye On looking left, the left eye must abduct If the left abducens nerve is weak, the left eye cannot move fully outward, causing horizontal diplopia that is worst on gaze toward the affected side Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Left 3rd cranial nerve Would cause ptosis, a "down and out" eye, and possibly a dilated pupil, not isolated diplopia only on left gaze. B. Right 3rd cranial nerve Also causes multiple extraocular movement deficits, not this isolated pattern. C. Right 4th cranial nerve Typically causes vertical diplopia, worse on looking down, not horizontal diplopia on left gaze. E. Right 6th cranial nerve Would impair abduction of the right eye, causing diplopia that is worse on looking to the right, not left. Key Exam Principle 👉 Binocular diplopia = ocular misalignment from extraocular muscle/cranial nerve palsy 👉 Horizontal diplopia worse on gaze to one side = abducens nerve palsy on that side 👉 "Can't look left properly = left 6th nerve"

question_text: A 33 year old man presents with outward gaze and ptosis of his right eye. He also complains of seeing double. Which is the SINGLE most likely nerve to be affected?
explanation: Why? This patient has a right oculomotor nerve (3rd cranial nerve) palsy. The combination of ptosis, outward deviation of the eye, and diplopia is classic for CN III dysfunction. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Right eye is deviated outward ✅ Ptosis of the right eyelid ✅ Diplopia These findings strongly point to oculomotor nerve palsy on the right side. Why Right Oculomotor Is Correct The oculomotor nerve supplies: - Levator palpebrae superioris → elevates the upper eyelid - Medial rectus, superior rectus, inferior rectus, and inferior oblique → control most eye movements When the oculomotor nerve is damaged: - Ptosis occurs due to paralysis of levator palpebrae superioris - The eye is pulled outward by the unopposed lateral rectus muscle - Diplopia occurs due to misalignment of the eyes Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Left trochlear Would affect the left superior oblique muscle and cause vertical diplopia, not right-sided ptosis with outward gaze. B. Left oculomotor Would affect the left eye, not the right eye. C. Right trochlear Trochlear nerve palsy causes difficulty looking down and in, leading to vertical diplopia, not ptosis with outward gaze. D. Right abducens Abducens nerve palsy causes failure of abduction, resulting in a medially deviated eye, not an outwardly deviated one, and does not cause ptosis. Key Exam Principle 👉 Ptosis + outward deviation of the eye + diplopia = oculomotor nerve palsy 👉 Oculomotor palsy causes a "down and out" or outwardly deviated eye because lateral rectus acts unopposed 👉 "Ptosis + outwards eye = CN III"

question_text: A 33 year old man presents with outward gaze and ptosis of his right eye. He also complains of seeing double. Which is the SINGLE most likely nerve to be affected?
explanation: Why? This patient has a right oculomotor nerve (3rd cranial nerve) palsy. The combination of ptosis, outward deviation of the right eye, and diplopia is classic for CN III dysfunction. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Right eye has outward gaze ✅ Ptosis of the right eyelid ✅ Diplopia These findings strongly localize to a right-sided oculomotor nerve lesion. Why Right Oculomotor Is Correct The oculomotor nerve supplies: - Levator palpebrae superioris → lifts the upper eyelid - Medial rectus, superior rectus, inferior rectus, and inferior oblique → most eye movements When the oculomotor nerve is damaged: - Ptosis occurs due to paralysis of levator palpebrae superioris - The eye deviates outward because the lateral rectus acts unopposed - Diplopia occurs because the eyes are no longer aligned Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Left trochlear Would cause vertical diplopia related to the left superior oblique muscle, not right-sided ptosis and outward gaze. B. Left oculomotor Would affect the left eye, not the right. C. Right trochlear Would cause difficulty depressing the adducted eye and vertical diplopia, not ptosis with outward deviation. D. Right abducens Would cause failure of abduction, producing a medially deviated eye, not an outwardly deviated eye, and would not cause ptosis. Key Exam Principle 👉 Ptosis + outwardly deviated eye + diplopia = oculomotor nerve palsy 👉 Same-side eye findings = same-side CN III lesion 👉 "Ptosis + out = right oculomotor"

question_text: A 53 year old man presents to his general practitioner (GP) with the complaint of a band of reduced sensation on the medial and posterior aspect of his lower left forearm running down to his little finger. He describes it as a tingling feeling and says that it feels like constant "pins and needles" in his left hand. Examination reveals a weakness of thumb extension and wrist ulnar deviation. There is also slight wasting of the muscles of the left hand. What is the SINGLE most likely structure affected?
explanation: Why? This patient has features most consistent with a C8 nerve root lesion. The sensory symptoms affect the medial forearm and little finger, while the motor findings include weakness of thumb extension and wrist ulnar deviation, which point to involvement beyond a single peripheral nerve. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Sensory symptoms extend from the medial/posterior forearm to the little finger ✅ Weakness of thumb extension ✅ Weakness of wrist ulnar deviation ✅ Slight wasting of hand muscles These findings suggest a root lesion rather than an isolated ulnar or median nerve lesion. Why C8 Nerve Root Is Correct C8 supplies sensation to the little finger and medial aspect of the forearm/hand region C8 contributes to finger flexors/extensors and intrinsic hand muscle function Thumb extension involves radial-innervated muscles, which would not be explained by an isolated ulnar nerve lesion A root lesion can affect multiple peripheral nerve territories at once Wrist ulnar deviation weakness can occur because muscles involved receive contributions from C8 Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Ulnar nerve at elbow Would cause sensory loss in the little finger and medial hand, but would not explain thumb extension weakness, since thumb extension is supplied by the radial nerve. B. Median nerve at elbow Would affect thumb opposition, forearm pronation, and sensation in the lateral palm/fingers, not the little finger. C. Median nerve at wrist Would cause carpal tunnel-type symptoms affecting the thumb, index, middle, and radial half of the ring finger, not the little finger or forearm. E. T1 nerve root n T1 mainly affects intrinsic hand muscles. It would be less likely to produce this broader pattern involving thumb extension and sensory symptoms extending along the forearm to the little finger. Key Exam Principle 👉 Sensory loss and weakness spanning more than one peripheral nerve territory suggests a nerve root lesion 👉 Little finger symptoms + thumb extension weakness = think C8 rather than isolated ulnar neuropathy 👉 "Multiple nerve territories in the hand/forearm = root lesion"

question_text: A 33 year old man complains of double vision when he looks to the right. When he closes either his right or left eye, his vision normalises. Which is the SINGLE most likely nerve to be involved?
explanation: Why? This patient has binocular diplopia, since the double vision resolves when either eye is closed. Diplopia that is worse on looking to the right suggests failure of right lateral gaze, most commonly due to a right abducens nerve (6th cranial nerve) palsy affecting the right lateral rectus muscle. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Diplopia only when both eyes are open (binocular diplopia) ✅ Symptoms occur when looking to the right These indicate a problem with coordinated eye movement. Why Right Abducens Is Correct The right abducens nerve supplies the right lateral rectus muscle The lateral rectus abducts the eye On right gaze, the right eye must abduct If the right abducens nerve is impaired, the right eye cannot move outward properly, causing horizontal diplopia that is worse when looking to the affected side Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Left abducens Would cause difficulty with left gaze, not right gaze. C. Left trochlear Trochlear nerve palsy causes vertical diplopia, worse on looking down, not horizontal diplopia on right gaze. D. Right trochlear Also causes vertical diplopia, not horizontal diplopia on lateral gaze. E. Right oculomotor Would cause ptosis, "down and out" eye position, and possibly a dilated pupil, not isolated diplopia on right gaze. Key Exam Principle 👉 Binocular diplopia = cranial nerve / extraocular muscle problem 👉 Horizontal diplopia worse on gaze to one side = ipsilateral abducens nerve palsy 👉 "Can't look right = right 6th nerve"

question_text: A 24 year old man presents with numbness and tingling over the left lower lip, chin, and lower teeth after being punched on the left jaw three days ago. He reports mild jaw pain and difficulty chewing but no facial weakness. On examination, there is reduced sensation in the affected areas with tenderness over the left mandible. Which nerve is most likely affected in this patient?
explanation: Why? This patient has trauma to the mandible with sensory loss over the lower lip, chin, and lower teeth—classic for injury to the inferior alveolar nerve, a branch of the mandibular division (V3) of the trigeminal nerve. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Trauma to the jaw (punch to mandible) ✅ Numbness of lower lip and chin ✅ Involvement of lower teeth ✅ No facial weakness (pure sensory issue) These findings localize specifically to the inferior alveolar nerve. Why Inferior Alveolar Nerve Is Correct Runs through the mandibular canal within the mandible Supplies sensation to lower teeth Gives rise to the mental nerve → supplies lower lip and chin Commonly injured in mandibular fractures or trauma Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Chorda tympani Carries taste from anterior 2/3 of tongue and parasympathetic fibers to salivary glands, not sensation of chin or teeth. B. Zygomatic nerve Supplies cheek and temple area, not lower lip or teeth. D. Hypoglossal nerve Motor nerve to tongue muscles; injury causes tongue deviation, not sensory loss. E. Mandibular nerve Main trunk (V3) carries both motor and sensory fibers; an isolated sensory deficit in this distribution localizes more specifically to the inferior alveolar branch. Key Exam Principle 👉 Lower lip + chin + lower teeth numbness = inferior alveolar nerve 👉 Mandibular trauma commonly injures this nerve 👉 "Jaw injury + numb chin = inferior alveolar nerve"

question_text: A 24 year old man presents with numbness and tingling over the left lower lip, chin, and lower teeth after being punched on the left jaw three days ago. He reports mild jaw pain and difficulty chewing but no facial weakness. On examination, there is reduced sensation in the affected areas with tenderness over the left mandible. Which nerve is most likely affected in this patient?
explanation: Why? This patient has trauma to the mandible with sensory loss over the lower lip, chin, and lower teeth, which is classic for injury to the inferior alveolar nerve. This nerve runs through the mandibular canal and gives rise to the mental nerve, which supplies the chin and lower lip. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Trauma to the jaw ✅ Numbness of the lower lip and chin ✅ Involvement of the lower teeth ✅ Tenderness over the mandible ✅ No facial weakness These findings localize to a sensory branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve. Why Inferior Alveolar Nerve Is Correct The inferior alveolar nerve supplies the lower teeth It continues as the mental nerve, which supplies sensation to the chin and lower lip It is commonly injured in mandibular trauma or fractures This explains the combined sensory loss in the lower teeth, lip, and chin Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Chorda tympani Carries taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and parasympathetic fibers to salivary glands, not sensation from the chin or teeth. B. Zygomatic nerve Supplies the cheekbone and temple region, not the lower jaw, chin, or lower teeth. D. Hypoglossal nerve A motor nerve to the tongue. Injury would cause tongue weakness, not sensory loss in the jaw. E. Mandibular nerve Although the inferior alveolar nerve is a branch of the mandibular nerve, the symptoms localize more specifically to the inferior alveolar branch rather than the whole mandibular nerve. Key Exam Principle 👉 Lower lip + chin + lower teeth numbness = inferior alveolar nerve injury 👉 Mandibular trauma commonly damages this nerve 👉 "Numb chin after jaw injury = inferior alveolar nerve"

question_text: A 72 year old man presents with sudden onset of double vision and drooping of the right eyelid. He denies headache or trauma. Examination reveals the right eye is deviated laterally and slightly downward. The right pupil is dilated and unresponsive to light. There is complete ptosis of the right eyelid, and eye movements show restricted adduction, elevation, and depression. Which cranial nerve is most likely affected?
explanation: Why? This patient has a classic complete oculomotor nerve (cranial nerve III) palsy. The key features are ptosis, a "down and out" eye, a dilated non-reactive pupil, and impaired adduction, elevation, and depression. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Sudden diplopia ✅ Ptosis of the right eyelid ✅ Eye deviated laterally and slightly downward ("down and out") ✅ Dilated, non-reactive pupil ✅ Impaired adduction, elevation, and depression These findings strongly indicate CN III palsy. Why Oculomotor Nerve Is Correct The oculomotor nerve supplies: - Levator palpebrae superioris → eyelid elevation (ptosis if damaged) - Medial rectus → adduction - Superior rectus → elevation - Inferior rectus → depression - Inferior oblique → elevation in adduction - Parasympathetic fibers → pupil constriction Loss of CN III function causes: - "Down and out" eye due to unopposed lateral rectus (CN VI) and superior oblique (CN IV) - Ptosis due to levator palpebrae paralysis - Dilated pupil due to loss of parasympathetic input Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Abducens nerve Would cause inability to abduct the eye (medial deviation), not ptosis or pupil dilation. B. Olfactory nerve Responsible for smell, not eye movement. D. Optic nerve Responsible for vision, not eye movement or eyelid position. E. Trochlear nerve Causes vertical diplopia, especially on looking down, without ptosis or pupil involvement. Key Exam Principle 👉 Ptosis + "down and out" eye + dilated pupil = oculomotor nerve palsy 👉 CN III controls most eye movements and parasympathetic pupil function 👉 "Down & out + blown pupil = CN III"

question_text: A 55 year old man with rheumatoid arthritis struck his hand against a door. On examination, he could extend the interphalangeal joint of his right thumb but the metacarpophalangeal joint of the thumb remained flex. What is the SINGLE most likely tendon to have been damaged?
explanation: Why? This patient can extend the interphalangeal (IP) joint of the thumb but cannot extend the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint. This indicates that extensor pollicis longus (which extends the IP joint) is intact, while extensor pollicis brevis (which extends the MCP joint) is damaged. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Thumb IP joint extension preserved ✅ Thumb MCP joint cannot extend (remains flexed) ✅ Local trauma with underlying rheumatoid arthritis (predisposes to tendon injury) These findings isolate the tendon responsible for MCP extension of the thumb. Why Extensor Pollicis Brevis Is Correct Extensor pollicis brevis (EPB) extends the thumb at the MCP joint Extensor pollicis longus (EPL) extends the IP joint Since IP extension is intact, EPL is functioning Loss of MCP extension indicates EPB tendon damage Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Extensor carpi ulnaris Acts on the wrist, not the thumb. B. Extensor digitorum Extends fingers (digits 2–5), not the thumb. C. Extensor indicis Extends the index finger, not the thumb. E. Extensor pollicis longus Would cause inability to extend the IP joint of the thumb, which is preserved here. Key Exam Principle 👉 Thumb MCP extension = extensor pollicis brevis 👉 Thumb IP extension = extensor pollicis longus 👉 "IP works, MCP doesn't = EPB injury"

question_text: A 32 year old patient presents to Accident & Emergency with a deep cut on the surface of her palm and the surface of the back of her wrist. She has an inability to extend the distal phalanx of her ring finger. What is the SINGLE most likely structure affected?
explanation: Why? This patient is unable to extend the distal phalanx of the ring finger, which points to damage to the extensor mechanism of that finger. Of the options given, the most likely structure affected is the extensor digitorum tendon. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Deep cut involving the back of the wrist ✅ Inability to extend the distal phalanx of the ring finger ✅ Problem is with extension, not flexion These findings indicate injury to the extensor apparatus rather than the flexor tendons or palmar muscles. Why Extensor Digitorum Is Correct Extensor digitorum is the main extensor tendon to the fingers It extends the fingers through the extensor expansion Damage can impair extension at the interphalangeal joints, including the distal phalanx A laceration on the dorsum of the wrist is a typical site for extensor tendon injury Why the Other Options Are Less Likely B. Branch of ulnar nerve Ulnar nerve injury affects intrinsic hand muscles and may cause clawing, but does not classically cause isolated loss of distal phalanx extension of one finger. C. Flexor digitorum profundus This flexes the distal phalanx. Injury would cause inability to flex the distal interphalangeal joint, not inability to extend it. D. Palmaris brevis This is a small muscle of the hand that wrinkles the skin over the hypothenar eminence and has no role in finger extension. E. Branch of median nerve Median nerve injury affects thenar muscles and lateral lumbricals, not isolated extension loss of the ring finger distal phalanx. Key Exam Principle 👉 Inability to extend a finger after a dorsal wrist laceration = extensor tendon injury 👉 Distal phalanx extension depends on the extensor mechanism 👉 "Dorsal cut + can't extend finger = extensor digitorum"

question_text: A 12 year old boy is brought to the Emergency Department after falling off his bicycle onto his outstretched left arm. He complains of severe left shoulder pain and is holding his arm in slight abduction and external rotation. He is unable to abduct his shoulder beyond 15 degrees due to pain. Sensory examination shows numbness over the lateral aspect of the upper arm and shoulder. Radiographs confirm an anterior dislocation of the left glenohumeral joint. Which nerve is most likely injured?
explanation: Why? This patient has an anterior shoulder dislocation with classic signs of axillary nerve injury. The axillary nerve is commonly injured in shoulder dislocations because it winds around the surgical neck of the humerus. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Anterior glenohumeral dislocation ✅ Inability to abduct shoulder beyond 15° (deltoid weakness) ✅ Numbness over lateral shoulder ("regimental badge" area) These findings strongly indicate axillary nerve involvement. Why Axillary Nerve Is Correct Supplies the deltoid muscle → responsible for shoulder abduction from 15° to 90° Supplies teres minor → assists with external rotation Provides sensation over the lateral upper arm (regimental badge area) Commonly injured in anterior shoulder dislocation Why the Other Options Are Less Likely B. Long thoracic nerve Injury causes winged scapula due to serratus anterior paralysis, not sensory loss over lateral shoulder. C. Musculocutaneous nerve Affects elbow flexion and sensation over lateral forearm, not shoulder abduction or lateral shoulder sensation. D. Radial nerve Causes wrist drop and sensory loss over posterior forearm/hand, not isolated shoulder findings. E. Suprascapular nerve Affects initial 0–15° abduction (supraspinatus) and external rotation, but does not supply sensation to the lateral shoulder. Key Exam Principle 👉 Shoulder dislocation + lateral shoulder numbness + weak abduction = axillary nerve injury 👉 "Regimental badge area + can't abduct = axillary nerve"

question_text: A patient is scheduled for an elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy. During the procedure, the surgeon plans to insert a trocar at the midway point between the anterior umbilicus and the mid-axillary line in the right lower quadrant. Which of the following anatomical structures is the first to be pierced by the trocar at this site?

options.a: Aponeurosis of the external oblique muscle and internal oblique muscle

explanation: Why? The trocar is inserted in the lateral abdominal wall (midway between the umbilicus and mid-axillary line), not in the midline. The first muscular/aponeurotic layer encountered after the skin and superficial fascia is the external oblique aponeurosis, followed by the internal oblique. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Entry point is lateral (not midline) ✅ Right lower quadrant, away from linea alba ✅ Typical laparoscopic port site in lateral abdominal wall These indicate the trocar will pass through the layered muscles of the abdominal wall. Why Aponeurosis of External and Internal Oblique Is Correct Layers of the lateral abdominal wall (superficial → deep): - Skin - Superficial fascia - External oblique (aponeurosis/muscle) - Internal oblique - Transversus abdominis - Transversalis fascia - Peritoneum The first deep layer encountered is the external oblique aponeurosis, followed by internal oblique Why the Other Options Are Less Likely B. Rectus abdominis muscle Located medially within the rectus sheath, not at this lateral entry point. C. Linea alba Midline structure, not involved in a lateral trocar insertion. D. Psoas major muscle Deep posterior abdominal wall muscle, not encountered in anterior abdominal wall entry. E. Transversus abdominis muscle Deeper layer, encountered after external and internal oblique muscles. Key Exam Principle 👉 Lateral abdominal wall entry = external oblique first 👉 Midline entry = linea alba (not here) 👉 "Lateral port → external oblique first"

question_text: A 38 year old man has lower back pain shooting down his right leg that started 5 days ago after lifting weights at the gym. He has weakness in dorsiflexion of the toes of his right foot. He has intact ankle and knee jerk reflexes. He has reduced sensory stimulus on the dorsum of the right foot. Which nerve root is likely affected?
explanation: Why? This patient has classic features of an L5 radiculopathy. The key findings are weakness of toe dorsiflexion, sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot, and preserved knee and ankle reflexes. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Lower back pain radiating down the leg ✅ Weakness in dorsiflexion of the toes ✅ Reduced sensation on the dorsum of the foot ✅ Knee jerk intact ✅ Ankle jerk intact These findings strongly localize to the L5 nerve root. Why L5 Is Correct L5 myotome is responsible for dorsiflexion of the toes, especially extension of the great toe L5 dermatome includes the dorsum of the foot L5 radiculopathy typically does not affect a major deep tendon reflex, so knee and ankle jerks may remain normal This pattern is very typical of an L4/L5 disc prolapse compressing the L5 root Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. L2 Would mainly affect hip flexion and sensation over the upper anterior thigh, not the dorsum of the foot. B. L3 Would affect knee extension and anterior thigh sensation, not toe dorsiflexion. C. L4 Would be associated with weakness of knee extension, reduced knee jerk, and sensory loss over the medial leg. E. S1 Would cause plantarflexion weakness, sensory loss over the lateral foot, and reduced ankle jerk. Key Exam Principle 👉 Toe dorsiflexion weakness + dorsum of foot sensory loss + preserved reflexes = L5 radiculopathy 👉 "Big toe up / dorsum foot = L5"

question_text: A 45 year old woman presents to the clinic with a 2-week history of double vision, particularly when looking to the right. She also reports intermittent headaches. On examination, her visual acuity is normal, and there is no ptosis. However, there is a noticeable limitation of abduction of the right eye when asked to follow the clinician's finger to the right side. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Why? This patient has impaired abduction of the right eye, which is the primary function of the lateral rectus muscle. The lateral rectus is supplied by the abducens nerve (cranial nerve VI), so this indicates a right abducens nerve palsy. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Diplopia worse on looking to the right ✅ Limitation of abduction of the right eye ✅ No ptosis (rules out oculomotor nerve palsy) These findings localize the problem to the right lateral rectus muscle. Why Right Abducens Nerve Palsy Is Correct The abducens nerve supplies the lateral rectus muscle The lateral rectus abducts the eye Injury leads to inability to move the eye outward (abduction) Diplopia is worse when looking toward the affected side Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Left abducens nerve palsy Would impair abduction of the left eye, not the right. C. Right oculomotor nerve palsy Would cause ptosis, "down and out" eye, and possibly pupil dilation, none of which are present. D. Right trochlear nerve palsy Causes vertical diplopia, especially on looking down, not horizontal diplopia with impaired abduction. E. Left trochlear nerve palsy Also causes vertical diplopia affecting the left eye, not right-sided abduction deficit. Key Exam Principle 👉 Failure of abduction = abducens nerve palsy 👉 Diplopia worse on gaze to one side = ipsilateral CN VI lesion 👉 "Can't abduct right eye = right 6th nerve"

question_text: A 31 year old pregnant woman in her third trimester presents to the GP surgery with complaints of numbness and tingling over her left little finger and half of the ring finger. It has been gradually worsening over months. She has had no injury to the arm or hand. There is no muscle weakness seen on examination. Which nerve is likely to be compressed?
explanation: Why? This patient has sensory symptoms affecting the little finger and medial half of the ring finger, which is the classic sensory distribution of the ulnar nerve. Gradual worsening without trauma suggests a compressive neuropathy. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Numbness and tingling ✅ Affects the little finger and half of the ring finger ✅ Gradual onset over months ✅ No injury ✅ No muscle weakness yet These findings point to early ulnar nerve compression. Why Ulnar Nerve Is Correct The ulnar nerve supplies sensation to the little finger and medial half of the ring finger Compression commonly causes tingling and numbness in this distribution before motor weakness appears Pregnancy can predispose to nerve compression due to fluid retention and soft tissue swelling Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Median nerve at the wrist Would cause symptoms in the thumb, index, middle, and lateral half of the ring finger, not the little finger. B. Median nerve at the elbow Also affects the median nerve distribution, not the little finger and medial ring finger. D. Radial nerve Primarily affects the dorsum of the hand and wrist/finger extensors, not this sensory pattern. E. Superficial branch of radial nerve Would cause sensory symptoms over the dorsolateral hand, not the little finger. Key Exam Principle 👉 Little finger + medial half of ring finger numbness = ulnar nerve compression 👉 Sensory symptoms may occur before motor weakness develops 👉 "Little finger symptoms = ulnar nerve"

question_text: A 37 year old woman presents to the GP surgery with a one-month history of numbness and weakness affecting her right hand. She describes difficulty in holding objects and has noticed a tendency to drop items, especially when attempting to grip with her thumb and index finger. Sensation is diminished over the palmar surface of the thumb, index finger, middle finger, and the lateral half of the ring finger. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Why? This patient has both sensory and motor symptoms affecting the classic distribution of the median nerve. The involvement of the palmar surface of the thumb, index, middle, and lateral half of the ring finger strongly points to median nerve pathology. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Numbness over thumb, index, middle, and lateral half of ring finger ✅ Weak grip, especially thumb and index finger (precision grip) ✅ Dropping objects ✅ Gradual onset over one month These findings indicate median nerve dysfunction affecting both sensation and motor function. Why Median Nerve Palsy Is Correct The median nerve supplies sensation to the palmar aspect of the thumb, index, middle, and lateral half of the ring finger It innervates muscles responsible for thumb opposition and precision grip (e.g., thenar muscles) Weakness in grip and dropping objects reflects impaired thumb-index pinch ("precision grip") Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Anterior interosseous nerve palsy Purely motor branch of the median nerve — no sensory loss. This patient has clear sensory deficits. C. Posterior interosseous nerve palsy A motor branch of the radial nerve — causes finger extension weakness, no sensory loss. D. Radial nerve palsy Typically causes wrist drop and sensory loss over the dorsum of the hand, not the palmar digits described. E. Ulnar nerve palsy Affects the little finger and medial half of the ring finger, not the thumb, index, and middle fingers. Key Exam Principle 👉 Thumb + index + middle + lateral ring finger sensory loss = median nerve 👉 Motor + sensory involvement = main nerve (not a pure motor branch) 👉 "Precision grip weakness = median nerve"

question_text: A 33 year old man presents to the orthopaedic clinic after experiencing persistent shoulder weakness and discomfort for several weeks following a fall onto his outstretched hand while playing football. He reports difficulty lifting weights and complains that his shoulder blade seems to "stick out" when he pushes against a wall. On examination, there is medial protrusion of the scapula when he presses his hands against a flat surface, especially on the right. What is the most likely nerve that has been injured?
explanation: Why? This patient has classic features of winged scapula, specifically medial scapular winging, which occurs due to paralysis of the serratus anterior muscle. This muscle is innervated by the long thoracic nerve. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Scapula "sticking out" (winging) ✅ Worse when pushing against a wall ✅ History of trauma (fall onto outstretched hand) ✅ Difficulty lifting weights (impaired shoulder stabilization) These findings are classic for long thoracic nerve injury. Why Long Thoracic Nerve Is Correct The long thoracic nerve innervates the serratus anterior muscle Serratus anterior holds the scapula against the thoracic wall Injury leads to medial winging of the scapula, especially when pushing against a wall Commonly injured in trauma or repetitive strain Why the Other Options Are Less Likely B. Radial nerve Causes wrist drop and affects forearm extensors, not scapular winging. C. Spinal accessory nerve Supplies trapezius — injury causes lateral winging and shoulder droop, not classic medial winging seen here. D. Suprascapular nerve Affects supraspinatus and infraspinatus — leads to weak abduction and external rotation, not winging. E. Thoracodorsal nerve Supplies latissimus dorsi — affects extension/adduction of the arm, not scapular stability. Key Exam Principle 👉 Medial winging of scapula = serratus anterior = long thoracic nerve 👉 Seen when pushing against a wall 👉 "Winged scapula = think long thoracic nerve"

question_text: A 45 year old man following an elbow injury develops loss of sensation of the dorsal and palmar surfaces of the ulnar border of his right hand. His hand is described as a "claw". Which of the following movement against resistance will help confirm an injury to the affected nerve?
explanation: Why? This patient has classic features of ulnar nerve injury — sensory loss over the ulnar side of the hand and a "claw hand" deformity. The ulnar nerve supplies the interossei muscles, which are responsible for finger abduction and adduction. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Sensory loss over ulnar border (little finger + medial ring finger) ✅ Both dorsal and palmar involvement ✅ "Claw hand" deformity ✅ Injury at the elbow (common site of ulnar nerve injury) These findings strongly indicate ulnar nerve damage. Why Abduction of the Fingers Is Correct Finger abduction is performed by the dorsal interossei muscles These muscles are innervated by the ulnar nerve Weakness or inability to abduct fingers against resistance confirms ulnar nerve injury Why the Other Options Are Less Likely B. Abduction of the thumb Performed by abductor pollicis brevis (median nerve), not ulnar nerve. C. Extension of the fingers Controlled by the radial nerve (extensor muscles), not ulnar nerve. D. Extension of the thumb Also radial nerve function. E. Flexion of the fingers Mainly mediated by flexor digitorum superficialis (median nerve) and partially by flexor digitorum profundus — not specific for ulnar nerve injury. Key Exam Principle 👉 Ulnar nerve = interossei muscles 👉 Interossei = finger abduction & adduction 👉 "PAD/DAB" → Palmar interossei ADduct, Dorsal interossei ABduct 👉 Loss of finger abduction = ulnar nerve injury

question_text: A 45 year old graphic designer presents to the clinic with complaints of numbness and tingling in the little finger and ring finger of his left hand. These symptoms have become worse over the past six months. Recently, he has noticed difficulty gripping objects and a slight clumsiness when performing fine motor tasks. On examination, there is weakness in the abduction and adduction of the fingers, and has difficulty pinching a piece of paper between the thumb and index finger. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.c: Ulnar nerve compression at the elbow

explanation: Why? This patient presents with both sensory and motor features in the classic distribution of the ulnar nerve, along with signs of interossei muscle weakness and Froment’s sign (difficulty pinching paper). The gradual progression suggests compressive neuropathy, most commonly at the elbow (cubital tunnel syndrome). Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Numbness in little finger and ring finger ✅ Progressive symptoms over 6 months ✅ Weak grip and fine motor difficulty ✅ Weak finger abduction/adduction (interossei) ✅ Difficulty pinching paper (Froment’s sign) These findings are classic for ulnar nerve compression. Why Ulnar Nerve Compression at the Elbow Is Correct The ulnar nerve supplies sensation to the little finger and medial half of the ring finger It innervates interossei muscles responsible for finger abduction and adduction Compression at the elbow (cubital tunnel) is a common cause, especially with repetitive use (e.g., prolonged elbow flexion in desk work) Froment’s sign indicates weakness of adductor pollicis (ulnar nerve) Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Carpal tunnel syndrome Median nerve compression — affects thumb, index, middle, and lateral ring finger, not the little finger. B. Radial nerve palsy Causes wrist drop and affects extension, not finger abduction/adduction or ulnar sensory distribution. D. Anterior interosseous nerve syndrome Pure motor branch of median nerve — no sensory loss. E. Cervical radiculopathy May cause mixed symptoms but would not produce isolated ulnar distribution with classic interossei weakness and Froment’s sign. Key Exam Principle 👉 Little finger + medial ring finger symptoms = ulnar nerve 👉 Interossei weakness (abduction/adduction) = ulnar nerve 👉 Froment’s sign = ulnar nerve (adductor pollicis) 👉 Most common site = elbow (cubital tunnel syndrome)

question_text: A 33 year old woman was injured by her seatbelt during a car accident. She has sustained injuries to her thigh and groin. Since the accident, she has noticed that she has reduced sensation and a mild burning sensation of the lateral side of her left thigh. What is the SINGLE most likely nerve that is affected?
explanation: Why? This patient has isolated sensory symptoms (numbness and burning pain) over the lateral thigh, which is the classic presentation of lateral femoral cutaneous nerve involvement. The history of seatbelt injury suggests compression at the inguinal ligament — a common mechanism. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Burning sensation (neuropathic pain) ✅ Reduced sensation ✅ Localized to lateral thigh ✅ Trauma involving groin/inguinal region (seatbelt injury) ✅ No motor weakness mentioned These features strongly indicate a purely sensory nerve injury. Why Lateral Femoral Cutaneous Nerve Is Correct The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve is a purely sensory nerve Supplies the skin of the lateral thigh Commonly compressed at the inguinal ligament → meralgia paraesthetica Seatbelt injury can compress or injure this nerve at the groin Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Femoral nerve Would cause motor weakness (quadriceps) and sensory loss over anterior thigh and medial leg, not isolated lateral thigh symptoms. B. Obturator nerve Supplies medial thigh and adductor muscles — not lateral thigh. C. Sciatic nerve Would cause posterior thigh/leg symptoms and significant motor deficits. E. Saphenous nerve Supplies medial leg and foot, not the lateral thigh. Key Exam Principle 👉 Lateral thigh burning/numbness = lateral femoral cutaneous nerve 👉 Pure sensory nerve → no weakness 👉 Think meralgia paraesthetica (compression at inguinal ligament) 👉 "Seatbelt injury + lateral thigh pain = LFCN"

question_text: A 65 year old man presents to the Emergency Department with a sudden onset of severe epigastric pain that radiates to his back. The pain began approximately 6 hours ago and is described as sharp and constant. He has a history of a posterior gastric ulcer. A chest X-ray reveals free air under the diaphragm. Which of the following anatomical locations can gastric contents leak to?
explanation: Why? This patient has a perforated posterior gastric ulcer. Posterior perforations of the stomach typically leak into the lesser sac (omental bursa), which lies directly behind the stomach. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Sudden severe epigastric pain radiating to the back ✅ History of posterior gastric ulcer ✅ Free air under diaphragm → perforation These findings indicate a perforated viscus, specifically a posterior gastric ulcer. Why Lesser Sac Is Correct The lesser sac lies posterior to the stomach Posterior gastric ulcers perforate into the lesser sac This allows gastric contents (and air) to collect in this space Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Anterior wall of the stomach Not a space where contents leak — this is a structure, not a compartment. C. Greater sac Anterior gastric perforations typically leak into the greater sac, not posterior ones. D. Retroperitoneal space Although the posterior stomach is near retroperitoneal structures (e.g., pancreas), perforation typically enters the lesser sac first. E. Anterior diaphragm Not a site for leakage — free air may be seen under the diaphragm but does not leak into it. Key Exam Principle 👉 Posterior gastric ulcer → perforates into lesser sac 👉 Anterior gastric ulcer → perforates into greater sac 👉 "Posterior = lesser sac, Anterior = greater sac"

question_text: A 35 year old woman presents to the clinic complaining of difficulty in lifting her foot and toes when walking, and an inability to turn her foot outward. She reports that these symptoms developed gradually after she tripped over a curb 2 weeks ago. On examination, there is noticeable weakness of dorsiflexíon and eversion of the foot. She also describes numbness over the dorsal aspect of her foot and lateral shin. No knee or thigh involvement is noted. Which nerve is most likely affected based on the clinical presentation?
explanation: Why? This patient presents with classic features of common peroneal (fibular) nerve injury — foot drop (loss of dorsiflexion), weakness of eversion, and sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot and lateral shin. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Difficulty lifting foot → foot drop (loss of dorsiflexion) ✅ Inability to evert foot ✅ Numbness over dorsum of foot and lateral shin ✅ History of minor trauma (trip) — common at fibular neck ✅ No thigh or knee involvement These findings strongly indicate a lesion of the common peroneal nerve. Why Peroneal Nerve Is Correct The common peroneal nerve supplies: • Deep peroneal nerve → dorsiflexion • Superficial peroneal nerve → eversion • Sensory → dorsum of foot and lateral leg It is vulnerable to injury at the fibular neck (common after trauma) Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Femoral nerve Affects anterior thigh muscles (knee extension) and medial leg sensation — not foot dorsiflexion. B. Sciatic nerve Would produce more extensive deficits involving both tibial and peroneal components. D. Obturator nerve Affects thigh adduction, not foot movements. E. Tibial nerve Responsible for plantarflexion and inversion — injury causes inability to plantarflex, not dorsiflex. Key Exam Principle 👉 Foot drop (loss of dorsiflexion) = peroneal nerve 👉 Eversion loss = superficial peroneal nerve 👉 Dorsum foot sensation = peroneal nerve 👉 "Foot drop = common peroneal nerve (fibular neck injury)"

question_text: A 33 year old man presents to the neurology clinic following a motorbike accident two weeks ago. He reports difficulty straightening his right arm at the elbow. On examination, there is marked weakness of elbow extension, but shoulder abduction and wrist extension are preserved. What is the most likely affected nerve root?
explanation: Why? This patient has weakness of elbow extension, which is primarily performed by the triceps muscle. The triceps is mainly supplied by the C7 nerve root via the radial nerve. Preserved shoulder abduction and wrist extension help localize the lesion more specifically to C7 rather than a broader brachial plexus or radial nerve lesion. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Difficulty straightening the arm at the elbow ✅ Marked weakness of elbow extension ✅ Shoulder abduction preserved ✅ Wrist extension preserved ✅ Post-traumatic presentation These findings point to isolated involvement of the C7 nerve root. Why C7 Is Correct The triceps muscle is the main extensor of the elbow Triceps is predominantly supplied by C7 Elbow extension weakness is a classic sign of C7 root involvement Preserved shoulder abduction suggests C5 is intact Preserved wrist extension makes a more extensive radial nerve palsy less likely Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. C4 C4 does not significantly contribute to elbow extension. B. C5 C5 is more associated with shoulder abduction and elbow flexion, not primary elbow extension. C. C6 C6 mainly contributes to elbow flexion and wrist extension. E. C8 C8 is more involved in finger flexion and intrinsic hand muscle function than elbow extension. Key Exam Principle 👉 Elbow extension = triceps = mainly C7 👉 Shoulder abduction = C5 👉 Wrist extension = mainly C6/C7 via radial nerve 👉 "Weak triceps reflex/elbow extension = think C7"

question_text: A 45 year old man was hit on his back by a chair during a fight. He presents with back pain and bruising. The back pain is specifically at the midpoint of the spine at the level of the iliac crest. Which vertebra is likely to be affected?
explanation: Why? The iliac crest is an important anatomical landmark used to identify vertebral levels. A line drawn between the highest points of the iliac crests (Tuffier’s line) typically intersects the spine at the level of the L4 vertebra. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Pain at level of iliac crest ✅ Midpoint of spine ✅ Surface anatomy landmark These point directly to the vertebral level corresponding to the iliac crest. Why L4 Is Correct The iliac crest aligns with the L4 vertebra Clinically used landmark for lumbar puncture (L3/L4 or L4/L5 space) Therefore, trauma at this level most likely affects L4 Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. L2 Located higher than the iliac crest level. B. L3 Also above the iliac crest level. D. L5 Below the iliac crest level. E. S1 Much lower, at the sacral region. Key Exam Principle 👉 Iliac crest line (Tuffier’s line) = L4 vertebra 👉 Used clinically for lumbar puncture landmark 👉 "Iliac crest = L4"

question_text: A 12 year old boy presents with a painful swollen knee after a sudden fall on his right knee. The pain is localized at the knee cap. There is localized swelling over the patella. Which SINGLE anatomical structure is most likely to be affected?
explanation: Why? This patient has swelling directly over the patella following trauma (a fall onto the knee). The prepatellar bursa lies superficially over the patella and is commonly affected in such injuries. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Direct trauma (fall onto knee) ✅ Pain localized to the kneecap (patella) ✅ Swelling directly over the patella These findings are classic for prepatellar bursitis. Why Prepatellar Bursa Is Correct The prepatellar bursa lies between the skin and the patella It is most commonly affected by direct trauma or repeated kneeling ("housemaid’s knee") Swelling appears directly over the patella Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Semimembranosus bursa Located posteriorly (back of knee), not over the patella. C. Pretibial bursa Located below the patella over the tibial tuberosity. D. Suprapatellar bursa Located above the patella, deep to the quadriceps tendon. E. Pes anserine bursa Located medially below the knee joint, not over the patella. Key Exam Principle 👉 Swelling over patella after trauma = prepatellar bursa 👉 "Housemaid’s knee" = prepatellar bursitis 👉 Location of swelling tells you the bursa involved

question_text: A 32 year old man presents to the clinic with right shoulder pain and difficulty raising his right hand above his shoulder. He cannot pinpoint an exact time of injury and only recalls that his shoulder had been feeling a little odd lately but in spite of this he has continued his weight training program. He has decided to seek help as it has not been improving and when he observed his upper back in the mirror, he noticed that his shoulder blade was protruding in an awkward manner. On physical exam, there is increased pain with elevation of the right arm and increased pain on tilting of his head to the left. On arm elevation scapula winging is noted which is exaggerated when the patient pushes against a wall with his arms extended. Which nerve is likely affected?
explanation: Why? This patient has classic scapular winging that becomes more obvious when pushing against a wall, which is the hallmark of serratus anterior weakness due to long thoracic nerve injury. Difficulty raising the arm above shoulder level also supports impaired upward rotation of the scapula. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Shoulder blade protruding abnormally ✅ Winging of scapula ✅ Worse when pushing against a wall ✅ Difficulty raising arm above shoulder level ✅ History of weight training / repetitive strain These findings strongly point to long thoracic nerve palsy. Why Long Thoracic Nerve Is Correct The long thoracic nerve supplies the serratus anterior muscle Serratus anterior holds the scapula against the thoracic wall It also helps rotate the scapula upward during arm elevation above shoulder level When this nerve is injured, the scapula wings, especially when pushing against a wall Patients also struggle to fully elevate the arm Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Accessory nerve Supplies trapezius. Injury causes shoulder droop and weakness in shrugging, with more lateral winging rather than the classic wall-push winging seen here. B. Thoracodorsal nerve Supplies latissimus dorsi, which is involved in extension, adduction, and medial rotation of the arm — not scapular winging. C. Posterior interosseus nerve A branch of the radial nerve affecting finger and wrist extension, not the scapula. D. Dorsal scapular nerve Supplies rhomboids and levator scapulae. Injury may affect scapular retraction but does not classically cause prominent wall-push winging. Key Exam Principle 👉 Scapular winging worse on pushing against a wall = serratus anterior weakness 👉 Serratus anterior = long thoracic nerve 👉 Difficulty lifting arm above shoulder level supports loss of scapular upward rotation 👉 "Winged scapula + wall push test = long thoracic nerve"

question_text: A 35 year old man sustains a deep laceration to the anterior aspect of his left ankle after stepping on broken glass. Following the injury, he is unable to dorsiflex his left foot. Sensation is reduced only in the web space between the big toe and second toe. Sensation over the remainder of the dorsum of the foot is intact. What is the SINGLE most likely anatomical structure affected?
explanation: Why? This patient has a very specific pattern of motor and sensory loss that localizes to the deep peroneal (fibular) nerve. Loss of dorsiflexion indicates involvement of the anterior compartment muscles, while sensory loss limited to the first web space is characteristic of the deep peroneal nerve. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Inability to dorsiflex foot (foot drop) ✅ Injury at anterior ankle (where deep peroneal nerve runs superficially) ✅ Sensory loss ONLY in first web space (between 1st and 2nd toes) ✅ Rest of dorsum sensation intact These findings precisely localize the lesion. Why Deep Peroneal Nerve Is Correct The deep peroneal nerve supplies: • Anterior compartment → dorsiflexion of foot • Sensory → first dorsal web space only Injury at the anterior ankle commonly affects this nerve Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Femoral nerve Supplies anterior thigh — not involved in foot movement or sensation. B. Sural nerve Supplies posterolateral leg and lateral foot, not the first web space. C. Sciatic nerve Would produce widespread deficits affecting both tibial and peroneal components. E. Superficial peroneal nerve Supplies most of the dorsum of the foot, not the first web space, and mainly controls eversion, not dorsiflexion. Key Exam Principle 👉 First web space sensation = deep peroneal nerve 👉 Dorsiflexion = anterior compartment = deep peroneal nerve 👉 Dorsum of foot (except web space) = superficial peroneal nerve 👉 "1st web space = deep peroneal nerve"

question_text: A 44 year old woman presents to the clinic complaining of progressive weakness in her right arm over the past three months. She reports difficulty in raising her arm above her head and a prominent winging' of her scapula when she presses against a wall. She denies any trauma or previous surgery. On examination, there is noticeable atrophy of the muscles around the scapula and diminished strength in shoulder abduction. Which nerve is most likely affected?
explanation: Why? This patient has classic features of serratus anterior weakness causing scapular winging, especially when pushing against a wall. The serratus anterior is supplied by the long thoracic nerve. Difficulty raising the arm above the head also occurs because the serratus anterior is essential for upward rotation of the scapula during arm elevation. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Progressive difficulty raising arm above head ✅ Prominent scapular winging ✅ Winging worsens when pressing against a wall ✅ Muscle wasting around the scapula ✅ Reduced shoulder abduction/elevation These findings strongly indicate long thoracic nerve palsy. Why Long Thoracic Nerve Is Correct The long thoracic nerve innervates the serratus anterior muscle Serratus anterior holds the scapula against the thoracic wall When it is weak or paralyzed, the scapula wings prominently, especially during the wall-push test It also assists with upward rotation of the scapula, which is necessary to raise the arm fully above the head Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Axillary nerve Supplies deltoid and teres minor. Injury causes impaired shoulder abduction and numbness over the regimental badge area, but does not cause classic wall-push scapular winging. B. Suprascapular nerve Supplies supraspinatus and infraspinatus. Injury causes weak initiation of abduction and weak external rotation, but not prominent scapular winging. C. Dorsal scapular nerve Supplies rhomboids and levator scapulae. Injury may affect scapular retraction, but classic wall-push winging is not typical. E. Spinal accessory nerve Supplies trapezius. Injury can cause shoulder droop and difficulty shrugging, with lateral winging rather than the classic medial winging seen on wall push. Key Exam Principle 👉 Scapular winging worse on wall push = serratus anterior weakness 👉 Serratus anterior = long thoracic nerve 👉 Difficulty raising arm above head supports loss of scapular upward rotation 👉 "Wall-push winging = long thoracic nerve"

question_text: A 22 year old man had a fall down a ladder and hit his shoulder and arm. He has weakness of right shoulder abduction and right shoulder external rotation. He has good strength in the forearm and hand muscles. He has numbness over the lateral part of the arm and forearm. Which structure is most likely affected?
explanation: Why? This patient has weakness of shoulder abduction and external rotation, which points to involvement of muscles supplied by C5-C6 fibers — especially the deltoid, supraspinatus, infraspinatus, and teres minor. The sensory loss over the lateral arm and forearm also fits a C5-C6/upper trunk brachial plexus lesion. Preserved forearm and hand strength makes a more distal nerve lesion less likely. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Weak shoulder abduction ✅ Weak shoulder external rotation ✅ Numbness over lateral arm and forearm ✅ Good forearm and hand muscle strength ✅ Trauma to shoulder region These findings localize to the upper brachial plexus (C5-C6). Why Upper Brachial Plexus Is Correct The upper trunk of the brachial plexus is formed by C5 and C6 roots C5-C6 contribute to: • Axillary nerve → deltoid, teres minor • Suprascapular nerve → supraspinatus, infraspinatus • Musculocutaneous nerve contribution → lateral forearm sensation Injury here causes weakness of shoulder abduction and external rotation, with sensory changes over the lateral arm/forearm Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Radial nerve Would mainly cause weakness of elbow, wrist, and finger extension, not isolated shoulder abduction/external rotation weakness. B. Axillary nerve Would explain shoulder abduction weakness and lateral arm numbness, but would not account for lateral forearm sensory loss or external rotation weakness as completely as an upper trunk lesion. C. Musculocutaneous nerve Would affect elbow flexion and sensation over the lateral forearm, but not shoulder abduction and external rotation. D. Lower brachial plexus Would mainly affect intrinsic hand muscles and finger flexors (C8-T1), not the shoulder. Key Exam Principle 👉 Shoulder abduction + external rotation weakness = C5-C6 involvement 👉 Lateral arm + lateral forearm sensory loss = upper trunk pattern 👉 Preserved hand function argues against lower plexus or widespread nerve injury 👉 "C5-C6 shoulder weakness = upper brachial plexus"

question_text: A 32 year old man presents to the Emergency Department after being involved in a road traffic accident. He reports double vision that worsens when looking downwards, such as when reading or descending stairs. The diplopia improves when he closes one eye. On examination, there is a noticeable difficulty in moving his eye downward, particularly when the eye is adducted. Which muscle is most likely involved?
explanation: Why? This patient has classic features of a superior oblique muscle dysfunction, typically due to trochlear nerve (CN IV) palsy. The superior oblique is responsible for depressing the eye when it is adducted, which explains the difficulty looking downwards, especially during activities like reading or descending stairs. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Diplopia worse when looking down ✅ Difficulty reading or going downstairs ✅ Problem depressing the eye when adducted ✅ Diplopia improves when one eye is closed (binocular diplopia) These are hallmark features of superior oblique dysfunction.
