Why Superior Oblique Is Correct The superior oblique muscle depresses the eye when it is adducted It also contributes to intorsion and abduction Damage leads to vertical diplopia, worse when looking down (e.g., stairs, reading) Commonly affected in trauma due to long intracranial course of CN IV Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Inferior oblique Elevates the eye in adduction — opposite function. B. Superior rectus Elevates the eye, not depresses it in adduction. C. Lateral rectus Abducts the eye — CN VI, not involved in vertical movement here. D. Medial rectus Adducts the eye — CN III, not responsible for depression in adduction. Key Exam Principle 👉 Depression in adducted eye = superior oblique 👉 Trouble reading/going downstairs = CN IV palsy 👉 "Down & in problem = superior oblique"

question_text: What is the lymphatic drainage of the testes?
explanation: Why? The testes originate embryologically in the posterior abdominal wall and descend into the scrotum during development. Because of this, their lymphatic drainage follows their original abdominal origin rather than their final position. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Testes (not scrotum) ✅ Embryological origin in posterior abdominal wall These point to abdominal (not inguinal) lymphatic drainage. Why Para-aortic Nodes Is Correct Testicular lymph drains to the para-aortic (lumbar) lymph nodes These nodes lie along the abdominal aorta near the level of the renal vessels This reflects the embryological origin of the testes Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Superficial inguinal nodes Drain the scrotal skin, not the testes. B. Deep inguinal nodes Also related to superficial structures of the lower limb and perineum, not testes. C. Internal iliac lymph nodes Drain pelvic organs, not the testes. D. External iliac lymph nodes Drain lower abdominal wall and some pelvic structures, not testes. Key Exam Principle 👉 Testes = para-aortic (lumbar) nodes 👉 Scrotum = superficial inguinal nodes 👉 "Testes follow abdomen, scrotum follows skin"

question_text: A 35 year old man sustained a fall while working as a window cleaner 6 months ago. He recalls grabbing onto a ledge with an outstretched left arm on his descent. On impact, he fractured his left elbow and injured his shoulder. He was managed surgically and has his arm in a sling. He has since suffered from a decreased sensation of his little finger. On examination, wasting of the interosseous muscles is observed. A loss of sensation is noted in the little finger and medial half of the ring finger. On assessing motor function, he is unable to cross the two fingers or abduct his little finger. Which is the SINGLE most likely structure to be damaged?

options.a: Inferior trunk of the brachial plexus
options.b: Superior trunk of the brachial plexus

explanation: Why? This patient has classic signs of an ulnar-sided hand deficit: sensory loss in the little finger and medial half of the ring finger, interosseous muscle wasting, inability to abduct the little finger, and inability to cross the fingers. These findings indicate involvement of C8-T1 fibers, which travel through the inferior trunk of the brachial plexus. The mechanism of injury — grabbing onto a ledge with an outstretched arm during a fall — is a traction injury that can damage the inferior trunk. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Traction injury from grabbing onto a ledge during a fall ✅ Sensory loss in little finger and medial half of ring finger ✅ Interosseous muscle wasting ✅ Cannot cross fingers ✅ Cannot abduct little finger These findings point to a lower brachial plexus lesion involving C8-T1 fibers. Why Inferior Trunk of the Brachial Plexus Is Correct The inferior trunk is formed by C8 and T1 roots These fibers contribute significantly to the ulnar nerve and intrinsic hand muscles Interossei muscles are supplied by the ulnar nerve Abduction of the little finger is performed by abductor digiti minimi (ulnar nerve) A traction injury to the upper limb can damage the inferior trunk, producing Klumpke-type features Why the Other Options Are Less Likely B. Superior trunk of the brachial plexus Would produce C5-C6 deficits such as weakness of shoulder abduction and elbow flexion, not intrinsic hand muscle wasting with ulnar sensory loss. C. Axillary nerve Would cause deltoid weakness and numbness over the regimental badge area, not little finger sensory loss or interosseous wasting. D. Median nerve Would affect thumb opposition and sensation of the lateral 3½ digits, not the little finger and interossei. E. Radial nerve Would cause weakness of extension at the elbow, wrist, or fingers, not ulnar-sided sensory loss and intrinsic hand weakness. Key Exam Principle 👉 Little finger + medial half of ring finger sensory loss = C8/T1-ulnar distribution 👉 Interossei wasting + inability to cross fingers = ulnar/intrinsic hand muscle involvement 👉 Traction injury to abducted arm = inferior trunk brachial plexus injury 👉 "Lower trunk lesion = Klumpke-type hand findings"

question_text: A 54 year old man attends your clinic with persistent neck pain, discomfort in his left arm, and increasing weakness in his left hand. He first noticed the neck pain about five months ago, with arm discomfort appearing one month later. The hand weakness began shortly afterwards and has progressively worsened, notably affecting his grip strength and dexterity, crucial for his job as a factory worker. On examination, all reflexes in his right arm are intact. Manual muscle testing shows significant weakness in the intrinsic muscles of his left hand, particularly affecting the finger abduction and adduction. Which cervical nerve root is most likely being compressed?
explanation: Why? This patient has neck pain radiating to the arm with progressive weakness of the intrinsic hand muscles, especially finger abduction and adduction. These muscles are mainly supplied by the ulnar nerve, which carries dominant fibers from the C8 nerve root. This pattern is most consistent with C8 radiculopathy. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Neck pain followed by arm discomfort ✅ Progressive hand weakness ✅ Reduced grip strength and dexterity ✅ Weak intrinsic hand muscles ✅ Finger abduction and adduction affected These findings point to C8 nerve root compression. Why C8 Is Correct C8 supplies many of the intrinsic hand muscles through the ulnar nerve contribution Finger abduction and adduction are performed by the interossei muscles Interossei weakness causes impaired dexterity and weak grip C8 radiculopathy commonly presents with neck pain radiating into the arm with hand weakness Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. C5 More associated with shoulder abduction and elbow flexion weakness, not intrinsic hand muscle weakness. B. C6 More associated with elbow flexion and wrist extension, with possible reduced biceps reflex. C. C7 More associated with elbow extension, wrist flexion, and reduced triceps reflex. E. T1 Also contributes to intrinsic hand muscles, but isolated cervical root compression causing this classic pattern is more commonly C8. Key Exam Principle 👉 Finger abduction/adduction = interossei = mainly C8/T1 👉 In cervical radiculopathy, intrinsic hand weakness usually points to C8 👉 Grip weakness + dexterity loss + neck pain = think C8 radiculopathy 👉 "Interossei weakness = C8 until proven otherwise"

question_text: A 21 year old girl has decreased taste sensation and decreased salivation 24 hours after having undergone a tympanoplasty. What is the SINGLE most likely nerve that is damaged?
explanation: Why? This patient developed decreased taste and salivation after ear surgery (tympanoplasty). The chorda tympani, a branch of the facial nerve (CN VII), runs through the middle ear and is vulnerable during such procedures. It carries taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and parasympathetic fibers to the submandibular and sublingual glands. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Recent tympanoplasty (middle ear surgery) ✅ Loss of taste sensation ✅ Reduced salivation These point directly to injury of the chorda tympani. Why Facial Nerve Is Correct The chorda tympani is a branch of the facial nerve (CN VII) It carries taste from the anterior 2/3 of the tongue It provides parasympathetic innervation to submandibular and sublingual salivary glands It passes through the middle ear → at risk in tympanoplasty Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Hypoglossal nerve Controls tongue movement only — no role in taste or salivation. B. Vagus nerve Carries taste from the epiglottis and innervates thoracoabdominal organs, not anterior tongue taste. D. Trigeminal nerve Provides general sensation to the face and oral cavity, not taste or salivation. E. Glossopharyngeal nerve Carries taste from the posterior 1/3 of the tongue and innervates the parotid gland, not the anterior 2/3. Key Exam Principle 👉 Tympanoplasty complication = chorda tympani injury 👉 Chorda tympani = facial nerve (CN VII) 👉 Anterior 2/3 taste + salivation (submandibular/sublingual) 👉 "Middle ear surgery → think facial nerve (chorda tympani)"

question_text: A 68 years old man attends the Emergency Department with a 3 hour history of sudden onset severe pain in the left leg. He reports that the leg became cold and numb shortly after the pain started. On examination, the left lower limb is pale and cool below the groin. Capillary refill is prolonged. The femoral pulse on the left is not palpable, and no distal pulses are detected. The right lower limb pulses are normal. Which artery is most likely to be affected?
explanation: Why? This patient has acute limb ischaemia of the left lower limb. The key clue is that the leg is ischaemic below the groin and the femoral pulse itself is absent. If the femoral pulse is not palpable, the arterial occlusion must be proximal to the femoral artery — most likely in the iliac artery. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Sudden severe leg pain ✅ Cold, pale, numb limb ✅ Prolonged capillary refill ✅ Left femoral pulse absent ✅ No distal pulses detected ✅ Right leg pulses normal These findings indicate an acute arterial occlusion proximal to the femoral artery on the left side. Why Iliac Artery Is Correct The iliac artery lies proximal to the common femoral artery An occlusion here would stop blood flow into the femoral artery This explains why the femoral pulse is absent and why the whole limb below the groin is ischaemic Acute occlusion of a major proximal artery causes the classic features of acute limb ischaemia Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Common femoral artery This is possible in some settings, but the question emphasizes ischaemia below the groin with absent femoral pulse, making a more proximal inflow lesion in the iliac artery the best answer. C. Inferior epigastric artery Supplies the anterior abdominal wall, not the lower limb. D. Deep femoral artery Supplies mainly the thigh. Its occlusion would not abolish the femoral pulse. E. Superficial femoral artery Would reduce distal pulses, but the femoral pulse would still be present because the obstruction is distal to the femoral pulse point. Key Exam Principle 👉 Absent femoral pulse = lesion proximal to femoral artery 👉 Proximal lower limb inflow lesion = iliac artery 👉 Acute pain + pallor + pulselessness + cold limb = acute limb ischaemia 👉 "No femoral pulse = think iliac occlusion"

question_text: A 75 year old woman was referred by her general practitioner to the same day ophthalmology clinic because of a 4 hour history of sudden painless loss of vision affecting her right eye. Her medical history includes hypertension and heavy smoking. Ophthalmic assessment showed visual acuity of light perception only in the right eye and 6/9 in the left eye. Apart from early cataracts, examination of the anterior segment was unremarkable. On further questioning, the patient admitted that she had previously experienced episodes of vision loss in the same eye, which lasted for a few seconds to a few minutes. What is most likely artery involved in this scenario?
explanation: Why? This patient has sudden painless monocular vision loss with a history of brief prior transient episodes of vision loss in the same eye. This is classic for central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO), often preceded by amaurosis fugax. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Sudden painless loss of vision in one eye ✅ Visual acuity reduced to light perception only ✅ Previous brief episodes of vision loss in the same eye ✅ Vascular risk factors: hypertension and heavy smoking ✅ Anterior segment examination essentially normal These findings strongly point to retinal arterial occlusion. Why Central Retinal Artery Is Correct The central retinal artery supplies the inner retina Acute occlusion causes sudden, severe, painless monocular visual loss Transient episodes beforehand suggest amaurosis fugax due to embolic or vascular insufficiency This is commonly associated with atherosclerotic disease and emboli Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Anterior communicating artery Associated with cerebral circulation and aneurysms, not isolated monocular retinal ischaemia. B. Anterior cerebral artery Supplies the medial frontal and parietal lobes; occlusion causes contralateral leg weakness/sensory loss, not isolated monocular blindness. C. Middle cerebral artery Causes contralateral face/arm weakness, sensory loss, aphasia, or neglect — not isolated painless monocular vision loss. E. Posterior inferior cerebellar artery Causes lateral medullary syndrome, not retinal ischaemia. Key Exam Principle 👉 Sudden painless monocular vision loss = central retinal artery occlusion until proven otherwise 👉 Transient prior episodes = amaurosis fugax 👉 Retina/optic pathway before chiasm causes monocular symptoms 👉 "Painless one-eye blindness = central retinal artery"

question_text: A 58 year old man underwent surgery for varicose veins of the leg. He is now complaining of numbness on the medial side of his foot. What is the SINGLE most likely nerve involved?
explanation: Why? This patient developed sensory loss on the medial side of the foot following varicose vein surgery. The saphenous nerve runs alongside the great saphenous vein and is commonly injured during such procedures, leading to sensory loss in this distribution. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ History of varicose vein surgery ✅ Numbness after surgery ✅ Medial side of foot affected These findings point to iatrogenic injury of a sensory nerve closely related to the great saphenous vein. Why Saphenous Nerve Is Correct The saphenous nerve is a branch of the femoral nerve It provides sensation to the medial leg and medial foot It runs with the great saphenous vein → vulnerable during vein surgery Injury leads to numbness along the medial aspect of the leg and foot Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Common peroneal nerve Supplies lateral leg and dorsum of foot, not medial foot. B. Tibial nerve Supplies plantar surface of the foot, not specifically medial cutaneous sensation of the foot dorsum/medial side. C. Sural nerve Supplies lateral foot, not medial foot. E. Medial plantar nerve Supplies plantar (sole) aspect of medial foot, not the medial surface described here and less likely in varicose vein surgery. Key Exam Principle 👉 Medial leg + medial foot sensation = saphenous nerve 👉 Great saphenous vein surgery → risk of saphenous nerve injury 👉 "Varicose vein surgery complication = saphenous nerve"

question_text: A 43 year old man presents to the Accident and Emergency Department after being stabbed in the back of the neck with a knife in the street. He was kicked several times on his neck and face while he was on the floor. He has an open wound on the back of his neck towards the left side with minimal bleeding. On examination, he has an asymmetrical rise and fall of his chest when breathing. He has noticeable stridor. What is the SINGLE most likely nerve that is damaged?
explanation: Why? This patient has trauma to the neck followed by asymmetrical chest movement, which strongly suggests hemidiaphragmatic paralysis due to phrenic nerve injury. The phrenic nerve arises from C3-C5 and supplies the diaphragm, so damage causes impaired movement of one side of the diaphragm and abnormal chest expansion. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Stab wound to the neck ✅ Asymmetrical rise and fall of the chest ✅ Respiratory difficulty ✅ Neck trauma involving an area where major cervical nerves may be damaged These findings point most strongly to phrenic nerve injury. Why Phrenic Nerve Is Correct The phrenic nerve supplies the diaphragm Unilateral injury causes paralysis of one hemidiaphragm This leads to asymmetrical chest movement during breathing The phrenic nerve runs through the neck and can be injured in penetrating neck trauma Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Recurrent laryngeal nerve Can cause hoarseness or stridor due to vocal cord paralysis, but would not explain asymmetrical chest movement. B. Vagus nerve May affect laryngeal function indirectly, but isolated vagus injury is less likely to produce the prominent asymmetrical chest rise described. D. Accessory nerve n Supplies sternocleidomastoid and trapezius. Injury causes shoulder droop and weak head turning, not breathing asymmetry. E. Superior laryngeal nerve Affects pitch and laryngeal sensation, not diaphragmatic movement. Key Exam Principle 👉 Asymmetrical chest movement after neck trauma = think phrenic nerve 👉 Phrenic nerve supplies the diaphragm 👉 C3, C4, C5 keep the diaphragm alive 👉 "Neck trauma + uneven breathing = phrenic nerve injury"

question_text: A 32 year old man presents to the Emergency Department with a fracture-dislocation of his right elbow. He complains of loss of sensation in his little finger and ring finger. Which is the SINGLE most likely nerve to be involved?
explanation: Why? This patient has sensory loss in the little finger and medial half of the ring finger, which is the classic distribution of the ulnar nerve. The ulnar nerve runs behind the medial epicondyle at the elbow, making it particularly vulnerable in elbow injuries such as fracture-dislocations. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Elbow fracture-dislocation ✅ Loss of sensation in little finger ✅ Involvement of ring finger (medial half) These findings localize to the ulnar nerve. Why Ulnar Nerve Is Correct The ulnar nerve supplies sensation to the little finger and medial half of the ring finger It passes behind the medial epicondyle ("funny bone") It is commonly injured in elbow trauma Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Median nerve Supplies thumb, index, middle, and lateral half of ring finger — not the little finger. C. Radial nerve Supplies the dorsum of the hand and extensor muscles — not this sensory distribution. D. Superficial branch of radial nerve Provides sensation to the dorsolateral hand, not the little finger. E. Axillary nerve Supplies the shoulder region, not the hand. Key Exam Principle 👉 Little finger + medial ring finger = ulnar nerve 👉 Elbow injury → think ulnar nerve (medial epicondyle) 👉 "Funny bone nerve = ulnar nerve"

question_text: A 45 year old man has been informed by his doctors that he has a carcinoma of the head of the pancreas. Which SINGLE structure is in close proximity with the head of pancreas?
explanation: Why? The head of the pancreas lies in close anatomical relation to the common bile duct, which passes through or along it. Tumors in the head of the pancreas commonly compress the common bile duct, leading to obstructive jaundice. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Head of pancreas ✅ Asking for closely related structure This points to structures anatomically embedded or directly adjacent to the pancreatic head. Why Common Bile Duct Is Correct The common bile duct runs through the head of the pancreas Pancreatic head tumors frequently compress it This causes obstructive jaundice (painless jaundice — classic exam finding) Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Pylorus Adjacent to the pancreas but not as closely related as the bile duct passing through the head. B. Aorta Located posteriorly in the abdomen, not directly related to the pancreatic head. C. Left kidney Located posteriorly and more lateral — not closely related to the head. D. Splenic artery Runs along the superior border of the pancreas, mainly associated with the body and tail. Key Exam Principle 👉 Head of pancreas → related to common bile duct 👉 Compression → obstructive jaundice 👉 "Painless jaundice = pancreatic head tumor"

question_text: A 42 years old man presents to the Emergency Department after sustaining a stab injury to the root of the neck during an assault. He reports numbness along the upper medial aspect of the forearm on the right side and weakness when attempting to grip objects. Which spinal nerve root is most likely to be affected?
explanation: Why? This patient has sensory loss over the medial forearm and weakness in grip strength. The medial forearm sensation is supplied by the medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm, which carries fibers predominantly from the T1 nerve root. Grip strength and intrinsic hand muscles also receive significant contribution from T1. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Stab injury at root of neck (brachial plexus region) ✅ Numbness over upper medial forearm ✅ Weak grip strength These findings point to involvement of lower brachial plexus fibers, particularly T1. Why T1 Is Correct T1 contributes to intrinsic hand muscles → important for grip strength Supplies medial forearm sensation via medial cutaneous nerve of forearm Injury at root of neck commonly affects lower plexus (C8-T1) T1 is especially responsible for medial forearm sensation Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. C5 Supplies shoulder (deltoid) and lateral arm — not medial forearm. B. C6 Supplies lateral forearm and thumb sensation, not medial forearm. C. C7 Supplies middle finger and triceps — not medial forearm. D. C8 Supplies medial hand and fingers, but medial forearm sensation is more specifically T1. Key Exam Principle 👉 Medial forearm sensation = T1 👉 Grip weakness + medial forearm numbness = lower plexus (T1) 👉 Root of neck injury → think brachial plexus (especially lower trunk) 👉 "Medial forearm = T1"

question_text: A 63 year old woman presents to the clinic with a one-week history of right thigh pain and weakness. The pain is described as a sharp sensation on the anterior aspect of the thigh, radiating to the medial leg. She reports difficulty in walking and an inability to extend her knee fully. On examination, there is a noticeable wasting of the quadriceps muscle, and the knee jerk reflex is absent on the right side. Sensation to light touch is diminished over the anterior and medial aspects of the thigh and medial side of the leg. The patient has a history of diabetes mellitus and recently underwent a hysterectomy. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Why? This patient has a classic femoral nerve lesion. The combination of anterior thigh pain, quadriceps weakness, inability to extend the knee, absent knee jerk reflex, and sensory loss over the anterior thigh and medial leg all point to femoral nerve involvement. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Anterior thigh pain radiating to medial leg ✅ Weakness in knee extension (quadriceps) ✅ Quadriceps muscle wasting ✅ Absent knee jerk reflex (L3-L4 via femoral nerve) ✅ Sensory loss over anterior thigh and medial leg ✅ Recent pelvic surgery (risk of femoral nerve injury) These findings strongly localize to the femoral nerve. Why Femoral Nerve Lesion Is Correct The femoral nerve supplies: • Quadriceps → knee extension • Sensation → anterior thigh and medial leg (via saphenous nerve) • Knee jerk reflex (L3-L4) It can be injured during pelvic or abdominal surgery (e.g., hysterectomy) Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Sciatica Affects posterior thigh and leg with sciatic nerve distribution, not anterior thigh or knee extension. C. Multiple sclerosis Would produce central neurological signs and is unlikely to present as an isolated peripheral nerve deficit. D. Lumbar radiculopathy Could mimic some features, but the clear distribution and association with surgery strongly favor a peripheral femoral nerve lesion. E. Peripheral neuropathy Typically bilateral and symmetric (e.g., diabetic neuropathy), not a focal unilateral deficit. Key Exam Principle 👉 Anterior thigh + medial leg sensation = femoral nerve 👉 Knee extension (quadriceps) = femoral nerve 👉 Absent knee jerk = L3-L4 (femoral nerve) 👉 Pelvic surgery → risk of femoral nerve injury 👉 "Quadriceps weakness + absent knee jerk = femoral nerve"

question_text: A man is undergoing elective laparoscopic appendicectomy. A port is inserted at the midway point between the anterior midline and the mid-axillary line, approximately at the level of the umbilicus. Which of the following structure(s) is pierced at this location?
explanation: Why? The described port site is lateral to the midline (not at the linea alba) and around the umbilical level. At this location, the abdominal wall consists of the lateral muscle layers, including the external oblique aponeurosis, internal oblique, and transversus abdominis. The most superficial structure pierced from the options given is the external oblique aponeurosis. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Midway between midline and mid-axillary line (lateral abdominal wall) ✅ Level of the umbilicus ✅ Laparoscopic port insertion through abdominal wall layers These indicate a lateral abdominal wall entry, not a midline structure. Why External Oblique Aponeurosis Is Correct The external oblique aponeurosis forms part of the anterior abdominal wall It is the most superficial muscle layer encountered in the lateral abdomen A port inserted here will pierce this layer first before deeper layers Why the Other Options Are Less Likely B. Iliacus muscle Located in the iliac fossa, deep and inferior — not at the umbilical level. C. Linea alba Located at the midline — not at a lateral port site. D. Serratus anterior muscle Located on the lateral thoracic wall, above this region. E. Thoracolumbar fascia Located posteriorly in the back, not at the anterior/lateral abdominal wall. Key Exam Principle 👉 Lateral abdominal wall entry → passes through muscle layers (external oblique first) 👉 Midline entry → linea alba 👉 "Not midline = not linea alba → think muscle layers"

question_text: A 32 year old man has complaints of pain on the medial side of his left forearm. There was also associated weakness of finger abduction and finger adduction, as well weakness upon adduction of his thumb. Finger flexion was normal. On inspection, atrophy of the muscles of his left hand was noted. What is the SINGLE most likely associated injury?
explanation: Why? This patient has classic signs of ulnar nerve dysfunction, including weakness of finger abduction and adduction (interossei muscles), weakness of thumb adduction (adductor pollicis), and wasting of intrinsic hand muscles. Sensory symptoms over the medial forearm further support involvement of the ulnar distribution. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Pain on medial forearm ✅ Weak finger abduction and adduction ✅ Weak thumb adduction ✅ Normal finger flexion ✅ Intrinsic hand muscle wasting These findings strongly indicate ulnar nerve involvement. Why Ulnar Nerve Injury Is Correct The ulnar nerve supplies: • Interossei → finger abduction and adduction • Adductor pollicis → thumb adduction • Intrinsic hand muscles → fine motor control Finger flexion remains relatively preserved (mainly median nerve for FDS and partial FDP) Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. T1 nerve root injury Could affect intrinsic hand muscles, but the presentation is more consistent with a peripheral ulnar nerve lesion rather than a root lesion. B. C8 vertebral injury Would produce broader neurological deficits, not isolated ulnar-pattern findings. C. Median nerve injury Would affect thumb opposition and lateral digits, not interossei or thumb adduction. E. C6 nerve root injury Affects lateral forearm and wrist extension, not intrinsic hand muscles. Key Exam Principle 👉 Finger abduction/adduction = interossei = ulnar nerve 👉 Thumb adduction = ulnar nerve (adductor pollicis) 👉 Intrinsic hand wasting = ulnar nerve 👉 "PAD/DAB + thumb adduction = ulnar nerve"

question_text: A 72 year old man with type 2 diabetes and a 40 pack-year smoking history presents with left thigh and calf pain when walking short distances, which resolves on rest. On examination, the left femoral pulse is not palpable, whereas the right femoral pulse is strong. Distal pulses in the left leg are also absent. What is the most likely site of the arterial occlusion?
explanation: Why? This patient has intermittent claudication with absent femoral and distal pulses on the left side, indicating a significant arterial occlusion proximal to the femoral artery but distal enough to affect only one limb. This localizes the lesion to the external iliac artery. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Claudication (pain on walking, relieved by rest) ✅ Left femoral pulse absent ✅ Distal pulses also absent ✅ Right femoral pulse normal (unilateral disease) These findings indicate an occlusion proximal to the femoral artery on the affected side. Why External Iliac Artery Is Correct The external iliac artery continues as the femoral artery An occlusion here will abolish the femoral pulse and all distal pulses It affects only one limb, unlike abdominal aortic occlusion Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Abdominal aorta Would typically affect both lower limbs, leading to bilateral absent femoral pulses. B. Internal iliac artery Supplies pelvic organs and gluteal region — does not significantly affect femoral pulse. D. Popliteal artery Would affect distal pulses, but the femoral pulse would still be present. E. Common femoral artery Possible, but the pattern of claudication involving both thigh and calf with a clear proximal inflow issue is more classically due to external iliac occlusion. Key Exam Principle 👉 Absent femoral pulse = lesion proximal to femoral artery 👉 Unilateral absence = iliac artery (not aorta) 👉 Claudication + absent pulses = peripheral arterial disease 👉 "No femoral pulse (one side) = external iliac artery"

question_text: A 54 year old man undergoes surgery for varicose veins involving ligation and stripping of the small saphenous vein. The procedure is uncomplicated, and his leg is placed in a compression bandage. Two weeks later, at his postoperative review, he reports numbness and tingling over the outer border of his left foot. Examination reveals reduced sensation over the lateral aspect of the foot. Which nerve is most likely to have been injured during the operation?
explanation: Why? This patient has sensory loss over the lateral (outer) border of the foot following small saphenous vein surgery. The sural nerve runs alongside the small saphenous vein in the posterior leg and is at risk during stripping procedures. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Surgery on small saphenous vein ✅ Postoperative numbness ✅ Sensory loss over lateral border of foot These findings point to injury of a nerve closely related to the small saphenous vein. Why Sural Nerve Is Correct The sural nerve runs with the small saphenous vein Provides sensation to the lateral aspect of the foot and lower leg Commonly injured during small saphenous vein surgery Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Common peroneal nerve Would cause foot drop and affect dorsum of foot, not isolated lateral border sensation. B. Saphenous nerve Supplies medial leg and foot, associated with great saphenous vein. D. Superficial peroneal nerve Supplies most of the dorsum of the foot, not specifically the lateral border. E. Tibial nerve Supplies the plantar surface of the foot, not the lateral border. Key Exam Principle 👉 Small saphenous vein surgery → sural nerve injury risk 👉 Lateral foot sensation = sural nerve 👉 Great saphenous vein → saphenous nerve (medial) 👉 "Small saphenous = sural nerve"

question_text: A surgeon is performing a laparoscopy. What anatomical structure(s) is pierced during insertion of a port at the midway point between umbilicus and anterior superior iliac spine?

options.b: External oblique and internal oblique muscles
options.c: Internal oblique muscle and external oblique aponeurosis

explanation: Why? The point midway between the umbilicus and the anterior superior iliac spine lies on the lateral abdominal wall (McBurney’s point region). At this site, the abdominal wall consists of muscle layers rather than midline aponeurotic structures. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Midway between umbilicus and ASIS ✅ Lateral abdominal wall (not midline) These indicate that the incision passes through muscular layers. Why External Oblique and Internal Oblique Muscles Are Correct At this location, the abdominal wall is composed of: • External oblique muscle • Internal oblique muscle • Transversus abdominis (deeper layer, not listed) Thus, the port passes through the external oblique and internal oblique muscles Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Linea alba Located at the midline, not lateral. C. Internal oblique muscle and external oblique aponeurosis The external oblique is muscle laterally, not aponeurosis. D. Internal oblique aponeurosis Aponeurosis forms closer to midline, not at this lateral point. E. Rectus abdominis Located near the midline, not at McBurney’s point. Key Exam Principle 👉 Lateral abdominal wall → muscle layers (external oblique → internal oblique → transversus) 👉 Midline → linea alba 👉 McBurney’s point = muscular wall 👉 "Lateral = muscle, Midline = aponeurosis"

question_text: A 33 year old man has lower back pain shooting down his right leg that started two days ago after lifting heavy boxes. He has intact ankle and knee jerk reflexes. He has reduced sensory stimulus on the dorsum of the right foot. Which nerve root is likely affected?
explanation: Why? This patient has radicular pain (sciatica) with sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot, which is the classic dermatome for L5 nerve root involvement. The preserved reflexes help exclude L4 and S1 involvement. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Lower back pain radiating down the leg (radiculopathy) ✅ Triggered by lifting (disc prolapse) ✅ Reduced sensation over dorsum of foot ✅ Knee jerk (L4) intact ✅ Ankle jerk (S1) intact These findings localize the lesion to L5. Why L5 Is Correct L5 dermatome supplies the dorsum of the foot L5 radiculopathy commonly presents with sciatica after lifting There is no reliable reflex for L5 → reflexes may remain normal Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. L3 Supplies anterior thigh, not the foot. B. L4 Affects medial leg and knee jerk reflex (which is normal here). D. S1 Affects lateral foot and ankle reflex (Achilles), which is intact. E. Cauda equina Would present with bilateral symptoms, saddle anesthesia, and bladder/bowel dysfunction. Key Exam Principle 👉 Dorsum of foot sensation = L5 👉 Normal reflexes + radicular pain = think L5 👉 L4 = knee jerk, S1 = ankle jerk, L5 = no reflex 👉 "Dorsum foot = L5"

question_text: A 60 year old man presents with complaints of persistent burning pain and sensitivity to touch on the upper inner aspect of his left arm, into the axilla and can extend across the chest. He mentions no recent injuries or surgeries but reports that the discomfort has been gradually worsening over the past few months. There is no evidence of motor dysfunction. Which dermatome is most likely involved in this patient's symptoms?
explanation: Why? The described sensory distribution involves the upper medial arm, axilla, and extension onto the chest wall — this corresponds to the T2 dermatome, particularly via the intercostobrachial nerve (branch of T2). Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Upper inner (medial) arm ✅ Involvement of axilla ✅ Extension across the chest wall ✅ Pure sensory symptoms (burning pain, allodynia) These findings are characteristic of T2 dermatome involvement. Why T2 Is Correct T2 dermatome supplies the upper medial arm and axilla The intercostobrachial nerve (T2) crosses into the arm from the chest This explains pain radiating from axilla to chest and medial arm Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. C5 Supplies lateral shoulder and upper arm, not medial arm or axilla. B. C6 Supplies lateral forearm and thumb. C. T1 Supplies medial forearm, not the axilla and upper medial arm. E. L1 Supplies groin region, not upper limb or chest. Key Exam Principle 👉 Upper medial arm + axilla = T2 dermatome 👉 Intercostobrachial nerve = T2 👉 Chest → axilla → medial arm radiation = T2 👉 "Axilla + medial arm = T2"

question_text: A 23 year old man is having difficulty in speaking following a stab wound to the right of his neck. On tongue protrusion test, the tip of tongue is deviated to the right. Which of the following nerve is the SINGLE most likely to be affected in this patient?
explanation: Why? Deviation of the tongue on protrusion indicates hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) injury. The tongue deviates toward the side of the lesion due to unopposed action of the contralateral genioglossus muscle. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Difficulty speaking (dysarthria) ✅ Tongue deviation on protrusion ✅ Deviation to the right side ✅ Neck stab wound (possible cranial nerve injury) These findings point to hypoglossal nerve damage. Why Hypoglossal Nerve Is Correct The hypoglossal nerve supplies all intrinsic and most extrinsic tongue muscles On protrusion, the genioglossus muscles push the tongue forward If one side is weak, the tongue deviates toward the side of the lesion Rightward deviation = right hypoglossal nerve injury Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Facial nerve Controls facial expression, not tongue movement. C. Vagus nerve Affects palate and voice, not tongue deviation. D. Trigeminal nerve Controls mastication and facial sensation, not tongue movement. E. Glossopharyngeal nerve Involved in taste (posterior 1/3) and swallowing, not tongue motor control. Key Exam Principle 👉 Tongue deviates TOWARD the side of lesion (LMN) 👉 CN XII = hypoglossal nerve = tongue movement 👉 Dysarthria + deviation = hypoglossal nerve 👉 "Tongue points to the lesion"

question_text: A 50 year old man presents to the GP surgery with neck pain, right arm discomfort and right-hand weakness. The neck pain developed around 5 weeks ago and a few weeks later he started having weakness in his hand. There is a tingling sensation on the medial aspect of his right upper arm. There is associated weakness in abduction and adduction of the fingers of the same arm. A X-ray of his neck shows cervical vertebrae degenerative changes. Which nerve root is most likely affected?
explanation: Why? This patient has features pointing to T1 nerve root involvement. The key clues are tingling on the medial aspect of the upper arm and weakness of finger abduction and adduction, which reflect involvement of the intrinsic hand muscles supplied largely by T1 fibers. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Neck pain with arm symptoms ✅ Progressive hand weakness ✅ Tingling on the medial aspect of the upper arm ✅ Weakness of finger abduction and adduction ✅ Cervical degenerative changes suggesting radiculopathy These findings are most consistent with T1 radiculopathy. Why T1 Is Correct The T1 dermatome includes the medial aspect of the upper arm T1 contributes significantly to the intrinsic muscles of the hand Finger abduction and adduction are performed by the interossei muscles, which are mainly supplied by the ulnar nerve with strong T1 contribution Therefore, sensory symptoms in the medial upper arm plus intrinsic hand weakness localize best to T1 Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. C5 Typically affects shoulder abduction and sensation over the lateral upper arm, not intrinsic hand muscles. B. C6 Usually affects the lateral forearm, thumb, and wrist extension/biceps function. C. C7 More associated with triceps, wrist flexion, and middle finger sensory symptoms. D. C8 Often affects the medial forearm and hand grip/finger flexion, but medial upper arm sensory symptoms point more specifically to T1. Key Exam Principle 👉 Medial upper arm sensation = T1 👉 Finger abduction/adduction = interossei = mainly T1 👉 Neck pain + dermatomal sensory loss + intrinsic hand weakness = cervical radiculopathy 👉 "Medial upper arm + interossei weakness = T1"

question_text: A 36 year old man arrives at the Emergency Department following a street fight. He complains of severe pain and presents with visible bruising and an obvious deformity in his lower right knee. The patient is given immediate pain relief, and an X-ray is ordered to assess the extent of the injury. The X-ray reveals a fracture of the neck of the fibula. What is the SINGLE most commonly associated nerve injury?
explanation: Why? The common peroneal (fibular) nerve winds around the neck of the fibula, making it highly vulnerable to injury in fractures at this site. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Fracture of the neck of fibula ✅ Location near lateral knee These point directly to the nerve that courses superficially around this region. Why Common Peroneal Nerve Is Correct The common peroneal nerve wraps around the fibular neck It lies superficially → easily injured in trauma Injury leads to: • Foot drop (loss of dorsiflexion) • Loss of eversion • Sensory loss over dorsum of foot and lateral leg Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Sciatic nerve Located more proximally in the thigh, not at the fibular neck. B. Femoral nerve Supplies anterior thigh, not near fibular head. C. Musculocutaneous nerve Supplies arm muscles, not lower limb. E. Tibial nerve Runs deeper in the posterior leg and is less likely to be injured at the fibular neck. Key Exam Principle 👉 Fibular neck fracture = common peroneal nerve injury 👉 Results in foot drop 👉 "Fibular neck = peroneal nerve"

question_text: A 64 year old woman has difficulty in moving her right shoulder on recovering from surgery of the posterior triangle of her neck. What is the SINGLE most likely anatomical structure to be affected?
explanation: Why? The spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) runs superficially through the posterior triangle of the neck and is highly vulnerable during surgical procedures in this region. Injury leads to weakness of the trapezius muscle, resulting in difficulty elevating the shoulder. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Surgery in posterior triangle of neck ✅ Difficulty moving shoulder These findings strongly suggest damage to a nerve supplying shoulder muscles in that region. Why Accessory Nerve Is Correct The accessory nerve innervates the trapezius and sternocleidomastoid muscles Trapezius is responsible for shoulder elevation (shrugging) Damage leads to shoulder droop and difficulty elevating the shoulder The nerve is superficial in the posterior triangle → easily injured in surgery Why the Other Options Are Less Likely B. Glossopharyngeal nerve Involved in swallowing and taste (posterior 1/3 of tongue), not shoulder movement. C. Hypoglossal nerve Controls tongue movement, not shoulder. D. Vagus nerve Supplies larynx and parasympathetic organs, not shoulder muscles. E. Brachial plexus Would cause broader upper limb deficits, not isolated shoulder movement difficulty following posterior triangle surgery. Key Exam Principle 👉 Posterior triangle surgery complication = accessory nerve injury 👉 Accessory nerve = trapezius → shoulder elevation 👉 "Shoulder droop after neck surgery = CN XI"

question_text: A 60 year old man attends the Oral and Maxillofacial surgery outpatient clinic for a postoperative follow-up. He has recently undergone a right submandibular gland excision for sialolithiasis under general anaesthesia. He complains of decreased tongue movements. There is no numbness of his tongue and sensation is intact. On protrusion, his tongue deviates to the right. What is the SINGLE most likely damaged nerve?
explanation: Why? This patient has a pure motor tongue deficit after submandibular gland surgery. Tongue deviation on protrusion with intact sensation strongly indicates hypoglossal nerve injury. The tongue deviates toward the side of the lesion. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Recent submandibular gland excision ✅ Decreased tongue movements ✅ Tongue sensation intact ✅ Tongue deviates to the right on protrusion These findings point to a motor nerve to the tongue being damaged. Why Hypoglossal Nerve Is Correct The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) supplies the intrinsic and most extrinsic muscles of the tongue Injury causes weakness of the ipsilateral side of the tongue On protrusion, the tongue deviates toward the side of the lesion due to unopposed action of the normal genioglossus muscle on the opposite side It is at risk during submandibular gland surgery because of its anatomical proximity Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Facial nerve Supplies muscles of facial expression, not tongue movement. C. Lingual nerve Carries general sensation from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue. This patient has intact sensation, so it is unlikely. D. Vagus nerve Affects palate, pharynx, and larynx, not primary tongue motor movement. E. Glossopharyngeal nerve Supplies taste and sensation to the posterior one-third of the tongue, not tongue motor control. Key Exam Principle 👉 Tongue deviation with intact sensation = hypoglossal nerve lesion 👉 Tongue deviates TOWARD the side of the lesion 👉 Submandibular gland surgery can injure CN XII 👉 "Tongue points to the lesion"

question_text: A 64 year old builder was screwing shelves when he suddenly felt a sharp tearing sensation at the cubital fossa followed by the presence of a swelling in the front of the elbow. His arm is very tender. What is the SINGLE most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Why? This patient has a classic presentation of distal biceps tendon rupture — sudden tearing pain at the cubital fossa followed by swelling and tenderness. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Sudden sharp tearing sensation ✅ Location: cubital fossa (anterior elbow) ✅ Immediate swelling ✅ Tenderness These findings strongly suggest an acute tendon rupture. Why Tendon Rupture Is Correct The distal biceps tendon inserts at the radial tuberosity and passes through the cubital fossa Rupture typically presents with a sudden "pop" or tearing sensation Followed by swelling, pain, and sometimes a visible bulge ("Popeye" deformity) Common in older individuals during forceful activity Why the Other Options Are Less Likely B. Cubital tunnel syndrome Chronic ulnar nerve compression causing numbness/tingling, not acute tearing pain and swelling. C. Muscle haematoma Can cause swelling, but usually follows trauma and does not present with a classic tearing sensation. D. Bursitis Typically presents with gradual swelling and inflammation, not acute tearing pain. E. Stress fracture Develops gradually due to repetitive stress, not sudden onset with tearing sensation. Key Exam Principle 👉 Sudden tearing pain + swelling = tendon rupture 👉 Cubital fossa → think distal biceps tendon 👉 Older patient + forceful movement = rupture risk 👉 "Pop + swelling at elbow = distal biceps rupture"

question_text: A 71 year old woman presents to the clinic complaining of severe lower back pain following a minor fall at home. Her medical history includes osteoporosis. On examination, there is notable tenderness over the midline of her lower back corresponding to the highest point of the iliac crest on palpation. Which vertebra is most likely to be affected?
explanation: Why? The highest point of the iliac crest corresponds to the L4 vertebral level. This is a key surface anatomy landmark (Tuffier’s line), commonly used in clinical practice. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Tenderness at level of iliac crest ✅ Midline lumbar spine ✅ Surface anatomy landmark These point directly to L4. Why L4 Is Correct A line drawn between the highest points of the iliac crests intersects the spine at L4 This landmark is used for lumbar puncture (L3/L4 or L4/L5 space) Therefore, pain at this level corresponds to L4 vertebra Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. L1 Located higher in the lumbar spine. B. L2 Also above the iliac crest level. C. L3 Slightly above the iliac crest level. E. L5 Below the iliac crest level. Key Exam Principle 👉 Iliac crest line (Tuffier’s line) = L4 👉 Important landmark for lumbar puncture 👉 "Iliac crest = L4"

question_text: A 28 year old man presents to the clinic with pain, numbness, and tingling radiating down the posterior aspect of his right arm into the middle finger. He describes difficulty in extending his elbow. On examination, there is reduced strength in elbow extension and diminished sensation over the dorsal aspect of the middle finger. Reflex testing reveals a diminished triceps reflex. Which nerve root is most likely affected?
explanation: Why? This patient has classic features of C7 radiculopathy. The middle finger is the key sensory clue for C7, while elbow extension and the triceps reflex are also predominantly supplied by C7. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Pain radiating down posterior arm ✅ Numbness/tingling into the middle finger ✅ Weak elbow extension ✅ Diminished triceps reflex These findings localize strongly to the C7 nerve root. Why C7 Is Correct C7 dermatome classically involves the middle finger C7 myotome contributes strongly to triceps function → elbow extension The triceps reflex is mainly mediated by C7 So the combination of middle finger sensory symptoms + weak elbow extension + reduced triceps reflex = C7 radiculopathy Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. C5 Typically affects shoulder abduction and lateral upper arm sensation, not the middle finger or triceps reflex. B. C6 n More associated with thumb/lateral forearm sensory symptoms and biceps/wrist extension involvement. D. C8 More associated with ring/little finger symptoms and finger flexion or intrinsic hand weakness. E. T1 Mainly affects intrinsic hand muscles and medial forearm/arm sensation, not the middle finger or triceps. Key Exam Principle 👉 Middle finger = C7 dermatome 👉 Elbow extension = triceps = mainly C7 👉 Triceps reflex = C7 👉 "Middle finger + triceps = C7"

question_text: A 63 year old woman presents to the Emergency Department with an inability to flex the proximal interphalangeal joint of her fingers of the left hand. Upon further questioning, she reveals that she has broken a wine glass and caused a cut on the surface of her left hand. She also had no previous procedure done to her hand. On examination, there was 2x2cm clean cut on the left hand. Extension at wrist joint was normal with no problem in adduction and abduction of the hand. However, she was unable to flex her first metacarpophalangeal joint. An X-ray of the left hand was done which was normal. What structure is most likely to be injured in her case?
explanation: Why? This patient is unable to flex the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joints of the fingers, which is the classic action of flexor digitorum superficialis. A glass laceration to the hand can injure the flexor tendons, and the normal X-ray makes a tendon injury much more likely than a bony injury. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Inability to flex the proximal interphalangeal joints ✅ Clean laceration to the hand after broken glass injury ✅ X-ray normal ✅ Wrist extension normal ✅ Hand adduction and abduction normal These findings point toward an isolated flexor tendon injury rather than nerve injury or fracture. Why Flexor Digitorum Superficialis Is Correct Flexor digitorum superficialis flexes the proximal interphalangeal joints of the medial four fingers Injury to this tendon causes inability to flex the PIP joints Sharp lacerations commonly damage flexor tendons in the hand Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Flexor digitorum profundus Flexes the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints, not the PIP joints. C. Lumbrical muscles Flex the metacarpophalangeal joints and extend the interphalangeal joints, but they do not produce primary PIP flexion. D. Flexor digiti minimi Acts on the little finger only, not the general finger flexion pattern described. E. First dorsal interossei Responsible for abduction of the index finger, not finger flexion at the PIP joint. Key Exam Principle 👉 PIP flexion = flexor digitorum superficialis 👉 DIP flexion = flexor digitorum profundus 👉 MCP flexion + IP extension = lumbricals 👉 "PIP problem = FDS"

question_text: A 63 year old woman presents to the Emergency Department with an inability to flex the proximal interphalangeal joint of her fingers of the left hand. Upon further questioning, she reveals that she has broken a wine glass and caused a cut on the surface of her left hand. She also had no previous procedure done to her hand. On examination, there was 2x2cm clean cut on the left hand. Extension at wrist joint was normal with no problem in adduction and abduction of the hand. However, she was unable to flex her first metacarpophalangeal joint. An X-ray of the left hand was done which was normal. What structure is most likely to be injured in her case?

A glass laceration to the hand can injure the flexor tendons, and the normal X-ray makes a tendon injury much more likely than a bony injury. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Inability to flex the proximal interphalangeal joints ✅ Clean laceration to the hand after broken glass injury ✅ X-ray normal ✅ Wrist extension normal ✅ Hand adduction and abduction normal These findings point toward an isolated flexor tendon injury rather than nerve injury or fracture. Why Flexor Digitorum Superficialis Is Correct Flexor digitorum superficialis flexes the proximal interphalangeal joints of the medial four fingers Injury to this tendon causes inability to flex the PIP joints Sharp lacerations commonly damage flexor tendons in the hand Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Flexor digitorum profundus Flexes the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints, not the PIP joints. C. Lumbrical muscles Flex the metacarpophalangeal joints and extend the interphalangeal joints, but they do not produce primary PIP flexion. D. Flexor digiti minimi Acts on the little finger only, not the general finger flexion pattern described. E. First dorsal interossei Responsible for abduction of the index finger, not finger flexion at the PIP joint. Key Exam Principle 👉 PIP flexion = flexor digitorum superficialis 👉 DIP flexion = flexor digitorum profundus 👉 MCP flexion + IP extension = lumbricals 👉 "PIP problem = FDS"

question_text: A 55 year old man presents with an ulcer of the scrotum. Which is the SINGLE most likely lymph node involved in its lymphatic drainage?
explanation: Why? The scrotum is part of the superficial external genitalia, and its lymphatic drainage follows the pattern of skin structures below the umbilicus. Therefore, it drains primarily into the superficial inguinal lymph nodes. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Ulcer located on the scrotum ✅ Asking about lymphatic drainage These features indicate a superficial structure, not a deep pelvic or abdominal organ. Why Inguinal Lymph Node Is Correct The scrotal skin drains into the superficial inguinal lymph nodes This is similar to other superficial structures such as the lower abdominal wall and perineum Clinically, scrotal infections, ulcers, or cancers commonly spread to inguinal nodes Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. External iliac lymph node Drains deeper pelvic structures such as the bladder and prostate, not superficial scrotal skin B. Pre-aortic lymph node Drains foregut, midgut, and hindgut organs (e.g., intestines) C. Aortic lymph node Receives drainage from structures like the testes (not the scrotum) E. Cervical lymph node Drains head and neck structures, unrelated to scrotal drainage Key Exam Principle 👉 Scrotum = superficial inguinal lymph nodes 👉 Testes = para-aortic (lumbar) lymph nodes 👉 "Skin goes inguinal, gonads go para-aortic"

question_text: A 52 year old woman with a history of Graves disease is seen in the Emergency Department with a 2-day history of hoarseness. She had undergone a total thyroidectomy 2 weeks prior for the treatment of her Graves' disease. She had been diagnosed with Graves' disease 10 years prior. She had been treated with carbimazole for several years, but her condition had worsened, and she had developed a large goitre. Her voice is hoarse and she has difficulty speaking in a loud voice. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Why? This patient developed hoarseness following a thyroidectomy, which strongly suggests injury to the recurrent laryngeal nerve — a well-known complication of thyroid surgery. This nerve supplies all intrinsic muscles of the larynx (except cricothyroid), and its injury leads to vocal cord paralysis and hoarseness. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Recent total thyroidectomy ✅ Hoarseness of voice ✅ Difficulty speaking loudly ✅ History of large goitre (increases surgical risk) These findings point toward damage to a nerve closely related to the thyroid gland. Why Recurrent Laryngeal Nerve Injury Is Correct The recurrent laryngeal nerve runs very close to the thyroid gland and is at risk during thyroidectomy It innervates most intrinsic laryngeal muscles responsible for vocal cord movement Injury causes vocal cord paralysis → hoarseness, weak voice May present days to weeks after surgery Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Vocal cord paralysis This is a consequence, not the underlying cause. The question asks for the diagnosis (cause). C. External laryngeal nerve injury Affects cricothyroid muscle → inability to produce high-pitched sounds, not primary hoarseness D. Laryngeal oedema Typically presents acutely post-op with airway compromise, not delayed isolated hoarseness E. Laryngeal cancer Unlikely with acute onset after surgery Key Exam Principle 👉 Thyroid surgery complication = think recurrent laryngeal nerve 👉 RLN injury → hoarseness + vocal cord paralysis 👉 External laryngeal nerve → loss of pitch (high notes) 👉 "Hoarseness after thyroidectomy = RLN injury"

question_text: A 24 year old man is hit by a baton just above the knee on his right leg. This is followed by loss of motor control of the leg. His foot drops and is unable to dorsiflex his foot. There is loss of sensation over the front and outer half of the leg and dorsum of the foot. What is the SINGLE most likely anatomical structure to be affected?
explanation: Why? This patient has classic features of common peroneal nerve injury: foot drop (loss of dorsiflexion) and sensory loss over the anterior and lateral leg and dorsum of the foot. The nerve is especially vulnerable where it winds around the neck of the fibula, just below the knee — a common site of trauma. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Trauma just above the knee (near fibular neck) ✅ Foot drop (inability to dorsiflex) ✅ Sensory loss over anterior + lateral leg ✅ Sensory loss over dorsum of foot These findings localize the lesion to the common peroneal nerve. Why Common Peroneal Nerve Is Correct Supplies muscles responsible for dorsiflexion (via deep peroneal nerve) Supplies sensation to anterior/lateral leg and dorsum of foot (via superficial + deep branches) Highly vulnerable at fibular neck → commonly injured in trauma Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Sural nerve Purely sensory → does not cause motor deficit or foot drop C. Tibial nerve Controls plantarflexion → injury causes inability to stand on toes, not foot drop D. Lateral plantar nerve Branch of tibial nerve → affects intrinsic foot muscles only E. Medial plantar nerve Also a branch of tibial nerve → affects plantar foot sensation and intrinsic muscles Key Exam Principle 👉 Foot drop = common peroneal nerve injury 👉 Fibular neck = danger zone 👉 Dorsiflexion loss = deep peroneal branch 👉 "Foot drop = peroneal nerve until proven otherwise"

question_text: A 68 year old man presents with sudden onset of double vision and drooping of the left eyelid. Examination shows the left eye positioned downwards and outwards, a dilated non-reactive pupil, and complete ptosis. Which cranial nerve is most likely affected?
explanation: Why? This patient has classic features of oculomotor nerve (CN III) palsy: ptosis, a 'down and out' eye position, and a dilated non-reactive pupil. The oculomotor nerve supplies most extraocular muscles, the levator palpebrae superioris (for eyelid elevation), and parasympathetic fibers to the pupil. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Ptosis (drooping eyelid) ✅ Eye deviated 'down and out' ✅ Dilated, non-reactive pupil ✅ Diplopia These findings are hallmark signs of CN III palsy. Why Oculomotor Nerve Is Correct Supplies superior, inferior, and medial recti, and inferior oblique muscles Supplies levator palpebrae superioris → ptosis when damaged Carries parasympathetic fibers → pupil dilation when affected Unopposed lateral rectus (VI) and superior oblique (IV) → 'down and out' eye Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Abducens nerve Controls lateral rectus → causes inability to abduct eye, not ptosis or pupil dilation B. Facial nerve Controls facial expression → does not affect eye movements or pupil D. Optic nerve Responsible for vision, not eye movement or eyelid position E. Trochlear nerve Controls superior oblique → causes vertical diplopia, not 'down and out' eye or ptosis Key Exam Principle 👉 CN III palsy = 'down and out' + ptosis + blown pupil 👉 Pupil involvement suggests compressive lesion (e.g., aneurysm) 👉 "Down & out + ptosis = oculomotor nerve"

question_text: A 68 year old woman is unable to extend the interphalangeal joint of her right thumb six weeks following a fracture of the right radius. The other fingers and thumb movements are unaffected. What is the SINGLE most likely tendon to be damaged?
explanation: Why? This patient cannot extend the interphalangeal (IP) joint of the thumb, which is the specific action of extensor pollicis longus (EPL). EPL tendon rupture is a well-known delayed complication of distal radius fractures, often occurring weeks after the injury. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Inability to extend thumb at IP joint ✅ Occurs 6 weeks after radius fracture (classic timing) ✅ Other thumb and finger movements are normal (isolated tendon injury) These findings point specifically to EPL tendon rupture. Why Extensor Pollicis Longus Is Correct Extends the interphalangeal joint of the thumb Runs around Lister's tubercle → vulnerable after distal radius fracture Prone to delayed rupture due to compromised blood supply Classic complication weeks after wrist fracture Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Abductor pollicis longus Abducts the thumb at the carpometacarpal joint, not IP extension B. Extensor pollicis brevis Extends the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint of the thumb, not the IP joint D. Flexor digitorum profundus Flexes DIP joints of fingers, unrelated to thumb IP extension E. Flexor pollicis longus Flexes the IP joint of the thumb (opposite action) Key Exam Principle 👉 Thumb IP extension = extensor pollicis longus 👉 Delayed complication of distal radius fracture = EPL rupture 👉 "Can't extend thumb IP → think EPL"

question_text: A 33 year old man suffered a mandibular fracture and now has loss of sensation over the chin and mucosal surface of the lower lip. Which SINGLE nerve is most likely to be involved?
explanation: Why? Loss of sensation over the chin and lower lip is characteristic of injury to the mental nerve, which is a terminal branch of the inferior alveolar nerve. A mandibular fracture commonly damages the inferior alveolar nerve as it runs within the mandibular canal. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Mandibular fracture ✅ Loss of sensation over chin ✅ Loss of sensation over lower lip mucosa These findings localize the lesion to the inferior alveolar nerve. Why Inferior Alveolar Nerve Is Correct Branch of mandibular nerve (V3) Runs within the mandibular canal → vulnerable in fractures Gives rise to the mental nerve → supplies chin and lower lip Damage causes numbness of chin and lower lip (“numb chin syndrome”) Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Mandibular nerve Too proximal → would cause more widespread deficits including muscles of mastication C. Buccal nerve Supplies cheek mucosa and skin, not chin or lower lip D. Lingual nerve Supplies anterior 2/3 of tongue sensation, not chin/lip E. Facial nerve Motor to facial muscles → does not carry sensory from chin/lip Key Exam Principle 👉 Chin + lower lip sensation = mental nerve 👉 Mental nerve ← inferior alveolar nerve 👉 Mandibular fracture → think inferior alveolar nerve injury 👉 "Numb chin = inferior alveolar nerve"

question_text: A 67 year old man presents with pain in his left leg on walking short distances which resolves with rest. On examination, the left femoral pulse is absent, while the contralateral femoral pulse is palpable. Distal pulses below the femoral artery are also absent on the affected side. His blood pressure is 148/84 mmHg. What is the most likely site of the arterial occlusion?
explanation: Why? This patient has intermittent claudication with absence of the femoral pulse on one side. If the femoral pulse is absent, the obstruction must be proximal to the femoral artery. The most likely site is the external iliac artery, which supplies the femoral artery. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Intermittent claudication (pain on walking relieved by rest) ✅ Absent femoral pulse on affected side ✅ Distal pulses also absent ✅ Normal pulse on the opposite side These findings localize the blockage proximal to the femoral artery but distal to the aorta. Why External Iliac Artery Is Correct The external iliac artery becomes the femoral artery after passing under the inguinal ligament Occlusion here → no femoral pulse + no distal pulses Fits unilateral presentation Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Internal iliac Supplies pelvis and gluteal region → would not abolish femoral pulse C. Popliteal Distal to femoral artery → femoral pulse would still be present D. Superficial femoral artery Also distal → femoral pulse would still be palpable E. Thoracic aorta Would affect both sides, not unilateral findings Key Exam Principle 👉 Absent femoral pulse = lesion proximal to femoral artery 👉 External iliac → femoral artery continuation 👉 Unilateral loss = localized arterial occlusion 👉 "No femoral pulse → think external iliac"

question_text: A 32 years old man attends the Emergency Department after falling awkwardly onto his right shoulder while playing football. He reports immediate pain around the shoulder and upper chest. Since the injury, he has noticed numbness along the medial aspect of his right forearm extending towards the wrist. He also describes difficulty with fine motor tasks such as buttoning his shirt. Power in the intrinsic muscles of the right hand is reduced compared with the left. Sensation to light touch is reduced over the upper medial aspect of the forearm. Which nerve root is most likely affected?
explanation: Why? This patient most likely has a T1 nerve root lesion, classically associated with injury to the lower brachial plexus. The key findings are weakness of the intrinsic hand muscles causing difficulty with fine motor tasks, together with sensory loss over the medial forearm. The T1 root contributes significantly to the intrinsic muscles of the hand and to sensation over the medial forearm via the medial cutaneous nerve of forearm. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Fall onto the shoulder with pain around the shoulder and upper chest ✅ Numbness along the medial forearm towards the wrist ✅ Difficulty with fine motor tasks like buttoning a shirt ✅ Weakness of intrinsic hand muscles ✅ Reduced sensation over the upper medial forearm These findings point to lower brachial plexus involvement, especially T1. Why T1 Is Correct T1 supplies many intrinsic muscles of the hand via the ulnar and median nerves T1 contributes sensory fibers to the medial forearm Injury causes hand muscle weakness and impaired fine finger movements Lower trunk / T1 lesions may follow traction injuries around the shoulder region Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. C5 Would mainly affect shoulder abduction and elbow flexion, with sensory loss over the lateral upper arm, not the medial forearm or intrinsic hand muscles. B. C6 Would affect elbow flexion and wrist extension, with sensory changes over the thumb/lateral forearm. C. C7 Typically affects triceps, wrist flexion/extension, and sensation over the middle finger. D. C8 Can affect finger flexion and sensation over the ring/little fingers, but isolated medial forearm sensory loss and intrinsic hand weakness point more strongly to T1. Key Exam Principle 👉 Medial forearm sensation = T1 👉 Intrinsic hand muscle weakness = lower brachial plexus / T1 involvement 👉 Fine motor difficulty + medial forearm numbness = think T1 👉 "Medial forearm and hand intrinsics = T1 until proven otherwise"

question_text: A 59 year old male with known lung cancer presents to his general practitioner (GP) with the complaint of a hoarse voice. He was diagnosed with lung cancer two months ago and is currently receiving chemotherapy. He also complains that the cough that he initially presented with has not abated since receiving treatment. The patient appears to be thin and gives a history of weight loss over the past month. What is the SINGLE most likely nerve affected in this patient's hoarseness of voice?
explanation: Why? This patient with lung cancer presents with hoarseness, which strongly suggests involvement of the recurrent laryngeal nerve. Lung tumors, especially in the upper lobes or mediastinum, can compress or invade this nerve, leading to vocal cord paralysis and hoarseness. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Known lung cancer ✅ Persistent cough ✅ Hoarseness of voice ✅ Weight loss (suggesting disease progression) These findings point toward nerve compression by a thoracic malignancy. Why Recurrent Laryngeal Nerve Is Correct Supplies all intrinsic muscles of the larynx (except cricothyroid) Damage leads to vocal cord paralysis → hoarseness The left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops under the aortic arch → vulnerable to thoracic tumors Commonly affected in lung cancer and mediastinal pathology Why the Other Options Are Less Likely B. Phrenic nerve Supplies diaphragm → injury causes breathing problems, not hoarseness C. External laryngeal nerve Affects pitch (cricothyroid muscle), not primary hoarseness D. Hypoglossal nerve Controls tongue movements → causes dysarthria, not hoarseness E. Lateral head of median nerve Not a recognized anatomical structure related to voice Key Exam Principle 👉 Hoarseness + thoracic pathology = recurrent laryngeal nerve 👉 Left RLN is especially vulnerable (loops under aortic arch) 👉 Vocal cord paralysis → hoarse voice 👉 "Hoarseness in lung cancer = RLN compression"

question_text: A 72 year old woman undergoes total hip replacement surgery under general anaesthesia. The procedure is uneventful, and she is transferred to the recovery unit. An hour later, during a routine post-operative assessment, she reports weakness in her right hand. On examination, there is difficulty with wrist extension and reduced sensation over the dorsum of the hand. Her right arm was inappropriately placed during the surgery. What is the most likely cause of this presentation?
explanation: Why? This patient has classic features of radial nerve palsy: weakness of wrist extension (wrist drop) and sensory loss over the dorsum of the hand. The history of improper arm positioning during surgery suggests compression injury, commonly affecting the radial nerve along its course in the spiral groove of the humerus. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Post-operative onset after improper positioning ✅ Difficulty with wrist extension (wrist drop) ✅ Sensory loss over dorsum of hand These findings strongly localize to the radial nerve. Why Radial Nerve Is Correct Supplies wrist and finger extensors → injury causes wrist drop Provides sensation to dorsum of hand Vulnerable to compression in the spiral groove during prolonged positioning Common perioperative nerve injury Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Brachial plexus injury Would cause more widespread deficits affecting multiple nerve territories B. Median nerve palsy Affects thumb opposition and palmar sensation of lateral digits, not wrist extension D. Ulnar nerve palsy Causes clawing of hand and sensory loss in little/ring fingers, not wrist drop E. Axillary nerve injury Affects deltoid muscle and shoulder abduction, not wrist or hand function Key Exam Principle 👉 Wrist drop = radial nerve palsy 👉 Dorsum of hand sensation = radial nerve 👉 Compression during surgery = common cause 👉 "Wrist drop = radial nerve until proven otherwise"

question_text: A 22 year old man presents to the clinic following a recent sports-related injury to his groin area. He is experiencing difficulty with knee extension and reports a significant loss of sensation in the anterior thigh and medial side of the lower leg. Which nerve is most likely affected by this injury?
explanation: Why? This patient has weakness of knee extension and sensory loss over the anterior thigh and medial leg, which are classic features of femoral nerve injury. The femoral nerve innervates the quadriceps muscles (responsible for knee extension) and provides sensation to the anterior thigh and medial leg (via the saphenous nerve). Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Groin injury (location of femoral nerve) ✅ Difficulty with knee extension ✅ Sensory loss over anterior thigh ✅ Sensory loss over medial lower leg These findings localize to the femoral nerve. Why Femoral Nerve Is Correct Innervates quadriceps → knee extension Provides sensation to anterior thigh Via saphenous nerve → sensation to medial leg Runs through the groin (femoral triangle) → vulnerable in groin injuries Why the Other Options Are Less Likely B. Obturator nerve Supplies adductor muscles → affects thigh adduction, not knee extension C. Saphenous nerve Purely sensory → would not cause motor weakness D. Sciatic nerve Affects posterior thigh and most of leg below knee, not isolated anterior thigh/knee extension E. Tibial nerve Controls plantarflexion and posterior leg muscles, not knee extension Key Exam Principle 👉 Knee extension = femoral nerve (quadriceps) 👉 Anterior thigh + medial leg sensation = femoral nerve 👉 Groin injury → think femoral nerve 👉 "Can't extend knee = femoral nerve"

question_text: A 24 year old patient was lying down on the operating table in a position with his arms hanging down for 3 hours. Soon after he woke up, he complains of numbness and weakness on his left hand and has a wrist drop. There is a loss of sensation over a small area between the dorsal aspect of 1st and 2nd metacarpals. What is the SINGLE most likely structure to be damaged?
explanation: Why? This patient has classic signs of radial nerve injury: wrist drop and sensory loss in the anatomical snuffbox region (between the first and second metacarpals). Prolonged compression of the arm (e.g., improper positioning during surgery) commonly injures the radial nerve in the spiral groove. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Arm hanging for prolonged period (compression injury) ✅ Wrist drop (loss of wrist extension) ✅ Sensory loss in dorsal web space between 1st and 2nd metacarpals These findings are highly specific for radial nerve injury. Why Radial Nerve Is Correct Supplies wrist and finger extensors → injury causes wrist drop Provides sensation to the dorsal web space between thumb and index finger Vulnerable to compression in the spiral groove (“Saturday night palsy”) Classic postoperative positioning complication Why the Other Options Are Less Likely B. Median nerve Affects thumb opposition and palmar sensation of lateral digits, not wrist extension or dorsal web space sensation C. Ulnar nerve Causes claw hand and sensory loss in little and ring fingers D. Axillary nerve Affects shoulder abduction (deltoid), not wrist or hand E. Suprascapular nerve Supplies supraspinatus and infraspinatus → affects shoulder movement, not hand function Key Exam Principle 👉 Wrist drop = radial nerve 👉 Dorsal web space (1st–2nd metacarpal) = radial nerve sensory area 👉 Compression injury = classic cause 👉 "Snuffbox numbness + wrist drop = radial nerve"

question_text: A 33 year old man complains of double vision, facial pain and pain in his right ear. The double vision is worse when he looks to his right. He finds difficulty trying to look outwards with his right eye. There is discharge from his right ear. Which is the SINGLE most likely nerve to be involved?
explanation: Why? This patient has difficulty abducting his right eye, and the diplopia is worse when he looks to the right. This is the classic pattern of a right abducens nerve palsy. The abducens nerve supplies the lateral rectus muscle, which is responsible for outward movement of the eye. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Double vision worse on looking to the right ✅ Difficulty looking outwards with the right eye ✅ Ear pain and discharge ✅ Facial pain These findings suggest abducens nerve involvement, likely related to spread of infection or inflammation from the ear. Why Abducens Nerve Is Correct The abducens nerve supplies the lateral rectus muscle Lateral rectus abducts the eye Injury causes failure of abduction and horizontal diplopia that worsens on looking toward the affected side Ear infection can sometimes lead to involvement of nearby cranial nerves Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Trochlear nerve Supplies superior oblique → causes vertical diplopia, especially on looking down, not inability to abduct the eye B. Facial nerve Controls muscles of facial expression → may be affected in ear disease, but does not abduct the eye C. Vestibulocochlear nerve Responsible for hearing and balance, not eye abduction E. Oculomotor nerve Would cause ptosis, a down-and-out eye, and often pupil abnormalities, none of which are described Key Exam Principle 👉 Failure to look laterally = abducens nerve palsy 👉 Lateral rectus = CN VI 👉 Horizontal diplopia worse on gaze toward affected side = abducens lesion 👉 "Can't abduct the eye = abducens nerve"

question_text: A 25 year old man presents to the Emergency Department with a self-inflicted wound to his left wrist. He reports he accidentally cut his wrist with a glass shard earlier this evening. On examination, there is a clean laceration over the volar aspect of the wrist. He is unable to oppose his thumb to the fifth digit and has numbness over the palmar aspect of his thumb, index finger, and middle finger. Which nerve is most likely injured?
explanation: Why? This patient has classic features of median nerve injury at the wrist: loss of thumb opposition and sensory loss over the palmar aspect of the thumb, index, and middle fingers. The volar wrist is a common site where the median nerve can be injured in lacerations. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Volar (anterior) wrist laceration ✅ Inability to oppose thumb to little finger ✅ Sensory loss over palmar thumb, index, and middle fingers These findings strongly localize to the median nerve. Why Median Nerve Is Correct Supplies thenar muscles → enables thumb opposition Provides sensation to palmar aspect of lateral 3½ digits Runs superficially at the wrist → vulnerable in cuts Injury leads to “ape hand” deformity and loss of precision grip Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Ulnar nerve Causes claw hand and sensory loss in medial 1½ fingers, not thumb opposition loss B. Axillary nerve Supplies deltoid → affects shoulder abduction, not hand function D. Radial nerve Controls extension → causes wrist drop, not loss of opposition or palmar sensory loss E.
