Why Prophylactic Mastectomy Is Correct BRCA1 mutation → very high lifetime risk of breast cancer (up to ~70%) Risk-reducing bilateral mastectomy significantly lowers risk (>90%) Recommended in high-risk individuals after counseling More definitive than surveillance alone Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Mammogram Already done recently and normal Not needed immediately B. Ultrasound of the breast No palpable breast lesion to evaluate C. Sentinel node biopsy Only indicated when cancer is diagnosed D. Fine needle aspiration Axillary lymph node is small, smooth, and likely benign/reactive Not first-line without suspicious features Key Exam Principle 👉 BRCA1/2 positive = very high cancer risk 👉 Offer risk-reducing strategies (mastectomy ± oophorectomy) 👉 Normal imaging does NOT eliminate risk 👉 "BRCA positive → think prevention, not just screening"

question_text: A 29 year old woman presents to her GP with a two-day history of pain and swelling in her left breast. She is three weeks postpartum and currently breastfeeding. She reports localised tenderness, redness, and a feeling of warmth over the affected area. She also describes feeling feverish with myalgia. On examination, there is an erythematous area on the outer quadrant of the left breast with localised induration and tenderness. Her temperature is 38.3°C. What is the most likely causative organism?
explanation: Why? This patient has classic features of lactational mastitis, which commonly occurs in breastfeeding women due to milk stasis and bacterial entry through cracked nipples. The most common causative organism is Staphylococcus aureus. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Postpartum (3 weeks) and breastfeeding ✅ Localised breast pain, redness, warmth ✅ Fever and systemic symptoms (myalgia) ✅ Induration and tenderness These findings strongly indicate infective (lactational) mastitis. Why Staphylococcus aureus Is Correct Most common organism in lactational mastitis Originates from skin flora entering through nipple cracks Causes localized infection with systemic symptoms Can progress to breast abscess if untreated Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Escherichia coli More common in urinary or gastrointestinal infections Not typical for mastitis B. Group B Streptococcus Common in neonates and perinatal infections Less common cause of mastitis C. Klebsiella pneumoniae Associated with hospital-acquired infections Rare in mastitis E. Streptococcus pneumoniae Typically causes respiratory infections Not a common cause of mastitis Key Exam Principle 👉 Breastfeeding + painful red breast + fever = lactational mastitis 👉 Most common organism = Staphylococcus aureus 👉 Early treatment prevents abscess formation 👉 "Mastitis → think Staph aureus"

question_text: A 53 year old lady was sent for investigations including biopsy after being found to have a breast lump and associated changes to the skin overlying this lump that appeared red and dimpled. The biopsy result was suggestive of cancer. What is the SINGLE most likely statement that would describe the histopathological findings?

options.a: Invasive intraductal carcinoma of the breast extending to the epithelium
options.b: In situ carcinoma involving the nipple epidermis
options.c: Encapsulated adipocytes within a fibrotic stroma
options.d: Proliferation and expansion of the stroma with low cellularity
options.e: Cystic formations with mild epithelial hyperplasia in ducts

explanation: Why? This patient has classic features of invasive breast carcinoma with skin involvement, evidenced by redness and dimpling (peau d’orange). This occurs due to tumor infiltration of lymphatics causing skin tethering and edema. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Breast lump ✅ Skin changes (red, dimpled → peau d’orange) ✅ Biopsy suggestive of malignancy These findings strongly indicate invasive breast carcinoma. Why Option A Is Correct Invasive ductal carcinoma is the most common type of breast cancer Tumor invades beyond ducts into surrounding stroma Can involve lymphatics → causes skin dimpling and edema Histology shows malignant epithelial cells invading surrounding tissue Why the Other Options Are Less Likely B. In situ carcinoma involving the nipple epidermis Describes Paget’s disease Presents with eczematous nipple changes, not dimpling of overlying skin C. Encapsulated adipocytes within a fibrotic stroma Suggests lipoma (benign) Does not cause skin changes or malignancy D. Proliferation and expansion of the stroma with low cellularity Suggests fibroadenoma (benign) No skin involvement E. Cystic formations with mild epithelial hyperplasia in ducts Suggests fibrocystic changes (benign) No malignant features or skin dimpling Key Exam Principle 👉 Skin dimpling (peau d’orange) = lymphatic obstruction by invasive carcinoma 👉 Most common type = invasive ductal carcinoma 👉 Invasive = beyond basement membrane 👉 "Peau d’orange → think invasive breast cancer"

question_text: A 32 year old woman, diagnosed with estrogen receptor-positive (ER+) invasive breast carcinoma, visits the pre-assessment clinic for a consultation regarding her upcoming mastectomy. During her evaluation, she mentions that her last menstrual period occurred 6 weeks ago. A subsequent pregnancy test confirms that she is pregnant. Which of the following is the most appropriate management plan for her breast cancer?

options.d: Plan for surgery in the second trimester

explanation: Why? This patient has breast cancer diagnosed during early pregnancy (~6 weeks, first trimester). The safest and most appropriate initial management is to delay definitive surgery until the second trimester, when the risk of miscarriage and teratogenicity is lower. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Confirmed invasive breast cancer ✅ Early pregnancy (6 weeks → first trimester) ✅ Planned surgical management These factors guide timing of treatment. Why Surgery in the Second Trimester Is Correct Second trimester is the safest period for surgery in pregnancy Lower risk of miscarriage compared to first trimester Allows timely cancer treatment while minimizing fetal risk Mastectomy can be safely performed during pregnancy Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Initiate chemotherapy immediately Contraindicated in the first trimester (teratogenic) May be considered in 2nd/3rd trimester B. Initiate radiotherapy Contraindicated in pregnancy due to fetal radiation exposure C. Termination of pregnancy Not routinely required Breast cancer can be managed during pregnancy E. Initiate hormonal therapy Tamoxifen is contraindicated in pregnancy (teratogenic) Key Exam Principle 👉 Breast cancer in pregnancy → do NOT delay treatment unnecessarily 👉 Surgery is safe in 2nd trimester 👉 Avoid chemo (1st trimester), radiotherapy, and hormonal therapy during pregnancy 👉 "Pregnant + cancer → surgery in 2nd trimester"

question_text: A 26 year old woman has breast tenderness for the past 3 months. It occurs on both sides of the breast equally. She has been taking combined oral contraceptives for the past 18 months. She notices it worsen a few days before her menstrual cycle starts and it resolves after her menstrual cycle finishes. She feels generalised swelling throughout both breasts. On examination, there are no palpable lumps and skin discolouration. What is the SINGLE most appropriate action?

options.b: Advice for a better-fitting bra during the day
options.c: Advice on the consumption of vitamin E
options.d: Stop combined oral contraceptives for a duration of 3 months and restart again
options.e: Stop combined oral contraceptives and start progestogen-only contraceptives

explanation: Why? This patient has classic cyclical mastalgia, characterized by bilateral breast pain that fluctuates with the menstrual cycle and resolves afterward. The first-line management is reassurance and supportive measures such as wearing a well-fitting bra. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Bilateral breast pain ✅ Cyclical pattern (worse premenstrual, resolves after menstruation) ✅ Generalised breast swelling ✅ No lumps or abnormal findings on examination These features strongly indicate cyclical mastalgia. Why Advice for a Better-Fitting Bra Is Correct First-line management is conservative Provides mechanical support and reduces discomfort Reassurance is key as condition is benign No need for medications initially Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Primrose oil Sometimes used but not first-line Limited evidence C. Vitamin E Not routinely recommended D. Stop combined oral contraceptives temporarily Not first-line Symptoms can be managed conservatively first E. Switch to progestogen-only contraceptives Consider only if symptoms are persistent and severe Key Exam Principle 👉 Cyclical mastalgia = bilateral, premenstrual pain 👉 First-line = reassurance + supportive bra 👉 No red flags → no imaging needed 👉 "Cyclical pain → reassure and support"

question_text: A 35 year old woman presents to the clinic with a complaint of painless bleeding from her left nipple that has persisted for the past seven days. She reports no associated breast pain or trauma. On examination, the breast tissue appears normal with no discernible masses, and the skin over the breast shows no changes or abnormalities. What is the SINGLE most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Why? This patient presents with classic features of an intraductal papilloma, which is the most common cause of painless bloody nipple discharge in women with no palpable mass. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Painless nipple bleeding ✅ No palpable mass ✅ No skin changes ✅ No history of trauma These features strongly point to intraductal papilloma. Why Intraductal Papilloma Is Correct Benign tumor within the lactiferous duct Classically presents with unilateral, spontaneous bloody nipple discharge Usually no associated lump Common in women aged 30–50 years Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Duct ectasia Typically causes green or brown discharge Often associated with periareolar inflammation B. Paget's disease Presents with eczematous changes of the nipple (itching, scaling) May have underlying malignancy D. Nipple abscess Painful, inflamed swelling with possible fever Not painless bleeding E. Fat necrosis Usually follows trauma Presents as a palpable lump, not nipple discharge Key Exam Principle 👉 Painless bloody nipple discharge = intraductal papilloma 👉 Green discharge = duct ectasia 👉 Eczematous nipple = Paget's disease 👉 "Bloody discharge, no lump → papilloma"

question_text: A 35 year old woman presents to the clinic with a 4-month history of intermittent discharge from her left nipple. She reports occasional discomfort and swelling beneath the nipple, which has recurred despite two previous courses of oral antibiotics. The discharge is sometimes bloody or purulent and appears spontaneously from a small opening near the nipple. She denies fever or systemic symptoms. She smokes 15 cigarettes a day and has done so for the past 17 years. On examination, there is mild erythema and induration in the subareolar region of the left breast, with a small opening lateral to the nipple. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Why? This patient has classic features of periductal mastitis complicated by fistula formation, strongly associated with smoking. Chronic inflammation of the subareolar ducts leads to recurrent infection, discharge, and eventually sinus/fistula formation. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Chronic recurrent subareolar symptoms (4 months) ✅ Smoker (major risk factor) ✅ Mixed discharge (bloody/purulent) ✅ Recurrent episodes despite antibiotics ✅ Small opening near nipple (fistula/sinus tract) ✅ Subareolar erythema and induration These findings strongly indicate periductal mastitis with fistula formation. Why Periductal Mastitis with Fistula Is Correct Smoking → duct damage → inflammation and obstruction Recurrent infections lead to abscess formation and sinus/fistula Discharge may be purulent or blood-stained Often chronic and relapsing External opening near areola is characteristic of fistula Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Inflammatory breast cancer Presents with diffuse redness, peau d’orange, rapid progression Not typically associated with fistula or chronic discharge C. Intraductal papilloma Causes painless bloody discharge No inflammation, induration, or fistula formation D. Fibrocystic changes Cause cyclical pain and nodularity No fistula or purulent discharge E. Breast abscess Usually acute, painful, with fever Does not typically form chronic fistula without prior history Key Exam Principle 👉 Smoker + recurrent periareolar infection = periductal mastitis 👉 Chronic disease → fistula/sinus formation 👉 Mixed (purulent/bloody) discharge supports infection 👉 "Smoker + recurrent discharge + opening near nipple = periductal mastitis with fistula"

question_text: A 38 year old woman presents with a noticeable, greenish, foul-smelling discharge from the right nipple. She recalls experiencing a similar episode approximately one year ago, which resolved without intervention. On examination, the right nipple appears slightly retracted with no palpable masses. What is the SINGLE most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Why? This patient has classic features of duct ectasia, a benign condition involving dilatation and inflammation of subareolar ducts, leading to characteristic green, foul-smelling discharge and nipple retraction. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Greenish, foul-smelling nipple discharge ✅ Recurrent episodes ✅ Nipple retraction ✅ No palpable mass These findings strongly indicate duct ectasia. Why Duct Ectasia Is Correct Dilatation of subareolar ducts → accumulation of secretions Leads to thick, green or brown, often foul-smelling discharge Chronic inflammation can cause nipple retraction Often recurrent and benign Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Breast abscess Would present with pain, redness, and fever Discharge is purulent, not typically green and foul-smelling without inflammation C. Duct papilloma Causes painless bloody discharge Not green or foul-smelling D. Fat necrosis Associated with trauma Presents as a lump, not nipple discharge E. Paget's disease of nipple Presents with eczematous nipple changes (itching, scaling) May have underlying malignancy Not associated with green discharge Key Exam Principle 👉 Green, foul-smelling discharge = duct ectasia 👉 Bloody discharge = intraductal papilloma 👉 Nipple retraction can occur in duct ectasia or cancer 👉 "Green discharge + recurrent + no mass = duct ectasia"

question_text: A 29 year old woman presents with a single 2 cm by 2 cm lump in the breast. The lump is mobile and hard in consistency. On examination, the mass is painless and there is also a palpable lymph node in the axilla. An ultrasound was performed which shows a mass with hypoechoic, ill-defined, spiculated, and microlobulated margins. A mammogram shows ill-defined, spiculated borders. A fine needle aspiration cytology was performed which results came back as normal. What is the SINGLE most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
explanation: Why? This patient has highly suspicious features of breast malignancy despite a normal FNAC result. The next step is to obtain a definitive tissue diagnosis using a core needle biopsy, which is more accurate and provides histological architecture. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Hard, painless breast lump ✅ Axillary lymph node (suggests possible spread) ✅ Ultrasound: hypoechoic, ill-defined, spiculated margins ✅ Mammogram: spiculated borders (classic for malignancy) ✅ FNAC normal (possible false negative) These features strongly suggest breast cancer. Why Core Biopsy Is Correct Gold standard for diagnosing breast cancer Provides tissue architecture (unlike FNAC) More sensitive and specific than cytology Essential when imaging is suspicious but FNAC is negative Part of triple assessment Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Repeat fine needle aspiration cytology Still limited by lack of tissue architecture Risk of repeated false negatives B. Magnetic resonance imaging Useful adjunct but does not confirm diagnosis Histology is required C. Punch biopsy Used for skin lesions (e.g., Paget’s disease) Not appropriate for breast masses D. Genetic testing and counselling Not part of immediate diagnostic confirmation Key Exam Principle 👉 Suspicious imaging overrides normal FNAC 👉 Always confirm with core biopsy 👉 Triple assessment must be concordant 👉 "Suspicious lump + negative FNAC = do core biopsy"

question_text: A 45 years old woman presents to her GP after feeling a lump in her left breast for 2 weeks. On examination, there is a 3 cm hard, irregular mass in the lower outer quadrant of the left breast. The lump is non-tender. No obvious skin erythema is present. A firm, enlarged ipsilateral axillary lymph node is palpable. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Why? This patient presents with classic features of invasive breast carcinoma. The presence of a hard, irregular, non-tender mass with associated axillary lymphadenopathy strongly suggests malignancy. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Age > 40 years ✅ Hard, irregular breast lump ✅ Non-tender mass ✅ Ipsilateral axillary lymph node enlargement These are red flag features for breast cancer. Why Carcinoma of the Breast Is Correct Invasive breast cancer commonly presents as a hard, irregular mass Often painless in early stages Spreads to axillary lymph nodes → palpable lymphadenopathy Most common type = invasive ductal carcinoma Why the Other Options Are Less Likely B. Ductal carcinoma in situ Non-invasive (confined within ducts) Usually detected on screening (microcalcifications) Does not typically present with lymph node involvement C. Breast abscess Painful, tender, with erythema and systemic symptoms D. Fat necrosis History of trauma May mimic cancer but often irregular and associated with bruising No lymph node involvement typically E. Phyllodes tumour Can be large and fast-growing but usually well-circumscribed Less commonly associated with lymph node involvement Key Exam Principle 👉 Hard, irregular, painless lump = malignancy until proven otherwise 👉 Axillary lymph nodes = likely metastatic spread 👉 Age > 40 increases suspicion 👉 "Hard + irregular + lymph node = carcinoma"

question_text: A 28 year old woman attends her GP surgery after noticing a lump in her right breast. She first noticed it three weeks ago and it has not changed in size. She denies any pain, discharge or skin changes. On examination, there is a firm, mobile lump in the upper outer quadrant of the right breast. Her grandmother was diagnosed with breast cancer at the age of 68 years old. Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
explanation: Why? This patient is a young woman (<30 years) presenting with a breast lump that has benign features (mobile, firm, no skin changes). The most appropriate initial investigation is an ultrasound of the breast. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Age 28 (young patient) ✅ Mobile, firm lump (suggestive of fibroadenoma) ✅ No pain, discharge, or skin changes ✅ Stable size over 3 weeks These features suggest a likely benign lesion. Why Ultrasound Is Correct First-line imaging in women under 30 Better at differentiating solid vs cystic lesions No radiation exposure Guides further management (e.g., biopsy if needed) Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Fine needle aspiration Not first-line without imaging B. Mammography Less sensitive in young women due to dense breast tissue Not first-line under 30 C. MRI of the breast Reserved for high-risk or complex cases Not initial test D. Core needle biopsy Done after imaging if suspicious findings Not first step Key Exam Principle 👉 Age < 30 → ultrasound first 👉 Age ≥ 40 → mammography first 👉 Triple assessment: exam + imaging + biopsy 👉 "Young patient + lump = ultrasound first"

question_text: A 29 year old woman has bilateral breast tenderness for the past 6 months. It occurs 2 weeks before her menstrual cycle starts and improves after her menses. She describes the pain as dull and achy in nature. She takes the combined oral contraceptive pills. On examination, there are no palpable lumps or skin discolouration. She drinks a cup of tea every morning. What is the SINGLE most appropriate action?

options.d: Advise to stop combined oral contraceptives

explanation: Why? This patient has classic cyclical mastalgia, characterized by bilateral, dull, aching breast pain that occurs premenstrually and resolves after menstruation. Conservative lifestyle modification is first-line, including reducing caffeine intake. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Bilateral breast pain ✅ Cyclical pattern (2 weeks before menses, improves after) ✅ Dull, aching pain ✅ No lumps or abnormal findings ✅ Caffeine intake (tea) These features strongly indicate cyclical mastalgia. Why Reducing Caffeine Is Correct Caffeine is associated with worsening breast pain in some patients Simple lifestyle modification is first-line Non-invasive and safe initial approach Often recommended before medications Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Primrose oil May be used but not first-line Limited evidence C. Start antibiotics No signs of infection D. Stop combined oral contraceptives Not first-line unless symptoms are severe or persistent E. Paracetamol Can help symptomatically but lifestyle modification is preferred first Key Exam Principle 👉 Cyclical mastalgia = bilateral, premenstrual, dull pain 👉 First-line = reassurance + lifestyle changes (reduce caffeine, supportive bra) 👉 No red flags → no imaging needed 👉 "Cyclical pain → lifestyle first (caffeine reduction)"

question_text: A 45 year old woman presents to the breast clinic with a six-month history of intermittent, unilateral bloody discharge from her right nipple. She has no personal or family history of breast cancer. On examination, there is no palpable mass, and the rest of the breast examination is unremarkable. An ultrasound of the breast shows a small lesion within the right central duct system. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Why? This patient presents with classic features of an intraductal papilloma, the most common cause of unilateral, spontaneous bloody nipple discharge without a palpable mass. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Unilateral bloody nipple discharge ✅ Intermittent but persistent (6 months) ✅ No palpable mass ✅ Ultrasound shows lesion in central duct These findings strongly indicate intraductal papilloma. Why Intraductal Papilloma Is Correct Benign tumor arising within a lactiferous duct Commonly presents with spontaneous, unilateral bloody discharge Often no palpable mass Usually located in central ducts (subareolar region) Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Breast cancer May cause discharge but usually associated with mass or other suspicious features Less likely with isolated duct lesion and no other signs B. Fibrocystic breast changes Cause cyclical pain and nodularity Not typically associated with bloody discharge D. Mammary duct ectasia Causes green or brown discharge Often associated with nipple retraction and inflammation E. Paget's disease of the breast Presents with eczematous nipple changes (itching, scaling) Not isolated bloody discharge Key Exam Principle 👉 Unilateral bloody discharge = intraductal papilloma until proven otherwise 👉 Central duct lesion supports diagnosis 👉 No lump does NOT exclude pathology 👉 "Bloody discharge + no mass = papilloma"

question_text: A 57 year old woman presents to the clinic with a concern regarding her skin. She underwent a mastectomy for breast cancer five years ago, followed by adjuvant chemotherapy and radiotherapy, and has since been in remission. On examination, a distinct blue tinge is noted on the skin overlying the mastectomy scar. This lesion is non-tender, measures approximately 3 cm in diameter, and has an irregular border. There is no associated lymphadenopathy or systemic symptoms. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Why? This patient has classic features of radiation-induced angiosarcoma, a rare but serious complication that can occur years after radiotherapy for breast cancer. It typically presents as a blue or purplish discoloration over the irradiated skin. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ History of breast cancer treated with radiotherapy ✅ Latency period (5 years later) ✅ Blue/purplish skin lesion ✅ Irregular borders ✅ Located over mastectomy scar (irradiated field) These findings strongly indicate angiosarcoma. Why Angiosarcoma Is Correct Malignancy of vascular endothelial cells Associated with prior radiotherapy (Stewart-Treves syndrome variant) Presents as bruised/blue/purple skin lesions Often arises years after treatment Can appear initially subtle but is aggressive Why the Other Options Are Less Likely B. Melanoma Usually pigmented (brown/black), not typically blue over irradiated scar Not specifically linked to prior radiotherapy in this context C. Lymphoma Typically presents with nodal enlargement or systemic symptoms Skin involvement is different (patches, plaques) D. Basal cell carcinoma Pearly papule with telangiectasia Not blue discoloration E. Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans Slow-growing firm nodules Not classically blue or linked to radiotherapy Key Exam Principle 👉 Blue/purple lesion on irradiated breast = angiosarcoma until proven otherwise 👉 Occurs years after radiotherapy 👉 Aggressive tumor → requires urgent evaluation 👉 "Post-radiation + blue lesion = angiosarcoma"

question_text: A 64 year old woman has been treated for breast cancer with tamoxifen. What SINGLE medication should be added to her regime?
explanation: Why? Postmenopausal women with breast cancer on endocrine therapy are at risk of osteoporosis and fractures. Bisphosphonates are recommended to protect bone density and reduce fracture risk, and they may also reduce the risk of bone metastases. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Age 64 (postmenopausal) ✅ Breast cancer treatment ✅ On tamoxifen (endocrine therapy context) These indicate a need for bone protection. Why Bisphosphonates Is Correct Inhibit osteoclast-mediated bone resorption Reduce risk of osteoporosis and fractures Provide additional benefit in reducing skeletal-related events in breast cancer Commonly used in postmenopausal breast cancer patients Why the Other Options Are Less Likely B. Calcium Helpful but insufficient alone for bone protection Usually used as adjunct, not primary therapy C. Vitamin D Supports calcium absorption but not adequate alone Adjunct rather than main treatment D. Calcitonin Less effective than bisphosphonates Rarely used E. Phosphate binders Used in renal disease, not relevant here Key Exam Principle 👉 Breast cancer + endocrine therapy → consider bone protection 👉 First-line = bisphosphonates 👉 Calcium/Vit D are supportive, not definitive 👉 "Protect bone → use bisphosphonates"

question_text: A 58 year old woman presents with a sore nipple and a peri-areolar rash. She has been complaining of a growing rash at her nipple which is itchy. She has clear fluid discharge from her left nipple over the past few months which has recently been a little bloodstained. On examination, her left nipple is dry, cracked and has a scaly erythematous area surrounding the nipple. Her right nipple appears normal and no lymphadenopathy was seen. A mammogram done 3 years ago was normal. What is the SINGLE most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Why? This patient has classic features of Paget’s disease of the breast, a form of breast cancer involving the nipple-areolar complex. It presents with eczematous changes and may be associated with underlying malignancy. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Unilateral nipple involvement ✅ Itchy, scaly, erythematous rash ✅ Nipple changes (dry, cracked) ✅ Blood-stained discharge ✅ Chronic progression over months These findings strongly indicate Paget’s disease. Why Paget's Disease Is Correct Malignant cells infiltrate the nipple epidermis Presents with eczema-like changes (itching, scaling, crusting) Often associated with underlying ductal carcinoma May have serous or blood-stained discharge Typically unilateral Why the Other Options Are Less Likely B. Contact dermatitis Usually bilateral and related to irritants No bloody discharge C. Invasive ductal carcinoma Typically presents as a palpable mass Does not primarily present with nipple eczema D. Intraductal papilloma Causes bloody discharge but no skin changes E. Bowen's disease Squamous cell carcinoma in situ of the skin Not specific to nipple and lacks classic Paget’s features Key Exam Principle 👉 Eczematous nipple + discharge = Paget’s disease until proven otherwise 👉 Always suspect underlying malignancy 👉 Unilateral nipple rash is cancer until excluded 👉 "Itchy, scaly nipple + discharge = Paget’s disease"

question_text: A 39 year old woman presents to the breast clinic with a painless lump in her right breast, which she first noticed six weeks ago. She reports no significant past medical history and no family history of breast or ovarian cancer. The lump is firm, immobile, and approximately 2 cm in diameter at the upper outer quadrant. There is no associated nipple discharge or skin changes. On clinical examination, the axillary lymph nodes are not palpable. An ultrasound of the breast is performed, revealing a solid, hypoechoic mass with irregular margins. What is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: Why? This patient has suspicious features of breast malignancy (firm, immobile lump with irregular margins on ultrasound). The next step is to confirm the diagnosis with a core needle biopsy as part of triple assessment. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Firm, immobile lump ✅ No pain (typical of malignancy) ✅ Ultrasound: hypoechoic, irregular margins ✅ No lymphadenopathy yet (early disease possible) These findings strongly suggest malignancy. Why Core Biopsy Is Correct Gold standard for diagnosing breast cancer Provides tissue architecture for definitive diagnosis Part of triple assessment (clinical + imaging + histology) Guides further management (surgery, chemo, etc.) Why the Other Options Are Less Likely B. FNAC Less accurate (no tissue architecture) Not preferred for suspicious solid lesions C. Chemotherapy Given only after histological confirmation D. Surgical excision Not done before tissue diagnosis E. Sentinel node biopsy Performed after cancer diagnosis for staging Key Exam Principle 👉 Suspicious lump → confirm with core biopsy 👉 Imaging alone is not diagnostic 👉 Always complete triple assessment 👉 "Irregular mass → core biopsy next"

question_text: A 56 years old woman attends the breast clinic with a 2 month history of intermittent green nipple discharge from both breasts. The discharge occurs spontaneously and is not painful. She also reports gradual inward pulling of her right nipple over the same period. Examination reveals mild right nipple retraction with a subareolar mass. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Why? This patient has classic features of duct ectasia, a benign condition involving dilatation and inflammation of subareolar ducts, commonly seen in older women. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Green nipple discharge (bilateral) ✅ Spontaneous, non-painful discharge ✅ Nipple retraction ✅ Subareolar mass ✅ Age > 50 These findings strongly indicate duct ectasia. Why Duct Ectasia Is Correct Dilatation of subareolar ducts → accumulation of secretions Leads to thick, green or brown discharge Chronic inflammation causes fibrosis → nipple retraction Often presents with subareolar mass Common in middle-aged to older women Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Fibroadenoma Occurs in younger women Presents as painless mobile lump, no discharge C. Intraductal Papilloma Causes unilateral bloody discharge Not green or bilateral D. Fat necrosis Associated with trauma Presents as irregular lump, not discharge E. Paget disease of the breast Presents with eczematous nipple changes Not green discharge Key Exam Principle 👉 Green discharge = duct ectasia 👉 Bilateral involvement supports benign cause 👉 Nipple retraction can occur due to fibrosis 👉 "Green discharge + retraction + subareolar mass = duct ectasia"

question_text: A 32 year old woman presents with a painless lump in her left breast, which she noticed three weeks ago. She has no history of previous breast lumps. She has no significant medical history but is concerned because her mother was diagnosed with breast cancer at the age of 45. On examination, a firm, mobile, well-circumscribed mass measuring approximately 1.5 cm is palpable in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast. What is the most appropriate investigation?
explanation: Why? This patient is a young woman (32 years) with a breast lump that has benign features (mobile, well-circumscribed). The most appropriate initial investigation is an ultrasound. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Age < 35 years ✅ Mobile, well-defined lump (likely fibroadenoma) ✅ No alarming features (no skin changes, no fixation) ✅ Short duration (3 weeks) These findings suggest a likely benign lesion. Why Ultrasound Is Correct First-line imaging in women under 35 Better for dense breast tissue Differentiates cystic vs solid masses Guides need for biopsy Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Serum prolactin Used for galactorrhea, not breast lumps B. Mammogram Less sensitive in younger women due to dense breast tissue Not first-line under 35 C. MRI breast Reserved for high-risk or complex cases Not initial test E. Watchful waiting Not appropriate without imaging in a new lump Key Exam Principle 👉 Age < 35 → ultrasound first 👉 Age ≥ 40 → mammogram first 👉 All lumps require imaging (no blind reassurance) 👉 "Young patient + lump = ultrasound"

question_text: A 39 year old smoker has a thick creamy brown discharge coming from her left nipple. It has been on going for the past two weeks. She has been experiencing left breast pain for the past few months. On examination, there is a palpable subareolar mass with nipple retraction on her left breast. There are no palpable lymph nodes. Her temperature is 37.1°C. What is the SINGLE most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Why? This patient has classic features of duct ectasia, a benign condition involving dilatation and inflammation of subareolar ducts, strongly associated with smoking. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Smoker (major risk factor) ✅ Thick creamy brown discharge ✅ Subareolar mass ✅ Nipple retraction ✅ Chronic symptoms (months) ✅ No fever (non-acute) These findings strongly indicate duct ectasia. Why Duct Ectasia Is Correct Dilatation of subareolar ducts → accumulation of secretions Leads to thick, creamy, green/brown discharge Chronic inflammation causes fibrosis → nipple retraction Often presents with subareolar mass and discomfort Common in middle-aged women and smokers Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Breast abscess Would present with acute pain, fever, erythema Patient is afebrile with chronic symptoms B. Fibroadenoma Painless, mobile lump No discharge or nipple retraction D. Duct papilloma Causes painless bloody discharge Not thick brown discharge E. Ductal fistula Would have an external opening/sinus near areola Not described here Key Exam Principle 👉 Smoker + thick brown/green discharge = duct ectasia 👉 Nipple retraction due to fibrosis 👉 Chronic, non-infective picture 👉 "Brown discharge + smoker + subareolar mass = duct ectasia"

question_text: A 65 year old woman presents to the breast clinic having noticed that she has had a blood stained discharge from the left nipple. She also has dry skin over the left areola which resembles eczema. On examination, a blood stained discharge with dry flaky skin is noted on the left areola and the nipple was ulcerated. What is the SINGLE most appropriate investigation?
explanation: Why? This patient has classic features of Paget’s disease of the breast (eczema-like nipple changes with bloody discharge and ulceration). The most appropriate investigation is a punch biopsy of the nipple/areolar skin to confirm the diagnosis. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Blood-stained nipple discharge ✅ Eczematous (dry, flaky) skin over areola ✅ Nipple ulceration ✅ Older age These findings strongly indicate Paget’s disease. Why Punch Biopsy Is Correct Samples skin of nipple/areola Confirms presence of Paget cells (malignant cells in epidermis) Essential for diagnosis Directly targets the lesion Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. FNAC Used for masses, not skin lesions B. MRI May be useful later but not diagnostic C. (Correct answer) D. Open biopsy Too invasive as first-line E. Stereotactic biopsy Used for non-palpable lesions (e.g., microcalcifications) Not for nipple skin changes Key Exam Principle 👉 Eczematous nipple lesion = biopsy the skin 👉 Punch biopsy confirms Paget’s disease 👉 Always suspect underlying malignancy 👉 "Nipple eczema → punch biopsy"

question_text: A 48 year old female with a history of breast carcinoma and a left-sided mastectomy with ipsilateral axillary lymph node clearance 2 years ago presents to her general practitioner (GP) with a three-day history of left upper limb swelling. An examination is unremarkable except for the presence of a small insect bite located in her left anterior upper arm. What is the SINGLE most likely mechanism for the swelling in this patient's upper limb?
explanation: Why? This patient has secondary lymphoedema due to prior axillary lymph node clearance. Damage/removal of lymph nodes impairs lymphatic drainage, leading to chronic swelling of the affected limb. The insect bite likely acted as a minor trigger but is not the primary mechanism. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ History of mastectomy with axillary lymph node clearance ✅ Unilateral upper limb swelling (same side) ✅ No significant signs of infection (no erythema, fever) ✅ Minor insect bite (trigger, not cause) These findings strongly indicate lymphoedema. Why Lymphoedema Is Correct Occurs due to disruption of lymphatic drainage Common after axillary node dissection in breast cancer Leads to accumulation of protein-rich interstitial fluid May be triggered or worsened by minor trauma/infection Usually painless, non-pitting (chronic) Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Ascending lymphangitis Would present with red streaks, fever, and systemic symptoms C. Cellulitis Painful, red, warm swelling with systemic features Not described here D. Hypoalbuminaemia Causes bilateral generalized oedema, not unilateral E. Delayed hypersensitivity Localized reaction (itching, redness), not whole limb swelling Key Exam Principle 👉 Axillary node clearance → risk of lymphoedema 👉 Unilateral arm swelling post-mastectomy = lymphoedema 👉 Minor trauma can trigger but not primary cause 👉 "Post-surgery + arm swelling = lymphoedema"

question_text: A 53 year old woman presents to the GP surgery with a 2 cm small smooth, firm mass in her left breast. The mass is non-tender and there is no nipple discharge or nipple retraction. She first noticed the lump 2 weeks ago. She has no family history of breast cancer. She is a non-smoker and does not have any medical problems. She had a mammogram 2 months ago which results have been satisfactory. There are no associated skin changes in the breast. The lump is slightly mobile on examination. What is the SINGLE most appropriate next step in management?

options.b: Request an ultrasound scan of the breast
options.c: Refer to the breast clinic for an appointment to be seen within 2 weeks
options.d: Refer to the breast clinic routinely

explanation: Why? Any new breast lump in a woman over 30–40 years must be considered malignant until proven otherwise, regardless of recent normal imaging. The most appropriate step is urgent referral to a breast clinic under the 2-week wait pathway. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Age 53 (high-risk age group) ✅ New breast lump (2 weeks duration) ✅ No reassuring features sufficient to exclude malignancy ✅ Recent normal mammogram does NOT rule out cancer These findings mandate urgent assessment. Why Urgent 2-Week Referral Is Correct All new breast lumps in women >30 require urgent specialist assessment Allows triple assessment (clinical exam + imaging + biopsy) Early detection of malignancy is critical GP should not delay with further primary care investigations Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Repeat mammography Not appropriate in primary care Specialist clinic will decide imaging B. Ultrasound Part of assessment but should be done in breast clinic C. (Correct answer) D. Routine referral Too slow for possible malignancy E. Reassure and reassess Unsafe — risk of missing cancer Key Exam Principle 👉 Any new breast lump in woman >30 = urgent 2-week referral 👉 Normal mammogram does NOT exclude cancer 👉 GP does NOT delay with reassurance or repeat imaging 👉 "New lump → urgent referral"

question_text: A 67 year old woman presents with a firm, round, painless 5 cm lump in her right breast. She has a bruise on the surface and there is no discharge. What is the SINGLE most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Why? This patient presents with a breast lump associated with bruising, which is highly suggestive of fat necrosis. Fat necrosis commonly follows trauma and can mimic malignancy but is benign. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Bruising over the lump (suggests prior trauma) ✅ Firm, round lump ✅ Painless ✅ No discharge These findings strongly point to fat necrosis. Why Fat Necrosis Is Correct Occurs following trauma to breast tissue Leads to inflammation and fibrosis of fat May present as a firm lump mimicking cancer Often associated with skin bruising or discoloration Why the Other Options Are Less Likely B. Fibroadenoma Occurs in younger women No associated bruising C. Fibroadenosis (fibrocystic change) Typically bilateral, cyclical pain Not a single large lump with bruising D. Duct ectasia Presents with green/brown discharge and nipple retraction Not a bruised lump E. Breast cancer Possible in this age group, but bruising strongly suggests trauma-related pathology Cancer does not typically present with surface bruising Key Exam Principle 👉 Breast lump + bruising = fat necrosis 👉 Always consider trauma even if not stated 👉 Can mimic malignancy clinically 👉 "Bruised lump → think fat necrosis"

question_text: A 58 years old woman attends the breast clinic after noticing a lump in her right breast for 1 month. She reports no pain or nipple discharge. On examination, there is a 2 cm firm, irregular mass in the upper outer quadrant of the right breast. The lump is non-tender and appears fixed to surrounding tissue. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Why? This patient presents with classic features of invasive breast carcinoma. A firm, irregular, non-tender lump that is fixed to surrounding tissue in an older woman is highly suspicious for malignancy. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Age 58 (higher risk for malignancy) ✅ Firm, irregular mass ✅ Non-tender ✅ Fixed to surrounding tissue (invasion) These are hallmark features of breast cancer. Why Carcinoma of the Breast Is Correct Invasive breast cancer commonly presents as a hard, irregular mass Fixation suggests local invasion Typically painless in early stages Upper outer quadrant is the most common site Why the Other Options Are Less Likely B. Ductal carcinoma in situ Non-invasive, usually detected on screening (microcalcifications) Does not present as a fixed mass C. Fibroadenoma Occurs in younger women Mobile, well-circumscribed D. Mastitis Painful, inflamed breast with fever E. Simple breast cyst Smooth, fluctuant, often tender Not fixed or irregular Key Exam Principle 👉 Hard + irregular + fixed = malignancy until proven otherwise 👉 Age > 50 increases suspicion 👉 Fixation = invasion 👉 "Irregular, fixed lump → carcinoma"

question_text: A 44 year old woman presents to the clinic with a three-month history of intermittent bloody discharge from her left nipple. She reports no pain, but notes that the discharge is unilateral and spontaneous. On examination, there is no palpable mass in either breast, and no skin changes or lymphadenopathy are evident. A mammogram reveals a small, well-circumscribed lesion in the left breast. An ultrasound-guided biopsy of the lesion is performed. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Why? This patient presents with classic features of an intraductal papilloma, the most common cause of unilateral, spontaneous bloody nipple discharge without a palpable mass. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Unilateral bloody nipple discharge ✅ Spontaneous and intermittent ✅ No palpable mass ✅ Well-circumscribed lesion on imaging These findings strongly indicate intraductal papilloma. Why Intraductal Papilloma Is Correct Benign tumor arising within a lactiferous duct Commonly presents with spontaneous, unilateral bloody discharge Often small and well-circumscribed on imaging Usually no associated mass on examination Why the Other Options Are Less Likely B. Invasive ductal carcinoma Typically presents with irregular, poorly defined mass Often associated with other suspicious features C. Fibroadenoma Painless lump, not associated with bloody discharge D. Duct ectasia Causes green/brown discharge, not bloody Often with nipple retraction E. Paget's disease of the breast Presents with eczematous nipple changes Not isolated bloody discharge Key Exam Principle 👉 Unilateral bloody discharge = intraductal papilloma until proven otherwise 👉 Well-circumscribed lesion supports benign cause 👉 No lump does not exclude duct lesion 👉 "Bloody discharge + no mass = papilloma"

question_text: A 50 year old woman presents to the GP with a complaint of a lump in her right breast that she noticed six weeks ago. She describes the lump as firm, non-tender, and it does not change in size with her menstrual cycle. On examination, a 2 cm hard, irregular mass is palpable in the upper outer quadrant of the right breast. There is no associated skin changes, nipple discharge, or axillary lymphadenopathy. The rest of the examination is unremarkable. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.c: Reassure and review in one month
options.d: Refer urgently to the breast clinic

explanation: Why? This patient presents with a suspicious breast lump (hard, irregular, non-tender) in a woman aged 50. The most appropriate next step is urgent referral to a breast clinic under the 2-week wait pathway for triple assessment. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Age ≥ 50 (high risk) ✅ Hard, irregular mass ✅ Non-tender and persistent ✅ No cyclical variation These are red flag features for malignancy. Why Urgent Referral Is Correct All suspicious breast lumps require urgent specialist assessment Allows triple assessment (clinical + imaging + biopsy) Ensures early diagnosis and management GP should not delay with investigations in primary care Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Arrange mammogram Imaging should be done in specialist clinic Doubles delay if done in primary care B. Antibiotics No signs of infection C. Reassure and review Unsafe — risk of missing cancer E. Ultrasound Part of triple assessment but should be done in breast clinic Key Exam Principle 👉 Suspicious lump in woman >30 = urgent referral 👉 GP should NOT delay with imaging or treatment 👉 Triple assessment done in breast clinic 👉 "Hard, irregular lump → urgent referral"

question_text: A 52 year old woman presents to her GP with a 6-month history of changes to the skin of her left nipple. She describes the area as red, itchy, and occasionally scaly. There is no discharge, and she denies any history of trauma or application of new creams or lotions. She has no pain or palpable masses within the breast. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Why? This patient has a chronic, unilateral eczematous change of the nipple, which is highly suspicious for Paget’s disease of the breast, even in the absence of discharge or a palpable mass. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Unilateral nipple involvement ✅ Chronic (6 months) ✅ Itchy, red, scaly lesion ✅ No obvious external cause (no creams, trauma) These features strongly indicate Paget’s disease. Why Paget's Disease Is Correct Malignant cells infiltrate the nipple epidermis Presents with eczema-like changes (itching, scaling, erythema) Often unilateral May occur without palpable mass initially Associated with underlying ductal carcinoma Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Bowen's disease Squamous cell carcinoma in situ of skin Not specifically localized to nipple or associated with breast malignancy B. Seborrheic dermatitis Usually bilateral and affects scalp, face, chest Responds to topical treatment C. Lichen sclerosus Typically affects genital areas D. Psoriasis Well-demarcated plaques with silvery scales Usually involves multiple sites (elbows, knees, scalp) Key Exam Principle 👉 Unilateral chronic nipple eczema = Paget’s disease until proven otherwise 👉 May occur without mass or discharge 👉 Always investigate for underlying malignancy 👉 "Unilateral nipple rash → Paget’s disease"

question_text: A 29 year old woman has breast tenderness for the past 3 months. It occurs on both sides of the breast but worse on the left side. She notices it worsen a few days before her menstrual cycle starts and it resolves after her menstrual cycle finishes. She feels generalised swelling throughout both breasts. On examination, there are no palpable lumps. What is the SINGLE most appropriate action?

options.b: Advice to wear a supportive bra

explanation: Why? This patient has classic cyclical mastalgia, characterized by bilateral breast pain that worsens premenstrually and resolves after menstruation. The most appropriate first-line management is reassurance and supportive measures such as wearing a well-fitting bra. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Bilateral breast pain ✅ Cyclical pattern (worse before menses, resolves after) ✅ Generalised swelling ✅ No palpable lumps These features strongly indicate cyclical mastalgia. Why Supportive Bra Is Correct First-line management is conservative Provides mechanical support and reduces discomfort Non-invasive and effective Reassurance is key as condition is benign Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Primrose oil Sometimes used but not first-line Limited evidence C. Gabapentin Used for neuropathic pain, not mastalgia D. Amitriptyline Not indicated for cyclical breast pain E. Pyridoxine Not standard treatment Key Exam Principle 👉 Cyclical mastalgia = bilateral, premenstrual pain 👉 First-line = reassurance + supportive bra 👉 No red flags → no imaging needed 👉 "Cyclical pain → support and reassure"

question_text: A 50 year old man had surgery to remove cancer in his left breast. The mass was removed successfully surgically, with safety margins, no penetration and no lymph node metastasis. What is the best adjunctive therapy to give?
explanation: Why? Male breast cancer is most commonly estrogen receptor-positive. Therefore, adjuvant hormonal therapy with tamoxifen is recommended even after successful surgical removal, as it reduces recurrence risk and improves survival. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Male patient with breast cancer ✅ Successful surgery with clear margins ✅ No lymph node involvement (early stage) These indicate need for adjuvant therapy to reduce recurrence. Why Tamoxifen Is Correct Selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM) Standard adjuvant therapy in male breast cancer Reduces recurrence and mortality Most male breast cancers are ER-positive Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Radiotherapy Used in breast-conserving surgery or high-risk cases Not routinely required after complete mastectomy with clear margins B. Bisphosphonates Used for bone protection, not primary cancer treatment D. Letrozole Aromatase inhibitors are less effective in men unless combined with suppression of testicular function Not first-line E. No further treatment Inappropriate — adjuvant therapy reduces recurrence risk Key Exam Principle 👉 Male breast cancer = usually ER+ 👉 First-line adjuvant therapy = tamoxifen 👉 Surgery alone is not sufficient 👉 "Male breast cancer → give tamoxifen"

question_text: A 45 year old woman presents to the breast clinic with a painless, mobile lump in her right breast, which she noticed 2 months ago. On clinical examination, the lump is firm, mobile well-circumscribed, and approximately 2 cm in diameter. An MRI is subsequently conducted, which shows a homogeneously enhancing lesion with well-defined borders. What is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?
explanation: Why? Although this lesion has benign features (mobile, well-circumscribed, homogeneous), the patient is 45 years old, and any breast lump in this age group requires histological confirmation as part of triple assessment. The most appropriate next step is a core needle biopsy. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Age 45 (higher risk group) ✅ Palpable breast lump ✅ Benign imaging features but not definitive These require confirmation. Why Core Biopsy Is Correct Gold standard for tissue diagnosis Provides histological architecture Part of triple assessment (clinical + imaging + histology) Required even if imaging suggests benign lesion in older patients Why the Other Options Are Less Likely B. FNAC Less accurate (no tissue architecture) Not preferred for solid lesions C. Repeat mammography Unnecessary — imaging already done Does not confirm diagnosis D. Reassurance and follow-up Unsafe without histological confirmation in >40 years E. Surgical excision Too invasive before confirming diagnosis Key Exam Principle 👉 Age > 40 + lump = biopsy required 👉 Imaging alone is not sufficient 👉 Core biopsy = gold standard 👉 "Breast lump → confirm with core biopsy"

question_text: A 37 year old woman had a right mastectomy with removal of axillary lymph nodes for a primary breast angiosarcoma 7 years ago. She also received chemotherapy and radiotherapy for her cancer. She presents to the breast clinic with a new development of purple coloured nodules on her right chest that she noticed 6 weeks ago. She has noticed enlargement of the nodule together with a discolouration surrounding it over the past few weeks. Clinical examination shows an irregular purple nodule with surrounding ring-shaped purple-blue pigmentation with indistinct borders. The diameter of the nodule is 0.9 by 1.1 cm. A biopsy was taken. What is the SINGLE most likely tissue diagnosis?
explanation: Why? This is a classic presentation of secondary (radiation-induced) angiosarcoma of the breast/chest wall. Angiosarcoma is a malignant tumour of vascular endothelial cells and is strongly associated with prior radiotherapy and chronic lymphoedema following breast cancer treatment. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ History of breast angiosarcoma ✅ Previous radiotherapy (major risk factor) ✅ Latency period of several years (7 years) ✅ Purple/bruise-like nodules on chest wall ✅ Rapid enlargement and surrounding discoloration These features are highly characteristic of angiosarcoma recurrence or radiation-induced angiosarcoma. Why Angiosarcoma Is Correct Typically presents as purple/blue skin nodules or plaques Associated with prior radiotherapy (Stewart-Treves-like phenomenon) Occurs years after treatment (latency period) Aggressive and locally recurrent Skin changes often resemble bruising Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Melanoma Usually pigmented (black/brown), not typically purple vascular lesions No strong link with radiotherapy in this pattern C. Lymphoma Presents as painless lymphadenopathy or systemic symptoms Skin involvement less likely to appear as vascular purple nodules D. Lipoma Soft, mobile, non-pigmented, benign fatty tumour Does not cause discoloration or rapid change E. Basal cell carcinoma Typically pearly nodules with telangiectasia Slow growing, not violaceous or bruise-like Key Exam Principle 👉 Purple/bruise-like skin lesion + prior radiotherapy = think angiosarcoma 👉 Latency of years after treatment is classic 👉 Highly aggressive vascular tumour with recurrence risk 👉 "Post-radiotherapy + purple nodules = angiosarcoma until proven otherwise"

question_text: A 52 years old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus presents to the Emergency Department with a 3 day history of high fever, rigors, and increasing pain in her left breast. She reports localised redness and swelling that has rapidly worsened. Examination reveals a tender, fluctuant lump beneath an area of erythema and warmth. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Why? This patient has features of an acute breast infection with systemic toxicity and a fluctuant mass, which is highly suggestive of a breast abscess. A fluctuant swelling indicates a localized collection of pus. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ High fever and rigors (systemic infection) ✅ Rapidly worsening pain and swelling ✅ Localised erythema and warmth (inflammation) ✅ Fluctuant lump (pus collection) ✅ Diabetes mellitus (risk factor for severe infection) Why Abscess Is Correct Fluctuation = hallmark of pus collection Associated with severe infection and systemic symptoms Common complication of untreated mastitis Requires drainage + antibiotics Why the Other Options Are Less Likely B. Cyst Usually painless, non-inflammatory No fever or systemic symptoms C. Fat necrosis Often painless, may follow trauma No systemic infection features D. Fibroadenoma Benign, firm, mobile, painless lump No redness, warmth, or fever E. Mastitis Inflammation without pus collection No fluctuation (key differentiator) May precede abscess formation Key Exam Principle 👉 Fluctuant lump = abscess until proven otherwise 👉 Mastitis = inflammation only; abscess = pus collection 👉 Fever + localized tender swelling + fluctuation = abscess 👉 "If it fluctuates → it’s an abscess"

question_text: A 58 year old lady with breast cancer has metastatic spread to her lower vertebrae. She describes the pain as being dull and constant and complains that the pain wakes her up at night. Her current medications include morphine sulphate, paracetamol, ibuprofen and senna. Despite taking her medications as prescribed, she still complains of moderate to severe pain in her back. A CT scan shows metastatic deposits at her fourth lumbar vertebra. What is the SINGLE best adjuvant to be added to manage her pain?
explanation: Why? This patient has bone metastasis causing persistent cancer-related pain despite adequate analgesia. The best adjuvant treatment for localized bone metastasis pain is palliative radiotherapy, which directly targets the tumour and provides effective pain relief. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Known breast cancer with bone metastasis ✅ Localized vertebral lesion (L4) ✅ Dull, constant pain worse at night (typical of bone metastasis) ✅ Pain not controlled with opioids and NSAIDs These indicate the need for targeted local therapy. Why Radiotherapy Is Correct Gold standard for pain control in localized bone metastases Reduces tumour burden Provides significant pain relief (often within days to weeks) Improves quality of life Why the Other Options Are Less Likely B. Bisphosphonates Helpful for preventing skeletal-related events Slower onset of pain relief Adjunct but not first-line for acute severe localized pain C. Dexamethasone Useful for spinal cord compression or nerve-related pain Not primary treatment for isolated bone pain D. Gabapentin Used for neuropathic pain This is somatic bone pain, not neuropathic E. Vertebroplasty Used for vertebral collapse/fracture No indication of fracture or instability here Key Exam Principle 👉 Localized bone metastasis pain → radiotherapy 👉 First-line adjuvant when analgesics are insufficient 👉 Night pain + known metastasis = tumour-related bone pain 👉 "Bone mets pain not controlled → give radiotherapy"

question_text: A 68 year old woman presents to her GP complaining of persistent "pins and needles" in her hands and feet. She has a history of breast cancer for which she completed chemotherapy three months ago. Additionally, she has noticed a slight difficulty in maintaining her balance. During the last few cycles of chemotherapy and for several weeks after, she experienced significant nausea and vomiting, leading to decreased oral intake. Her neurological examination shows decreased sensation in a glove-and-stocking distribution. What is the most likely cause of this woman's symptoms?
explanation: Why? This patient has a classic glove-and-stocking sensory neuropathy occurring after chemotherapy, which strongly suggests chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN). Many chemotherapeutic agents (e.g., taxanes, platinum drugs) are neurotoxic and commonly cause this pattern. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Recent chemotherapy (3 months ago) ✅ Persistent "pins and needles" (paresthesia) ✅ Glove-and-stocking distribution ✅ Balance difficulty (sensory ataxia) These are hallmark features of chemotherapy-induced neuropathy. Why Chemotherapy-Induced Peripheral Neuropathy Is Correct Common adverse effect of many chemotherapy agents Typically presents as symmetric distal sensory neuropathy Can persist after treatment has ended Causes paresthesia, numbness, and gait instability Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Calcium deficiency Causes tetany, muscle cramps, perioral numbness Not glove-and-stocking neuropathy B. B12 deficiency Can cause similar neuropathy and ataxia BUT no strong evidence here (no anemia, no long-standing malnutrition, clear chemo trigger) CIPN is more directly supported by the timeline D. Diabetic neuropathy Requires history of diabetes Not mentioned in the question E. Hypothyroidism Can cause neuropathy but usually mild and with other systemic features (weight gain, fatigue, cold intolerance) Key Exam Principle 👉 Glove-and-stocking neuropathy + recent chemotherapy = CIPN 👉 Common exam trap vs B12 deficiency — look at timeline and risk factors 👉 Cancer treatment history is a major clue 👉 "Post-chemo neuropathy → think CIPN first"

question_text: A 68 year old man is reviewed in the Oncology Department. He has metastatic colorectal cancer and has just started chemotherapy using capecitabine as monotherapy 7 days ago. He has also prescribed loperamide which he started a few days ago. He has been complaining of severe diarrhoea over the past few days with nausea. He passes around 6 watery stools a day. He has difficulty tolerating drinking a sufficient amount of fluids due to nausea. His medications also include allopurinol which he was prescribed as prophylaxis of hyperuricaemia associated with chemotherapy. He takes regular codeine for pain relief. He has been taking rivaroxaban for recurrent pulmonary embolisms for the past 15 years. What is the SINGLE most appropriate medication to stop?
explanation: Why? This patient is taking capecitabine, a prodrug of 5-fluorouracil (5-FU). Allopurinol significantly reduces the efficacy of 5-FU by interfering with its activation and metabolism. Therefore, allopurinol should be stopped. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Capecitabine chemotherapy (prodrug of 5-FU) ✅ Concurrent use of allopurinol ✅ Known drug interaction reducing chemotherapy efficacy Why Allopurinol Is Correct Interferes with activation of 5-FU Reduces effectiveness of capecitabine Should not be co-administered Stopping it improves chemotherapy efficacy Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Capecitabine Diarrhoea is a known side effect May require dose adjustment, but not immediate cessation as the primary step here B. Loperamide Used to treat chemotherapy-induced diarrhoea Should be continued or even optimized D. Codeine Can help reduce diarrhoea (constipating effect) Not harmful here E. Rivaroxaban Indicated for recurrent pulmonary embolism Stopping it risks thrombosis Key Exam Principle 👉 Capecitabine (5-FU) + allopurinol = avoid combination 👉 Allopurinol reduces chemotherapy efficacy 👉 Always check for drug interactions in oncology patients 👉 "5-FU drugs + allopurinol = STOP allopurinol"

question_text: A 59 year old man attends the GP surgery with extreme fatigue over the past 3 months. He has now been experiencing thirst and increased urinary frequency. He has lost significant weight over this period of time. The only medications that he takes are his multivitamins which he takes 4 times a day. His blood results show the following: Sodium 139 mmol/L (135-145), Potassium 3.8 mmol/L (3.5 - 5), Creatinine 89 umol/L (70-150), eGFR >90 mL/min, Thyroid stimulating hormone 5.0 mU/L (0.5-5.7), Serum corrected calcium 3.0 mmol/L (2.1-2.6), ALT 30 U/L (5-35), AST 32 U/L (5-35), ALP 210 U/L (30-150), yGT 58 U/L (8-60), Parathyroid hormone (PTH) 0.7 pmol/L (0.8-8.5). What is the SINGLE most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Why? This patient has hypercalcaemia with a suppressed PTH, indicating a non–PTH-mediated cause. The key clue is excessive intake of multivitamins (4 times daily), which likely contain vitamin D, leading to vitamin D toxicity and increased calcium absorption. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Marked hypercalcaemia (Ca = 3.0 mmol/L) ✅ Suppressed PTH (rules out primary hyperparathyroidism) ✅ Symptoms of hypercalcaemia: fatigue, polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss ✅ Excess multivitamin intake (possible vitamin D overdose) Why Vitamin D Excess Is Correct Vitamin D increases intestinal calcium absorption Excess leads to hypercalcaemia with low PTH Often due to supplementation overdose Explains biochemical pattern and history Why the Other Options Are Less Likely B. Multiple myeloma Can cause hypercalcaemia, but usually with bone pain, anaemia, renal impairment No supporting features here C. Sarcoidosis Can cause hypercalcaemia via increased vitamin D activation But no systemic features (e.g., cough, lymphadenopathy) D. Metastatic bone cancer Would expect more significant symptoms (bone pain, malignancy history) No cancer history provided E. Primary hyperparathyroidism Would have elevated PTH, not suppressed Key Exam Principle 👉 Hypercalcaemia + low PTH = non-parathyroid cause 👉 Always check medication/supplement history 👉 Vitamin D toxicity is a common exam trap 👉 "High Ca + low PTH + supplements = vitamin D excess"

question_text: A 68 year old man with a known diagnosis of renal cell carcinoma presents with progressively worsening bilateral lower limb swelling over the past three months. The swelling is pitting in nature and extends to the mid-thighs. Examination reveals dilated abdominal wall veins and bilateral lower limb oedema. What is the most likely cause of his oedema?
explanation: Why? Renal cell carcinoma is well known to invade the renal vein and extend into the inferior vena cava (IVC), leading to obstruction of venous return. This results in bilateral lower limb oedema and dilated abdominal wall veins due to collateral circulation. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Known renal cell carcinoma ✅ Bilateral pitting oedema extending to thighs ✅ Dilated abdominal wall veins ✅ Progressive course over months These are classic for IVC obstruction. Why Inferior Vena Cava Obstruction Is Correct RCC commonly invades renal vein → IVC Causes impaired venous return from lower limbs Leads to bilateral oedema (not unilateral) Dilated abdominal wall veins = collateral circulation Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Hypoalbuminaemia Causes generalized oedema (including face) No mention of liver disease, nephrotic syndrome, or low protein C. Lymphatic infiltration Typically causes non-pitting oedema (lymphedema) Not associated with dilated superficial veins D. Portal vein occlusion Causes ascites, splenomegaly, portal hypertension signs Does not primarily cause bilateral leg oedema with abdominal wall veins E. Venous thromboembolism Usually unilateral leg swelling Acute presentation rather than gradual progression Key Exam Principle 👉 RCC + bilateral leg oedema + abdominal wall veins = IVC obstruction 👉 Think tumour invasion into venous system 👉 Bilateral oedema = central venous obstruction 👉 "RCC → renal vein → IVC → obstruction → oedema"

question_text: A 35 year old man presents to the clinic with a painless swelling of his left testis. An ultrasound of the testes shows a heterogeneous lesion with areas of calcification. A biopsy of the lesion is performed, and histopathological examination reveals the presence of mature cartilage, and epithelial tissue forming glands. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Why? This is a classic description of a testicular teratoma, which is a germ cell tumour composed of multiple tissue types derived from different germ layers (ectoderm, mesoderm, endoderm). Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Painless testicular swelling (typical of testicular tumour) ✅ Heterogeneous lesion with calcification on ultrasound ✅ Presence of mature cartilage (mesoderm) ✅ Presence of glandular epithelial tissue (endoderm) These indicate multiple differentiated tissue types → hallmark of teratoma. Why Teratoma Is Correct Contains tissues from multiple germ layers Often shows calcifications on imaging Histology shows differentiated structures (cartilage, glands, etc.) Common non-seminomatous germ cell tumour Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Leydig cell tumour Sex cord-stromal tumour Produces hormones (e.g., gynecomastia) No mixed tissue types B. Lymphoma Typically in older men Diffuse infiltration, not heterogeneous with calcifications C. Seminoma Uniform cells, no differentiated tissues No cartilage or gland formation E. Yolk sac tumour Common in children Associated with AFP and Schiller-Duval bodies No mature tissue differentiation Key Exam Principle 👉 Multiple tissue types (cartilage, glands) = teratoma 👉 Calcifications + heterogeneous mass support diagnosis 👉 Non-seminomatous germ cell tumour clue 👉 "Different tissues in one tumour → think teratoma"

question_text: A 75 year old man presents with a worsening headache over the past few weeks. He has been diagnosed with an inoperative high-grade glioblastoma 3 months ago. He feels nauseous and has been vomiting daily over the past week. The head pain can wake him up in the morning. He has been prescribed oral morphine but has very little pain relief from it. A recent brain CT shows an enhanced lesion with surrounding oedema. What is the SINGLE most appropriate management?
explanation: Why? This patient has raised intracranial pressure due to vasogenic oedema from a glioblastoma. The most effective treatment is dexamethasone, which reduces tumour-associated cerebral oedema and rapidly improves symptoms such as headache, nausea, and vomiting. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Known high-grade glioblastoma ✅ Morning headaches (raised ICP) ✅ Persistent vomiting and nausea ✅ Poor response to opioids ✅ CT showing surrounding oedema These point to raised intracranial pressure from tumour-related oedema. Why Dexamethasone Is Correct Reduces vasogenic cerebral oedema Rapidly relieves ICP symptoms First-line in brain tumour-related swelling Improves headache and vomiting Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Mannitol Used in acute emergency (e.g., impending herniation) Short-term measure, not routine management C. Cyclizine Antiemetic only Does not treat underlying cause (oedema) D. Prochlorperazine Also antiemetic Symptomatic relief only E. Oxycodone Another opioid Ineffective because pain is due to raised ICP, not nociceptive pain Key Exam Principle 👉 Brain tumour + oedema → give dexamethasone 👉 Morning headache + vomiting = raised ICP 👉 Steroids reduce vasogenic oedema 👉 "Raised ICP from tumour → dexamethasone first"

question_text: A 61 year old man is admitted into the medical ward following face and arm swelling, difficulty breathing and headaches. He is known to have bronchogenic carcinoma which has metastasised to his vertebrae. On examination, there is distention of the veins on his neck. His oxygen saturation is 91%, heart rate is 70 beats/minute and respiratory rate is 26 breaths/minute. He is given oxygen by a face mask. A CT scan shows a well defined heterogeneously enhancing mass measuring 5 cm by 4.5 cm by 3.8 cm in the apical segment of the right upper lobe compressing the superior vena cava. What is the SINGLE most appropriate management?
explanation: Why? This patient has superior vena cava (SVC) syndrome due to compression by a lung tumour. The most appropriate immediate management is dexamethasone, which reduces tumour-related inflammation and oedema, helping to relieve venous obstruction and symptoms. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Known bronchogenic carcinoma ✅ Facial and arm swelling ✅ Distended neck veins ✅ Dyspnoea and headache ✅ CT showing tumour compressing SVC These are classic features of SVC syndrome. Why Dexamethasone Is Correct Reduces tumour-associated oedema Provides rapid symptomatic relief First-line initial management in malignant SVC obstruction Stabilizes patient before definitive therapy (e.g., radiotherapy/stenting) Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Furosemide May reduce fluid overload but does not address venous obstruction B. Diamorphine Symptomatic relief of breathlessness only Does not treat underlying cause C. Metoprolol No role in SVC syndrome D. Apixaban n Useful in thrombotic causes, not tumour compression Key Exam Principle 👉 SVC syndrome (face swelling + distended neck veins) = oncologic emergency 👉 Initial management = steroids (dexamethasone) 👉 Follow with definitive treatment (radiotherapy/stenting) 👉 "SVC compression → give dexamethasone immediately"

question_text: A 59 year old man is followed up by his oncology team. He has a background of small cell lung cancer. Over the past few weeks, he has been experiencing headaches throughout the day. He has been having nausea throughout the day with loss of appetite. He has been vomiting several times a day for the past two days. His last neuroimaging shows brain metastasis with substantial surrounding oedema. His regular medications include cyclizine. What is the SINGLE most appropriate medication to prescribe?
explanation: Why? This patient has symptoms of raised intracranial pressure due to brain metastases with surrounding vasogenic oedema. The most appropriate treatment is dexamethasone, which reduces cerebral oedema and rapidly improves symptoms such as headache, nausea, and vomiting. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Known small cell lung cancer ✅ Brain metastases on imaging ✅ Significant surrounding oedema ✅ Headache, nausea, vomiting (raised ICP) ✅ Already on antiemetic (cyclizine) with poor control These indicate that the cause is oedema, not just nausea. Why Dexamethasone Is Correct Reduces vasogenic cerebral oedema First-line for brain metastasis-related symptoms Rapidly improves headache and vomiting Addresses the underlying cause Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Haloperidol Used for nausea/delirium Does not treat raised ICP C. Hydrocortisone Steroid but less potent for cerebral oedema Not first choice D. Metoclopramide Antiemetic only Does not address oedema E. Prednisolone Steroid but less effective than dexamethasone for brain oedema Key Exam Principle 👉 Brain metastasis + oedema + headache/vomiting = dexamethasone 👉 Always treat cause, not just symptoms 👉 Dexamethasone is steroid of choice for cerebral oedema 👉 "Raised ICP from mets → give dexamethasone"

question_text: A 35 year old woman presents for her blood test results. She reports that she is constantly feeling tired and has heart palpitations. Three years ago she underwent a thyroidectomy for papillary carcinoma of the thyroid. The patient is taking levothyroxine. Her blood results are as follows: Corrected calcium 2.6 mmol/L (2.1-2.6), Free T3 5.5 pmol/L (3.5-6.5), Free T4 17.2 pmol/L (9-18), Thyroid-stimulating hormone 0.1 (0.5-5.7), Thyroglobulin 5.6 (1.50-38.5). Which of the above laboratory values would be of most concern?
explanation: Why? In a patient who has undergone total thyroidectomy for papillary thyroid carcinoma, thyroglobulin should be very low or undetectable, as it is a tumour marker for residual or recurrent thyroid tissue/cancer. A detectable thyroglobulin level raises concern for recurrence. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ History of papillary thyroid carcinoma ✅ Total thyroidectomy ✅ On levothyroxine therapy ✅ Detectable thyroglobulin level These point toward possible residual or recurrent disease. Why Thyroglobulin Is Correct Used as a tumour marker after thyroidectomy Should be undetectable or very low Detectable level suggests recurrence or residual tissue Most clinically concerning finding here Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. FT3 Within normal range Not concerning B. FT4 Within normal range Appropriate for replacement therapy C. TSH Suppressed intentionally with levothyroxine Part of cancer management (TSH suppression therapy) D. Calcium At upper limit of normal but not elevated No acute concern Key Exam Principle 👉 Post-thyroidectomy → thyroglobulin is key tumour marker 👉 Detectable thyroglobulin = possible recurrence 👉 TSH is intentionally suppressed in thyroid cancer patients 👉 "After thyroid cancer → worry about thyroglobulin, not TSH"

question_text: A 77 year old man is seen in the Oncology Department for a follow up with his advanced prostate cancer. He has been on chemotherapy which had stopped 3 weeks ago. He has been suffering with worsening constipation over the past few weeks. He finds himself feeling depressed most of the day and extremely tired. His appetite is poor. He has noticed that he has been drinking more fluids over the past week. He drank 5 litres of water the day before. On examination, his abdomen is mildly distended with hypoactive bowel sounds. What is the SINGLE most appropriate investigation?

options.d: Computerised tomography scan of the head

explanation: Why? This patient has classic symptoms of hypercalcaemia, which is common in advanced malignancy. Features include constipation, depression, fatigue, polyuria/polydipsia, and reduced bowel activity. Key Clues in the Question: ✅ Advanced cancer (prostate cancer) ✅ Constipation with hypoactive bowel sounds ✅ Depression and fatigue ✅ Increased thirst and fluid intake (polydipsia) These strongly suggest hypercalcaemia. Why Serum Calcium Is Correct Confirms suspected hypercalcaemia Common paraneoplastic/metastatic complication Explains all symptoms ("stones, bones, groans, moans") Requires urgent detection and management Why the Other Options Are Less Likely A. Serum potassium May affect bowel motility but does not explain full symptom cluster C. Urea May reflect dehydration but not primary cause D. CT head No neurological focal signs to suggest intracranial pathology E. CRP Non-specific inflammatory marker Does not explain symptoms Key Exam Principle 👉 Cancer patient + constipation + depression + polyuria = hypercalcaemia 👉 Always check calcium urgently 👉 Hypercalcaemia is an oncologic emergency 👉 "Groans + moans + thirst → check calcium"

question_text: A 69 years old man with a known diagnosis of metastatic non small cell lung cancer attends the oncology clinic with a 2 week history of worsening thoracic back pain. The pain is constant, worse at night and not relieved by regular paracetamol and oral morphine. Over the past 48 hours he reports new onset bilateral leg weakness and difficulty climbing stairs. On examination, there is midline tenderness over the mid thoracic spine. Previous investigations include: Thoracic spine X ray shows lytic lesion consistent with bony metastasis. What is the most appropriate investigation?
explanation: Why? This patient has suspected metastatic spinal cord compression (MSCC), a medical emergency. The best investigation is an urgent MRI of the whole spine, which is the gold standard for assessing spinal cord compression and extent of disease.
